_Why must every motion a robot follows already contain the stop it will probably never use?_

A moving robot cannot pause its momentum while a learned policy computes the next piece of its motion. Each new plan must take over from motion already under way, and a plan that matches only the arm's position leaves a jump in velocity or acceleration that the motors can meet only with a sudden step in torque, which a real drive refuses or converts into vibration, wear, and a spilled load. A path that clears every obstacle can still ask for more joint speed, torque, or current than the body can supply, and the fastest timing along that path demands exactly the abrupt changes a drive cannot make. The next plan can also arrive late, because inference time has a long tail, and a machine that keeps moving while it waits spends the distance it needs to stop. Without trajectory planning, a correct decision about where to go becomes a command the body cannot follow, or motion that cannot be halted in the room that remains. Planning attaches timing, a smooth join to the present state, and a stop that runs without the proposer, and those three properties decide whether a command that crosses the causal boundary can still be brought to rest before its energy reaches something that cannot be undone.

{{< pagebreak >}}

::: {.callout-learning-objectives}

- Distinguish prediction horizon, executed prefix, renewal cadence, and evidence age when budgeting trajectory replacement
- Map tool-space speed limits to joint rates through the manipulator Jacobian, explain why the mapping fails near a singularity, and bound an inverse-kinematics step there with damped least squares
- Evaluate a timed trajectory and its time parameterization against actuator torque, current-slew, and voltage limits, including reflected rotor inertia ($\GearReductionRatio^2 \RotorInertia$)
- Synthesize closed-form quintic spline bridges, anchored at the projected seam state rather than a stale sampled pose, that eliminate acceleration steps and bound commanded jerk across replanning seams
- Size a jerk-limited $\DifferentiabilityClass^2$ stopping suffix from deceleration and jerk bounds and verify stopping clearance ($\StoppingDistance \le \ClearDistance$)
- Compare sampling-based search, trajectory optimization, and learned action chunking by the work each performs and the checks its output still requires
- Construct trajectory records whose two-tier deadlines (high-rate chunk lease and hardware commitment cutoff) keep motion out of inevitable collision states (ICS) and support independent per-tick permission decisions

:::

## Continuous Trajectory Generation {#sec-planning-continuous-trajectories}

```{python}
#| label: calc-planning-opening-machine
#| echo: false
#| warning: false
#| message: false
# ┌─────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────
# │ THE MACHINE'S ARM LOOP AND CHUNK-POLICY LATENCY
# ├─────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────
# │ Context: @sec-planning-continuous-trajectories (opening paragraph).
# │
# │ Goal:    Pin the arm tracking rate and chunk inference latency the opening
# │          quotes for the warehouse mobile manipulator.
# │ Show:    1 kHz joint loop; 40 ms P99 chunk inference; 150 ms interference tail.
# │ How:     RM registry fields; the tail is a scenario assumption.
# └─────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────
from mlsysim import *
from mlsysim.core.units import millisecond
from mlsysim.fmt import check, fmt_frequency, fmt_latency

RM = Embodied.MobileManipulator.WarehouseMobileManipulator

class PlanningOpeningMachine:
    """Arm tracking rate and chunk-policy inference latency on the machine."""

    # ┌── 1. LOAD (Constants) ──────────────────────
    f_track = RM.arm.control_frequency  # category: datasheet; arm joint loop, registry
    t_chunk = RM.chunk_inference_latency  # category: illustrative; P99 incl. vision, registry
    t_tail = 150 * millisecond  # category: illustrative; interference tail

    # ┌── 2. EXECUTE (The Compute) ─────────────────
    tail_over_nominal = (t_tail / t_chunk).to("dimensionless").magnitude

    # ┌── 3. GUARD (Invariants) ────────────────────
    check(abs(f_track.to("hertz").magnitude - 1000.0) < 1e-9, "arm loop rate changed")
    check(abs(t_chunk.to(millisecond).magnitude - 40.0) < 1e-9, "chunk inference latency changed")
    check(tail_over_nominal > 3, "interference tail no longer several times the nominal pass")

    # ┌── 4. OUTPUT (Formatting) ───────────────────
    f_track_str = fmt_frequency(f_track)
    t_chunk_str = fmt_latency(t_chunk, unit=millisecond)
    t_tail_str = fmt_latency(t_tail, unit=millisecond)
```

The arm of the warehouse mobile manipulator is reaching for a mug that drifts along a moving conveyor when an inference pass is delayed by operating-system scheduling contention. The intent lease still names the mug as a valid target, but a lease grants a target, never a path. A target coordinate paired with an expiration timestamp specifies neither velocity nor acceleration, so it cannot tell the arm what to do while the next pass is late. The arm cannot freeze abruptly, and it cannot extrapolate blind setpoints into space no check has covered. Planning must supply a concrete, time-parameterized path, an admissible transition from the motion already under way, and a precomputed stop that runs even if the next inference pass never returns.

::: {.column-margin .margin-pointer}
↩ The intent lease, whose expiry bounds the validity window of every trajectory, is established in @sec-intent-lease.
:::

Classical robotics split this problem into two stages. A search first finds a collision-free geometric path through a configuration space, and a time parameterization then assigns timing that respects kinematic and torque limits. Learned sensorimotor policies change both stages. Instead of searching a static, pre-mapped scene, a policy emits short chunks of future setpoints conditioned directly on live camera observations, and because it replans while the machine moves, each new trajectory must splice into motion already under way rather than start from rest. Neural inference also has variable, heavy-tailed latency, and the hardware keeps moving along its previous trajectory while it waits. Geometric clearance therefore does not settle a plan. A plan must also establish how long the proposed motion remains executable, how it joins the retiring trajectory, and how the machine comes to a controlled stop if later inference passes stall.

The machine meets these obligations in a fixed order. What the planner hands to the tracking controller and the permission path comes first, together with the map from tool coordinates to the joint limits the drives enforce. Replacement timing is then sized against the inference tail, a timed candidate and its seams are checked against what the actuators can follow, and the jerk-limited stop that every admitted plan must carry is sized. The generators that propose candidates, from sampling-based search to learned action chunks, can be compared only after those obligations are fixed.

On this machine, the arm's low-level joint tracking loop evaluates feedback and setpoints at `{python} PlanningOpeningMachine.f_track_str` (datasheet; see the Reader Guide); however, this high-rate servo clock does not specify the physical stopping response. Above this loop sits the Brain, where learned policies such as Action Chunking with Transformers (ACT) [@zhao2023learning] or Diffusion Policy [@chi2024diffusionpolicy] process sensory observations on the host application processor to synthesize future reference paths.[^fn-plan-action-chunking] The machine's chunk policy operates with an illustrative budget of `{python} PlanningOpeningMachine.t_chunk_str` per pass at p99, vision included. Even so, memory contention, direct memory access (DMA) traffic, or thread preemption can stretch tail latency beyond `{python} PlanningOpeningMachine.t_tail_str`. The real-time controller therefore cannot block synchronously on policy execution; it requires both buffered nominal motion and an immediately dispatchable, pre-validated stop.

::: {.column-margin .margin-pointer}
↩ The kinetic energy a trajectory commits, and the stopping distance that energy demands, are established in @sec-body-stopping-distance-prebrake.
:::

A geometric path specifies where the arm must pass, but a trajectory also specifies when it passes each point. Time parameterization exposes instantaneous velocity, acceleration, and jerk to dynamic validation against actuator torque limits and structural thresholds. While sampling-based search, numerical trajectory optimization, and learned action chunking propose candidate motions through distinct mechanisms (@sec-planning-paradigms), every proposal confronts identical execution constraints on physical hardware.

A learned neural policy serves strictly as an unprivileged proposer. Although a downstream trajectory generator can shape and filter raw policy outputs into a continuous candidate profile, the independent safety permission path must formally validate that profile before any motion is admitted. A smooth geometric reference alone provides no guarantee that motor windings can generate the necessary torques under dynamic load, nor does it confirm that sufficient clearance exists along the arm's swept stopping volume.

::: {.column-margin .margin-pointer}
↪ The runtime gatekeeper that checks every admitted setpoint against live state is developed in @sec-enforcement-deterministic-gatekeeper.
:::

A multi-step action chunk delivers a finite horizon of future setpoints that the low-level tracking controller consumes sequentially while the proposer computes the next chunk. Splicing successive chunks introduces an **execution seam**: the temporal and kinematic boundary where the retiring setpoints hand off control to the incoming plan. Matching position alone across this seam leaves a discontinuous velocity step, and matching velocity while neglecting acceleration leaves an instantaneous acceleration step. Because physical links and payloads carry inertia, discontinuous accelerations demand instantaneous steps in motor torque, exciting mechanical vibrations and risking overcurrent faults. The trajectory generator must therefore enforce continuity through position, velocity, and acceleration (the $\DifferentiabilityClass^2$ continuity condition) while verifying that dynamic torques and swept clearance throughout the transition segment remain within safe physical envelopes.[^fn-plan-c2-spline]

Decoupling the execution rate from the inference rate allows the low-level tracking controller to service motor loops on a rigid real-time clock while neural inference runs asynchronously. Setpoint buffering absorbs latency jitter, but buffered motion cannot remain valid indefinitely. Sensor observations age, dynamic obstacles shift, and localization drift accumulates over time. Consequently, the planner's replacement deadline must account for the worst-case inference tail, guaranteeing sufficient lead time to commit to a feasible, controlled stop before either the buffered trajectory drains or the supporting environmental evidence expires.

[^fn-plan-action-chunking]: **Action chunking representations**\index{Action chunking!architectures}\index{Policy learning!temporal horizons}: ACT and Diffusion Policy, the 2023-era chunk policies, carry no boundary-derivative constraints. Real-time chunking [@black2025realtime] conditions each new chunk on the actions already committed, which makes a consistent join more likely without guaranteeing one, so the planner still proposes a transition bridge across each replanning seam and the permission path checks it before admission.

Every admitted proposal must therefore arrive as a self-contained bundle: the active trajectory segment continuous through acceleration ($\DifferentiabilityClass^2$), its explicit validity deadlines, and a pre-verified stopping suffix whose required deceleration distance fits within verified obstacle clearance ($\StoppingDistance \le \ClearDistance$). An isolated safety microcontroller (MCU) inspects and validates this bundle across the proposal boundary before arming actuator outputs, caching the emergency stopping continuation in local real-time memory so it can be autonomously dispatched if communications falter.

[^fn-plan-c2-spline]: **$\DifferentiabilityClass^2$ continuity at the motor**\index{C2 continuity@$\DifferentiabilityClass^2$ continuity}\index{Drivetrain!jerk dynamics}: In permanent-magnet synchronous motors, electromagnetic torque couples directly to quadrature stator current ($\MotorTorque = \MotorTorqueConstant \TorqueProducingCurrent$). Under this model an acceleration step requires a finite step in torque and current, while a velocity step implies an ideal acceleration impulse, which no drive can supply.

Momentum, long-tailed inference latency, and seam continuity therefore shape every trajectory plan, starting at the interface where the high-level planner hands motion to the joint tracking controller and the safety permission path while the machine is moving.

## The Planning Handoff and the Trajectory Record {#sec-planning-handoff}

If the planner hands over raw joint setpoints for the reach toward the mug without binding them to the obstacle geometry, the active intent lease, and a pre-checked stop, the arm can chase an expired target or coast past its clearance the moment the next inference cycle stalls. To prevent that failure, the planner consumes the belief record, which supplies obstacle geometry and clearance, and the intent lease, which supplies the grounded goal, task tolerances, effort ceilings, and time-bounded intent lease ($\IntentLeaseExpiry$), while respecting the actuator and transmission limits of the physical body. The handoff connects those inputs to the checks that permit execution, and two things must be fixed before any replacement timing can be budgeted. The first is the map between the tool coordinates in which clearance is measured and the joint coordinates whose limits the drives enforce. The second is the record that carries a candidate across the proposal boundary, with the deadlines and the stop that bound its authority.

::: {.column-margin .margin-pointer}
↩ The belief record and the state invariants it carries are established in @sec-memory-handoff.
:::

### Mapping tool motion to joint limits {#sec-planning-handoff-kinematics}

A path that keeps the tool inside its speed limit and clear of obstacles in workspace can still command a joint near a straightened elbow to spin faster than its drive allows, tripping a velocity fault mid-reach. Catching that mismatch requires translating workspace motion into the manipulator's joint coordinates. A configuration $(\JointPosition_1, \dots, \JointPosition_n)$ collects the joint positions into a single point in the **configuration space**\index{Configuration space!definition}[^fn-configuration-space-origin] $\ConfigurationSpace$, and removing configurations occupied by obstacles leaves the collision-free subset $\FreeConfigurationSpace = \ConfigurationSpace \setminus \ObstacleConfigurationSet$ [@lozanoperez1983spatial]. Because a geometric path through $\FreeConfigurationSpace$ still lacks timing, an **executable trajectory**\index{Executable trajectory!definition} assigns physical timestamps to the path, generating continuous state references $\MechanicalPlantState(\TimeInstant) = [\GeneralizedCoordinates(\TimeInstant)^\top, \GeneralizedVelocities(\TimeInstant)^\top]^\top$ and acceleration profiles $\GeneralizedAccelerations(\TimeInstant)$ alongside feedforward torque profiles $\FeedforwardJointTorque(\TimeInstant)$. Whereas the kinematic references state the intended position, velocity, and acceleration, the feedforward terms supply the torque predicted by the rigid-body model. The complete candidate crosses the proposal boundary for independent checking, and only admitted actuator commands cross the causal boundary to the drives.

[^fn-configuration-space-origin]: **Configuration space**\index{Configuration space!history}: @lozanoperez1983spatial shrank the moving body to a point by growing each obstacle by the body's shape, and in the same year @schwartz1983piano treated the "piano movers' problem" as a search of exactly this space. The reduction turns a collision query into a membership test on $\ObstacleConfigurationSet$, but the space gains a dimension with every joint, which is why collision queries dominate the run time of the sampling planners in @sec-planning-paradigms.

```{python}
#| label: calc-planning-two-link-arm
#| echo: false
#| warning: false
#| message: false
# ┌─────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────
# │ JOINT SPACE VERSUS TOOL SPACE FOR A PLANAR TWO-LINK ARM
# ├─────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────
# │ Context: @sec-planning-handoff (kinematics paragraph),
# │          @sec-planning-future-state-conditioning (tool displacement),
# │          @sec-planning-rigidbody-dynamics (one-joint reduction).
# │
# │ Goal:    Show that a tool-speed limit does not bound joint speed near a
# │          singularity, using the arm's published link lengths.
# │ Show:    l1 = 0.316 m, l2 = 0.384 m, reach 0.700 m; det J = l1 l2 sin q2;
# │          1.0 m/s in the weakest direction needs |qdot| = 4.90 rad/s at a
# │          90 degree elbow (one joint >= 3.46 rad/s > 2.175 rad/s) and
# │          37.8 rad/s at a 10 degree elbow.
# │ How:     Franka FER kinematic chain (d3, d5) and joint velocity limit from
# │          the registry (franka2023robot); smallest singular value of the
# │          2x2 Jacobian.
# └─────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────
import numpy as np
from mlsysim import *
from mlsysim.core.units import meter, radian, second
from mlsysim.fmt import check, fmt, fmt_length, fmt_angular_velocity, fmt_velocity, fmt_int

RM = Embodied.MobileManipulator.WarehouseMobileManipulator

def _two_link_sigma_min(l1_m, l2_m, q2_deg):
    """Smallest singular value of the planar two-link Jacobian at q1 = 0 (rank depends only on q2)."""
    q2 = np.radians(q2_deg)
    jac = np.array([[-l2_m * np.sin(q2), -l2_m * np.sin(q2)], [l1_m + l2_m * np.cos(q2), l2_m * np.cos(q2)]])
    return float(np.linalg.svd(jac, compute_uv=False)[-1])

class PlanningTwoLinkArm:
    """Planar two-link abstraction of the arm: forward kinematics and Jacobian conditioning."""

    # ┌── 1. LOAD (Constants) ──────────────────────
    l1 = RM.arm.upper_arm_length  # category: datasheet; FER DH d3, shoulder to elbow, registry (franka2023robot)
    l2 = RM.arm.forearm_length  # category: datasheet; FER DH d5, elbow to wrist, registry (franka2023robot)
    qd_max = RM.arm.joint_velocity_limits[1]  # category: datasheet; FER joints 1-4 velocity limit, registry (franka2023robot)
    v_tool = RM.tcp_speed_limit  # category: chosen; free-space TCP limit, registry
    q2_good_deg = 90  # category: illustrative; right-angle elbow
    q2_bad_deg = 10  # category: illustrative; nearly straight elbow

    # ┌── 2. EXECUTE (The Compute) ─────────────────
    reach = (l1 + l2).to(meter)
    sig_good = _two_link_sigma_min(l1.magnitude, l2.magnitude, q2_good_deg)
    sig_bad = _two_link_sigma_min(l1.magnitude, l2.magnitude, q2_bad_deg)
    qd_norm_good = (v_tool / (sig_good * meter)).to(second**-1).magnitude * radian / second
    qd_norm_bad = (v_tool / (sig_bad * meter)).to(second**-1).magnitude * radian / second
    qd_one_good = qd_norm_good / np.sqrt(2)  # some joint must reach at least ||qdot|| / sqrt(2)

    # ┌── 3. GUARD (Invariants) ────────────────────
    check(abs(reach.magnitude - 0.700) < 1e-12, "planar reach changed")
    check(abs(qd_norm_good.magnitude - 4.8968) < 1e-3, "right-angle joint-rate norm changed")
    check(abs(qd_norm_bad.magnitude - 37.760) < 1e-2, "near-singular joint-rate norm changed")
    check(qd_one_good > qd_max, "right-angle weakest direction no longer exceeds the joint limit")

    # ┌── 4. OUTPUT (Formatting) ───────────────────
    l1_str = fmt_length(l1, unit=meter, precision=3)
    l2_str = fmt_length(l2, unit=meter, precision=3)
    reach_str = fmt_length(reach, unit=meter, precision=2)
    qd_max_str = fmt_angular_velocity(qd_max, precision=3)
    v_tool_str = fmt_velocity(v_tool)
    q2_good_str = fmt_int(q2_good_deg)
    q2_bad_str = fmt_int(q2_bad_deg)
    qd_norm_good_str = fmt_angular_velocity(qd_norm_good, precision=1)
    qd_norm_bad_str = fmt_angular_velocity(qd_norm_bad, precision=1)
    qd_one_good_str = fmt_angular_velocity(qd_one_good, precision=1)
```

The drives track joint angles, but clearance is measured in the task space where the tool, the mug, and the conveyor guard sit. In a planar two-link abstraction of the arm's shoulder, elbow, and wrist with upper-arm length $\LinkLength_1$ and forearm length $\LinkLength_2$, **forward kinematics**\index{Forward kinematics!two-link arm} gives the tool position directly as a function of the joint angles:

$$\ToolPlanarAbscissa = \LinkLength_1\cos \JointPosition_1 + \LinkLength_2\cos(\JointPosition_1+\JointPosition_2), \qquad \ToolPlanarOrdinate = \LinkLength_1\sin \JointPosition_1 + \LinkLength_2\sin(\JointPosition_1+\JointPosition_2)$$ {#eq-plan-two-link-kinematics}

Differentiating @eq-plan-two-link-kinematics gives tool velocity $\EndEffectorVelocity = \ManipulatorJacobian(\GeneralizedCoordinates)\,\GeneralizedVelocities$, where the manipulator Jacobian\index{Jacobian!manipulator}[^fn-jacobian-autograd-bridge] $\ManipulatorJacobian = \partial\CartesianPosition/\partial\GeneralizedCoordinates$ changes with configuration. It is the same map that showed, in @sec-data-kinematic-topology, why a Cartesian action label can force a different arm through a singularity; here it prices the arm's own reach. For the two-link arm its determinant is $\LinkLength_1 \LinkLength_2 \sin \JointPosition_2$, which vanishes when the elbow straightens, the singular pose at which no joint motion moves the tool along the arm.

Consider the link lengths from the arm's published kinematic chain: `{python} PlanningTwoLinkArm.l1_str` and `{python} PlanningTwoLinkArm.l2_str`, which yield a `{python} PlanningTwoLinkArm.reach_str` planar reach [@franka2023robot]. In the arm's weakest direction (the tool direction that a unit of joint rate moves least, set by the smallest singular value $\SmallestJacobianSingularNumber$ of $\ManipulatorJacobian$, so that $\|\GeneralizedVelocities\| = \ToolSpeedLimit/\SmallestJacobianSingularNumber$), moving the tool at the `{python} PlanningTwoLinkArm.v_tool_str` tool center point (TCP) limit requires a joint-rate vector of magnitude `{python} PlanningTwoLinkArm.qd_norm_good_str` at a `{python} PlanningTwoLinkArm.q2_good_str`° elbow. With two joints, the larger component of a vector is at least its norm divided by $\sqrt{2}$, so at least one joint must then turn at `{python} PlanningTwoLinkArm.qd_one_good_str`, above the published `{python} PlanningTwoLinkArm.qd_max_str` limit of the shoulder and elbow joints. Straightening the arm makes the demand far worse. The image of a unit joint-rate circle under $\ManipulatorJacobian$, the manipulability ellipse of tool velocities, is broad at the `{python} PlanningTwoLinkArm.q2_good_str`° elbow and collapses into a narrow sliver across the links at `{python} PlanningTwoLinkArm.q2_bad_str`° (@fig-11-two-link-singularity). Sustaining `{python} PlanningTwoLinkArm.v_tool_str` along the arm, the ellipse's minor axis, then needs a joint-rate magnitude of `{python} PlanningTwoLinkArm.qd_norm_bad_str`. Because a tool-speed limit bounds no joint speed near a singularity, every tool-space quantity this chapter checks (the TCP limit, the stopping distance, and the swept clearance) must be mapped back through $\ManipulatorJacobian$ to the joint limits the drives enforce, even on a seven-joint arm whose extra degrees of freedom help the planner steer around singular poses that this planar abstraction omits.

[^fn-jacobian-autograd-bridge]: **Manipulator Jacobian**\index{Jacobian!automatic differentiation}: It is the same object automatic differentiation builds, the matrix of first derivatives of an output with respect to its inputs, here tool position with respect to joint angles. Reverse-mode autograd never forms the matrix; it computes products $\ManipulatorJacobian^\top\UpstreamGradientVector$, and the manipulator equation uses that same transpose product to map a tool wrench into joint torques (@eq-plan-rigidbody-dynamics). A planner is the unusual consumer that must *invert* $\ManipulatorJacobian$, and it is the inverse, not the Jacobian, that fails at a singularity.

::: {.column-margin .margin-pointer}
↪ Forward kinematics, the manipulator Jacobian, singularities, and the damped least-squares inverse are developed for $\JointCount$ joints in @sec-appendix-control-kinematics.
:::

::: {#fig-11-two-link-singularity fig-env="figure" fig-pos="t" fig-cap="**The same tool speed, two elbows**: The planar two-link arm drawn to scale with its `{python} PlanningTwoLinkArm.l1_str` and `{python} PlanningTwoLinkArm.l2_str` links. Each ellipse is the set of tool velocities that a unit joint-rate vector can produce, drawn at one scale in both panels; its short axis is the weakest direction (arrow). At a right-angle elbow the ellipse is round enough that `{python} PlanningTwoLinkArm.v_tool_str` in that direction needs `{python} PlanningTwoLinkArm.qd_norm_good_str` of joint rate. Near the straight elbow the ellipse collapses toward a line across the arm, and the same tool speed along the arm needs `{python} PlanningTwoLinkArm.qd_norm_bad_str`." fig-alt="Two panels, each showing a two-link arm drawn from a shoulder joint through an elbow joint to a tool point, with a dashed arc marking the arm's reach. In the left panel the elbow is bent at a right angle and a wide shaded ellipse surrounds the tool point, with a double arrow along its short axis. In the right panel the arm is nearly straight, the tool sits near the reach arc, and the ellipse is a thin sliver across the arm with the double arrow pointing along the arm. Text in each panel gives the joint rate needed for 1 meter per second along the arrow: 4.9 and 37.8 radians per second."}

```{python}
#| label: plot-planning-two-link-singularity
#| echo: false
#| warning: false
#| message: false
# ┌─────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────
# │ TWO-LINK ARM AT TWO ELBOW ANGLES (FIGURE)
# ├─────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────
# │ Context: @fig-11-two-link-singularity in @sec-planning-continuous-trajectories.
# │
# │ Goal:    Make the Jacobian's conditioning visible: the same tool speed costs
# │          little joint rate at a right-angle elbow and much more near straight.
# │ Show:    the arm to scale at q2 = 90 and 10 degrees; the tool-velocity
# │          ellipse J * (unit joint-rate circle); the weakest direction.
# │ How:     PlanningTwoLinkArm link lengths, elbow angles, TCP limit, and
# │          joint-rate norms; the guard ties the drawn ellipses to the cell.
# └─────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────
from mlsysim import viz
import numpy as np

TL = PlanningTwoLinkArm
R = viz.VOL4_ROLES
l1, l2 = TL.l1.to(meter).magnitude, TL.l2.to(meter).magnitude
v_tool = TL.v_tool.to(meter / second).magnitude
k_ell = 0.25  # drawing scale: meters of page per (m/s) of tool speed

def _jac(q1, q2):
    return np.array(
        [[-l1 * np.sin(q1) - l2 * np.sin(q1 + q2), -l2 * np.sin(q1 + q2)], [l1 * np.cos(q1) + l2 * np.cos(q1 + q2), l2 * np.cos(q1 + q2)]]
    )

cases = [(TL.q2_good_deg, TL.qd_norm_good), (TL.q2_bad_deg, TL.qd_norm_bad)]
viz.set_book_style()
import matplotlib.pyplot as plt
from mlsysim.core.units import meter, second

fig, axes = plt.subplots(1, 2, figsize=(6.4, 3.1))
drawn = []
for ax, tag, (q2d, qd_need) in zip(axes, ("a", "b"), cases):
    q2 = np.radians(q2d)
    q1 = np.radians(45) - np.arctan2(l2 * np.sin(q2), l1 + l2 * np.cos(q2))  # tool direction at 45 degrees
    elbow = np.array([l1 * np.cos(q1), l1 * np.sin(q1)])
    tool = elbow + l2 * np.array([np.cos(q1 + q2), np.sin(q1 + q2)])
    # reach circle
    arc = np.radians(np.linspace(-14, 80, 120))
    th = np.linspace(0, 2 * np.pi, 200)
    ax.plot(TL.reach.magnitude * np.cos(arc), TL.reach.magnitude * np.sin(arc), color=R["neutral"], lw=0.6, ls=(0, (3, 3)))
    # links
    ax.plot([0, elbow[0], tool[0]], [0, elbow[1], tool[1]], color=R["structural"], lw=3.2, solid_capstyle="round", zorder=3)
    for p in ((0, 0), elbow):
        ax.plot(*p, "o", ms=6.5, mfc="white", mec=R["structural"], mew=1.4, zorder=4)
    ax.plot(*tool, "o", ms=3.5, color=R["structural"], zorder=4)
    # velocity ellipse: image of the unit joint-rate circle, scaled so the tool speed per (rad/s)
    J = _jac(q1, q2)
    U, s, Vt = np.linalg.svd(J)
    circ = np.vstack([np.cos(th), np.sin(th)])
    ell = (J @ circ) * k_ell
    ax.fill(tool[0] + ell[0], tool[1] + ell[1], color=R["measured"], alpha=0.14, lw=0, zorder=2)
    ax.plot(tool[0] + ell[0], tool[1] + ell[1], color=R["measured"], lw=1.0, zorder=2)
    # weakest direction
    u_min = U[:, 1]
    ax.annotate("", xy=tool + u_min * 0.13, xytext=tool - u_min * 0.13, arrowprops=dict(arrowstyle="<->", color=R["proposal"], lw=1.2), zorder=5)
    drawn.append((s[1], qd_need.magnitude))
    ax.text(0.0, 1.0, f"({tag}) elbow {q2d}°", transform=ax.transAxes, ha="left", va="bottom", fontsize=9, fontweight="bold", color=R["neutral"])
    ax.text(
        0.97,
        0.03,
        f"weakest direction:\n{v_tool:g} m/s needs {qd_need.magnitude:.1f} rad/s",
        transform=ax.transAxes,
        ha="right",
        va="bottom",
        fontsize=9,
        color=R["proposal"],
        bbox=dict(boxstyle="square,pad=0.1", fc="white", ec="none"),
    )
    ax.set_aspect("equal")
    ax.set_xlim(-0.12, 0.82)
    ax.set_ylim(-0.22, 0.74)
    ax.axis("off")
    ax.text(0.03, -0.035, "shoulder", fontsize=9, color=R["neutral"], ha="left", va="top")
axes[0].text(
    TL.reach.magnitude * np.cos(np.radians(12)) + 0.035,
    TL.reach.magnitude * np.sin(np.radians(12)),
    f"reach\n{TL.reach.magnitude:.2f} m",
    fontsize=9,
    color=R["neutral"],
    ha="left",
    va="center",
)
check(
    abs(drawn[0][1] - v_tool / drawn[0][0]) < 1e-6 and abs(drawn[1][1] - v_tool / drawn[1][0]) < 1e-6,
    "Two-link figure: drawn ellipse minor axes must give the cell's joint-rate norms.",
)
plt.tight_layout()
plt.show()
```

:::

```{python}
#| label: calc-planning-dls-step
#| echo: false
#| warning: false
#| message: false
# ┌─────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────
# │ ONE DAMPED-LEAST-SQUARES INVERSE-KINEMATICS STEP ON THE TWO-LINK ARM
# ├─────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────
# │ Context: @sec-planning-handoff (inverse-kinematics paragraphs after
# │          @fig-11-two-link-singularity).
# │
# │ Goal:    Show that damping bounds the joint command near the singularity
# │          the figure shows, and what it costs in tool motion.
# │ Show:    lambda = 50 mm; weakest-direction 1.0 m/s request needs 4.6 rad/s
# │          (was 4.9) at a 90 degree elbow, 94.3 percent of the request realized;
# │          8.3 rad/s (was 37.8) at a 10 degree elbow, 21.9 percent realized;
# │          bound v / (2 lambda) = 10 rad/s at any configuration.
# │ How:     Per singular direction the DLS gain is sigma / (sigma^2 + lambda^2)
# │          and the realized fraction sigma^2 / (sigma^2 + lambda^2)
# │          (wampler1986manipulator; nakamura1986inverse); sigma_min from
# │          PlanningTwoLinkArm. Chapter-local: promote to MLSysIM only if a
# │          second chapter reuses it.
# └─────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────
from mlsysim.core.units import dimensionless, meter, millimeter, radian, second
from mlsysim.fmt import check, fmt_length, fmt_angular_velocity, fmt_percent

class PlanningDLSStep:
    """Damped-least-squares IK gain and realized tool motion in the arm's weakest direction."""

    # ┌── 1. LOAD (Constants) ──────────────────────
    lam = 50 * millimeter  # category: chosen; illustrative damping, not a vendor setting
    v_tool = PlanningTwoLinkArm.v_tool  # category: chosen; free-space TCP limit, registry
    qd_max = PlanningTwoLinkArm.qd_max  # category: datasheet; shoulder and elbow limit, registry
    sig_good = PlanningTwoLinkArm.sig_good * meter  # derived; 90 degree elbow
    sig_bad = PlanningTwoLinkArm.sig_bad * meter  # derived; 10 degree elbow

    # ┌── 2. EXECUTE (The Compute) ─────────────────
    def _gain(sig, lam):
        return (sig / (sig**2 + lam**2)).to(meter**-1)

    def _realized(sig, lam):
        return (sig**2 / (sig**2 + lam**2)).to(dimensionless).magnitude

    rad_s = radian / second
    qd_dls_good = (v_tool * _gain(sig_good, lam)).to(second**-1).magnitude * rad_s
    qd_dls_bad = (v_tool * _gain(sig_bad, lam)).to(second**-1).magnitude * rad_s
    qd_bound = (v_tool / (2 * lam)).to(second**-1).magnitude * rad_s
    frac_good = _realized(sig_good, lam)
    frac_bad = _realized(sig_bad, lam)

    # ┌── 3. GUARD (Invariants) ────────────────────
    check(qd_dls_good < PlanningTwoLinkArm.qd_norm_good, "damping must not raise the joint command")
    check(qd_dls_bad < PlanningTwoLinkArm.qd_norm_bad / 4, "damping no longer cuts the near-singular command by 4x")
    check(qd_dls_bad <= qd_bound and qd_dls_good <= qd_bound, "DLS gain exceeded its 1/(2 lambda) bound")
    check(abs(qd_bound.magnitude - 10.0) < 1e-9, "DLS joint-rate bound changed")
    check(frac_good > 0.9 and frac_bad < 0.3, "damping no longer spares the good pose and taxes the bad one")
    check(qd_dls_bad > qd_max, "damped command now within the joint limit; revise the feasibility sentence")
    # margin_dls_joint_rate_knee.svg fig-alt hand-types 4.9, 37.8, 4.6, 8.3 and 10 rad/s.
    check(
        [
            round(PlanningTwoLinkArm.qd_norm_good.magnitude, 1),
            round(PlanningTwoLinkArm.qd_norm_bad.magnitude, 1),
            round(qd_dls_good.magnitude, 1),
            round(qd_dls_bad.magnitude, 1),
        ]
        == [4.9, 37.8, 4.6, 8.3],
        "DLS knee margin fig-alt values are stale",
    )

    # ┌── 4. OUTPUT (Formatting) ───────────────────
    lam_str = fmt_length(lam, unit=millimeter)
    qd_dls_good_str = fmt_angular_velocity(qd_dls_good, precision=1)
    qd_dls_bad_str = fmt_angular_velocity(qd_dls_bad, precision=1)
    qd_bound_str = fmt_angular_velocity(qd_bound, precision=0)
    frac_good_str = fmt_percent(frac_good, precision=1, style="prose")
    frac_bad_str = fmt_percent(frac_bad, precision=1, style="prose")
```

The same map must also run in reverse. A proposal stated in tool space, whether a grasp pose from the intent lease or a Cartesian velocity from a policy or a teleoperation device, leaves the planner to find the joint motion that produces it, the **inverse kinematics**\index{Inverse kinematics!differential step} problem. The two-link arm has a closed-form inverse, but a seven-joint arm replanning chunk by chunk is solved by differential steps: linearize at the current configuration and solve $\ManipulatorJacobian\,\FiniteChange\GeneralizedCoordinates = \FiniteChange\CartesianPosition$ for the joint step that moves the tool by $\FiniteChange\CartesianPosition$, then repeat from the new configuration. Where $\ManipulatorJacobian$ is invertible the exact step is $\FiniteChange\GeneralizedCoordinates = \ManipulatorJacobian^{-1}\FiniteChange\CartesianPosition$. Written along the singular directions of $\ManipulatorJacobian$, this step divides the part of $\FiniteChange\CartesianPosition$ along each tool direction by that direction's singular value $\JacobianSingularNumber$. The weakest direction therefore receives the largest joint step, $1/\SmallestJacobianSingularNumber$ per unit of tool motion, which is exactly the joint-rate demand that @fig-11-two-link-singularity charts diverging along the minor axis as the elbow straightens. An exact inverse passes the singularity's arithmetic straight to the drives.

**Damped least squares**\index{Damped least squares!inverse kinematics} gives up exactness to bound the step [@wampler1986manipulator; @nakamura1986inverse]. Instead of demanding $\ManipulatorJacobian\,\FiniteChange\GeneralizedCoordinates = \FiniteChange\CartesianPosition$, it chooses the joint step that best trades tool error against joint motion, with a damping length $\InverseKinematicsDamping$ that sets the exchange rate:

$$\FiniteChange\DampedStepConfiguration = \arg\min_{\FiniteChange\GeneralizedCoordinates} \left(\|\ManipulatorJacobian\,\FiniteChange\GeneralizedCoordinates-\FiniteChange\CartesianPosition\|^2 + \InverseKinematicsDamping^2\|\FiniteChange\GeneralizedCoordinates\|^2\right) = \ManipulatorJacobian^\top\!\left(\ManipulatorJacobian\ManipulatorJacobian^\top+\InverseKinematicsDamping^2\IdentityMatrix\right)^{-1}\FiniteChange\CartesianPosition$$ {#eq-plan-dls-ik}

Setting the gradient of the objective to zero gives $(\ManipulatorJacobian^\top\ManipulatorJacobian+\InverseKinematicsDamping^2\IdentityMatrix)\,\FiniteChange\GeneralizedCoordinates = \ManipulatorJacobian^\top\FiniteChange\CartesianPosition$, and moving $\ManipulatorJacobian^\top$ through the inverse yields the form in @eq-plan-dls-ik, which needs only a $2 \times 2$ solve for the planar arm. A reader who has trained a model will recognize ridge regression, with $\InverseKinematicsDamping^2$ as the weight-decay coefficient. Along each singular direction the gain changes from $1/\JacobianSingularNumber$ to $\JacobianSingularNumber/(\JacobianSingularNumber^2+\InverseKinematicsDamping^2)$. Far from the singularity, where $\JacobianSingularNumber \gg \InverseKinematicsDamping$, the two agree. As $\JacobianSingularNumber$ falls toward zero the damped gain falls with it instead of diverging, and it never exceeds $1/(2\InverseKinematicsDamping)$, reached where $\JacobianSingularNumber = \InverseKinematicsDamping$. The damping thus places a configuration-independent ceiling on the joint step, which no choice of pose can breach.

With an illustrative $\InverseKinematicsDamping$ of `{python} PlanningDLSStep.lam_str`, the weakest-direction request at the `{python} PlanningTwoLinkArm.v_tool_str` TCP limit needs `{python} PlanningDLSStep.qd_dls_good_str` of joint rate at the `{python} PlanningTwoLinkArm.q2_good_str`° elbow, against `{python} PlanningTwoLinkArm.qd_norm_good_str` undamped, and the tool still realizes `{python} PlanningDLSStep.frac_good_str` of the requested motion. At the `{python} PlanningTwoLinkArm.q2_bad_str`° elbow the damped command is `{python} PlanningDLSStep.qd_dls_bad_str` instead of `{python} PlanningTwoLinkArm.qd_norm_bad_str`, and no pose can demand more than `{python} PlanningDLSStep.qd_bound_str`. The price is paid where the damping acts: the tool realizes only `{python} PlanningDLSStep.frac_bad_str` of the requested motion along the arm, so the step lags its target in exactly the direction the arm cannot move well. That residual is a tracking error the planner must carry into the trajectory's timing and clearance checks rather than discard. A larger $\InverseKinematicsDamping$ lowers the ceiling and enlarges the error everywhere, which is why practical solvers raise the damping only as $\SmallestJacobianSingularNumber$ approaches it.

::: {.column-margin}
![](images/svg/margin_dls_joint_rate_knee.svg){width="100%" fig-alt="Joint-rate norm needed for 1 meter per second in the weakest direction, plotted on a log scale against elbow angle from 90 degrees down to near straight. The exact-inverse curve climbs steeply from 4.9 at 90 degrees to 37.8 radians per second at 10 degrees. The damped curve stays below a dashed ceiling at 10 radians per second, reading 4.6 and 8.3 at the same two elbows."}

*As the elbow straightens, the exact inverse climbs from `{python} PlanningTwoLinkArm.qd_norm_good_str` to `{python} PlanningTwoLinkArm.qd_norm_bad_str`; damping caps it at `{python} PlanningDLSStep.qd_bound_str`.*
:::

Damping bounds the inverse-kinematics step; it does not make the step feasible. Even the damped `{python} PlanningDLSStep.qd_dls_bad_str` exceeds the `{python} PlanningTwoLinkArm.qd_max_str` joint limit, so the planner must still slow the tool through time parameterization (@sec-planning-time-parameterization), and the permission path still checks every joint rate against the limits the drives enforce. Damped least squares is a better proposal, not a permission.

### The trajectory record and its deadlines {#sec-planning-handoff-record}

```{python}
#| label: calc-planning-lease-rule
#| echo: false
#| warning: false
#| message: false
# ┌─────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────
# │ ONE CHUNK LEASE FOR BOTH BODIES: THE ARM'S LEASE PATH AND ALTERNATE CUTOFF
# ├─────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────
# │ Context: @sec-planning-handoff (TRACK/STOP paragraph),
# │          @sec-planning-behavior-seam (arm lease path),
# │          @sec-planning-trajectory-contract (record expiry, filled record).
# │
# │ Goal:    Charge the arm's stop from the last admitted chunk when the
# │          shared chunk lease lapses; separately derive the alternate cutoff.
# │ Show:    60 ms lease, renewed every 50 ms; lease path 60 + 1 + 1 + 20 =
# │          82 ms, 82 mm at 1.0 m/s; with the 137.5 mm S-curve stop (275 ms),
# │          219.5 mm of 300 mm, leaving 80.5 mm; alternate path leaves
# │          102.5 mm from its later epoch; alternate admission cutoff
# │          300 - 22 = 278 ms from schedule origin.
# │ How:     AISLE lease, tick, bus, and brake onset (charged as the arm's
# │          onset, conservative); RM TCP limit; the arm's jerk bound is the
# │          peak jerk of the reference C2 polynomial at the same peak
# │          (calc_c2_stop_suffix), and the stop is calc_scurve_stop_distance
# │          / calc_scurve_stop_time. The arm's worked deadlines and clearance
# │          are defined here and read by calc-planning-arm-timeline and
# │          calc-planning-c2-stop-clearance.
# └─────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────
from mlsysim import *
from mlsysim.core.units import millisecond, meter, millimeter, second
from mlsysim.fmt import check, fmt_latency, fmt_length, fmt_velocity

RM = Embodied.MobileManipulator.WarehouseMobileManipulator
AISLE = Embodied.Scenario.WarehouseAisle

class PlanningLeaseRule:
    """The arm lease path and the alternate schedule admission cutoff."""

    # ┌── 1. LOAD (Constants) ──────────────────────
    t_lease = AISLE.t_lease  # category: chosen; chunk lease (@sec-nervous-lease-sizing), registry
    f_renew = RM.chunk_rate  # category: chosen; admitted-chunk renewal rate, registry
    t_tick = AISLE.t_tick  # category: derived; permission-loop period, registry
    t_bus = AISLE.t_bus  # category: illustrative; fieldbus cycle, registry
    t_onset = AISLE.t_brake_onset  # category: illustrative; brake onset, charged as the arm's onset
    v_arm = RM.tcp_speed_limit  # category: chosen; free-space TCP limit, registry
    t_blend = 240 * millisecond  # category: chosen; blend deadline
    t_commit = 300 * millisecond  # category: chosen; physical suffix onset
    a_arm_stop = 5.0 * meter / second**2  # category: illustrative; arm stop deceleration bound
    d_arm_clear = 300 * millimeter  # category: illustrative; obstacle clearance

    # ┌── 2. EXECUTE (The Compute) ─────────────────
    t_renew = (1 / f_renew).to(millisecond)
    t_lease_slack = (t_lease - t_renew).to(millisecond)
    t_dispatch = (t_tick + t_bus + t_onset).to(millisecond)
    t_lease_path = (t_lease + t_dispatch).to(millisecond)
    d_lease_path = (v_arm * t_lease_path).to(millimeter)
    j_arm_stop = calc_c2_stop_suffix(v_arm, a_arm_stop)["peak_jerk"]  # jerk bound: reference polynomial's peak
    t_arm_stop = calc_scurve_stop_time(v_arm, a_arm_stop, j_arm_stop).to(millisecond)
    arm_stop_dist = calc_scurve_stop_distance(v_arm, a_arm_stop, j_arm_stop).to(millimeter)
    lease_total = d_lease_path + arm_stop_dist
    lease_margin = d_arm_clear - lease_total
    commit_margin = d_arm_clear - (v_arm * (t_commit - t_blend)).to(millimeter) - arm_stop_dist
    t_alt_admission_cutoff = (t_commit - t_dispatch).to(millisecond)

    # ┌── 3. GUARD (Invariants) ────────────────────
    check(abs(t_lease.to(millisecond).magnitude - 60.0) < 1e-9, "chunk lease changed")
    check(abs(t_renew.magnitude - 50.0) < 1e-9, "renewal period changed")
    check(t_renew < t_lease, "lease no longer outlasts one renewal period")
    check(abs(t_lease_slack.magnitude - 10.0) < 1e-9, "lease slack beyond one renewal period changed")
    check(abs(t_lease_path.magnitude - 82.0) < 1e-9, "arm lease path changed")
    check(abs(d_lease_path.magnitude - 82.0) < 1e-9, "arm lease-path travel changed")
    check(abs(j_arm_stop.to(meter / second**3).magnitude - 200.0 / 3.0) < 1e-9, "arm jerk bound changed")
    check(abs(t_arm_stop.magnitude - 275.0) < 1e-9, "arm S-curve stop duration changed")
    check(abs(arm_stop_dist.magnitude - 137.5) < 1e-9, "arm S-curve stop distance changed")
    check(abs(lease_total.magnitude - 219.5) < 1e-9, "arm lease-path stop total changed")
    check(abs(lease_margin.magnitude - 80.5) < 1e-9, "arm lease-path margin changed")
    check(abs(commit_margin.magnitude - 102.5) < 1e-9, "arm commitment-path margin changed")
    check(abs(t_dispatch.magnitude - 22.0) < 1e-9, "tick + bus + onset changed")
    check(abs(t_alt_admission_cutoff.magnitude - 278.0) < 1e-9, "alternate admission cutoff changed")
    check(lease_total <= d_arm_clear, "running lease-path stop exceeds illustrative clearance")

    # ┌── 4. OUTPUT (Formatting) ───────────────────
    t_lease_str = fmt_latency(t_lease, unit=millisecond)
    t_renew_str = fmt_latency(t_renew, unit=millisecond)
    t_lease_slack_str = fmt_latency(t_lease_slack, unit=millisecond)
    t_dispatch_str = fmt_latency(t_dispatch, unit=millisecond)
    t_lease_path_str = fmt_latency(t_lease_path, unit=millisecond)
    d_lease_path_str = fmt_length(d_lease_path, unit=millimeter)
    v_arm_str = fmt_velocity(v_arm)
    arm_stop_dist_str = fmt_length(arm_stop_dist, unit=millimeter, precision=1)
    lease_total_str = fmt_length(lease_total, unit=millimeter, precision=1)
    lease_margin_str = fmt_length(lease_margin, unit=millimeter, precision=1)
    commit_margin_str = fmt_length(commit_margin, unit=millimeter, precision=1)
    d_arm_clear_str = fmt_length(d_arm_clear, unit=millimeter)
    t_alt_admission_cutoff_str = fmt_latency(t_alt_admission_cutoff, unit=millisecond)
```

If a candidate trajectory crosses from the planner to the controller without an immutable expiration time and a pre-checked stop, a hung host process leaves the drives tracking the last command into an obstacle. What the planner hands over is therefore a **trajectory record**\index{Trajectory record!definition}, the ninth record in the record chain and the immutable proposal that the tracking controller follows and the permission path admits. Consuming the geometric obstacle bounds from the belief record and the task target and lease window from the intent lease, the trajectory record binds an untrusted sequence proposal to checked physical limits across the formal boundary between the unprivileged, asynchronous Brain and the deterministic, hard real-time Nervous System. Its header names its coordinate frame $\TrajectoryRecordFrame$, evidence time $\EvidenceEpoch$, initial reference state, active intent lease expiry $\IntentLeaseExpiry$, and four deadlines defined in the **MCU monotonic clock domain** (into which host and sensor timestamps are converted with a bounded synchronization error): nominal tracking begins at $\TrackingStartInstant$, the nominal setpoints end at $\NominalPlanExpiry$, the matched stop must physically begin at $\CommitmentInstant$, and the admitted stop finishes at $\StopCompletionInstant$. Beside these header fields, an assumption sidecar declares the payload, friction, obstacle-map epoch, and other conditions under which the candidate was checked (@sec-planning-trajectory-contract). Within the planner itself, each replacement is scheduled against an earlier internal milestone, the blend deadline $\BlendDeadline$, by which a preferred successor should clear validation, while the latest replacement-admission decision on the MCU precedes physical stop onset at $\CommitmentInstant$ by the reserved decision, transport, and actuator delay.

The permission path permits nominal **TRACK** only while the intent lease and trajectory record remain valid, so an expired intent lease terminates nominal tracking immediately, regardless of what the trajectory's own timestamps allow. To manage asynchronous inference latency tails and hardware faults without compromising safety, the architecture enforces a strict **two-tier deadline hierarchy**:

1.  **Fast Nervous System periodic chunk lease ($\ChunkLease$, `{python} PlanningLeaseRule.t_lease_str`):** This high-rate heartbeat governs the real-time execution contract between Brain and Nervous System. The chunk policy proposes base velocity and arm joint targets together, so one chunk lease governs both bodies, and only an admitted replacement chunk renews it, with a desired admission interval of `{python} PlanningLeaseRule.t_renew_str` on this machine. Qualification must bound successful-admission interarrival, not merely inference or request cadence. If an upstream inference pass hangs or communication drops, the lease lapses `{python} PlanningLeaseRule.t_lease_slack_str` after its expected renewal, immediately requesting a controlled stop whose onset follows the reserved response delay.
2.  **Trajectory commitment deadline:** The record names the latest physical onset of its matched stop. Replacement admission must close early enough to dispatch that stop and absorb actuator response delay. This geometric limit does not replace the running machine's shorter chunk lease; the later worked timeline examines an explicitly different, longer-lease configuration.

::: {.column-margin .margin-pointer}
↩ The chunk lease and its sizing from the stopping budget are established in @sec-nervous-lease-sizing.
:::

Two stopping responses back these deadlines. A matched stop suffix, latched at admission, begins at $\CommitmentInstant$ if no successor has been admitted; a state-matched fallback, built from the measured state, answers any earlier invalidation, such as a lapsed lease (@sec-planning-two-tier-deadlines). Either stop remains authorized after nominal tracking expires, provided its own state, clearance, sensing, and drive-energy premises still hold.

::: {#dfn-planning-stopping-suffix .callout-definition title="Stopping suffix"}

***Stopping suffix***\index{Stopping suffix!definition} is the bounded continuation, checked and latched with a trajectory at admission, that brings the machine from a declared entry state to rest along the already-checked path, within the clearance that remains and without further input from the proposer.

1.  **Significance**: It is the term that makes $\StoppingDistance \le \ClearDistance$ checkable before motion begins. From the arm's `{python} PlanningLeaseRule.v_arm_str` TCP limit, the worked suffix sized in @sec-planning-c2-stopping-suffix travels `{python} PlanningLeaseRule.arm_stop_dist_str` of an illustrative `{python} PlanningLeaseRule.d_arm_clear_str` of clearance, the free distance along the checked path between the tool and the nearest obstacle, so the stop alone claims nearly half the room before any response delay is charged.
2.  **Distinction**: The matched suffix is anchored at the nominal state expected at $\CommitmentInstant$; the state-matched fallback is built from the measured state when authority ends earlier. Both are controlled stops along the checked path, unlike a drive inhibit or brake, whose motion is not planned.
3.  **Common pitfall**: Treating the last nominal setpoint, or a hold at the final position, as the stop. A hold is not a deceleration profile, and a suffix sized with constant deceleration understates the distance any drive that ramps its deceleration will travel.

:::

The two execution consumers read distinct subsets of the trajectory record. The downstream tracking controller interpolates admitted setpoints, timestamps, and feedforward torque terms to drive the motor inverters along a continuous profile fetched from the real-time execution jitter buffer. Simultaneously, the independent permission path inspects the record's lineage, timing bounds, dynamic assumptions, validity envelopes, and verified stopping continuation ($\StoppingDistance \le \ClearDistance$). The permission path monitors current limits and physical tracking error on every millisecond tick without inheriting the planner's feasibility claim as proof. An unmodeled obstacle, payload slip, or contact wrench immediately revokes TRACK authority and activates the state-matched fallback. Because every contract field maps to an explicit hardware or software gate, the Nervous System safely executes fast physical motion without presuming that subsequent neural inference cycles will complete on schedule. A record of this kind is short-lived by design, so the next constraint is how often a successor must arrive and how long producing one takes.

## Replacement Timing and the Planning Horizon {#sec-planning-goal-to-trajectory}

On the mug reach, the arm needs an admitted replacement every `{python} PlanningLeaseRule.t_renew_str` and loses tracking authority `{python} PlanningLeaseRule.t_lease_str` after the last one. Whether a replacement can arrive that often depends on how long it takes to produce one, and producing one is more than a single inference pass. The observation behind the candidate must be captured, the proposer must run, and the candidate must cross to the safety MCU and pass validation before it is admitted. Every generator, from numerical trajectory optimization to an autoregressive policy, pays for that pipeline, so the timing questions come before the choice of generator: how long a replacement takes, how deep into its latency tail the design must look, how much motion one record must cover, and from which state the next candidate must be planned.

### Action chunk horizons and reaction lag {#sec-planning-horizon-tradeoff}

If a replacement chunk takes longer from camera capture to MCU admission than the active chunk's lease allows, the arm drops into its stopping fallback before the new plan arrives; if the executed prefix is stretched to hide that latency, the arm reacts too slowly when the mug or an obstacle shifts. Sizing the prediction horizon $\ActionChunkHorizon$ therefore starts from an end-to-end latency budget for replacement, one that spans host accelerator memory, the inter-processor link, and real-time microcontroller firmware.

```{python}
#| label: calc-planning-replacement-budget
#| echo: false
#| warning: false
#| message: false
# ┌─────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────
# │ REPLACEMENT-LATENCY STAGE BUDGET FOR THE MACHINE'S CHUNK POLICY
# ├─────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────
# │ Context: @sec-planning-horizon-tradeoff (replacement-latency paragraph),
# │          @eq-plan-replacement-latency; rows 1 + 2 of @tbl-04-event-timing.
# │
# │ Goal:    Read replacement latency L as capture to admission from the
# │          shared timing table, not from a stage list of this chapter's own.
# │ Show:    L = t_age 51.6 + Delta_da 63.3 = 114.9 ms; inside Delta_da the
# │          40 ms inference and the 18 ms whole-plan validation.
# │ How:     AISLE.perception_age (Ch8), AISLE.t_dispatch_to_admission (Ch13),
# │          AISLE.t_capture_to_admission (MLSysIM). 2026-09-29: replaced the
# │          15 + 5 + 40 + 2 + 18 + 1 = 81 ms chapter-local stage list, whose
# │          sensing stages disagreed with the registry's capture-to-dispatch age.
# └─────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────
from mlsysim import *
from mlsysim.core.units import millisecond
from mlsysim.fmt import check, fmt_latency

RM = Embodied.MobileManipulator.WarehouseMobileManipulator
AISLE = Embodied.Scenario.WarehouseAisle

class PlanningReplacementBudget:
    """Replacement latency L: capture to admission, from the two registry intervals."""

    # ┌── 1. LOAD (Constants) ──────────────────────
    t_age = AISLE.perception_age  # category: derived; capture to dispatch (@sec-perception-latency-waterfall)
    t_da = AISLE.t_dispatch_to_admission  # category: derived; dispatch to admission allocation (@sec-placement-dispatch-admission)
    t_infer = RM.chunk_inference_latency  # category: illustrative; P99 incl. vision, registry (inside t_da)
    t_validate = AISLE.t_plan_validate  # category: illustrative; whole-plan validation, registry (inside t_da)

    # ┌── 2. EXECUTE (The Compute) ─────────────────
    t_sum = AISLE.t_capture_to_admission.to(millisecond)

    # ┌── 3. GUARD (Invariants) ────────────────────
    check(abs(t_infer.to(millisecond).magnitude - 40.0) < 1e-9, "chunk inference latency changed")
    check(abs((t_age + t_da - t_sum).to(millisecond).magnitude) < 1e-9, "L must be capture-to-dispatch plus dispatch-to-admission")
    check(abs(t_sum.magnitude - 114.91072) < 1e-6, "replacement latency changed")
    check(t_validate < t_da, "validation is counted once, inside Delta_da")
    # margin_replacement_latency_envelope.svg fig-alt hand-types 51.6, 114.9, 50 and 60 ms.
    check(
        [
            round(t_age.to(millisecond).magnitude, 1),
            round(t_sum.magnitude, 1),
            round(PlanningLeaseRule.t_renew.magnitude),
            round(PlanningLeaseRule.t_lease.to(millisecond).magnitude),
        ]
        == [51.6, 114.9, 50, 60],
        "replacement-latency margin fig-alt values are stale",
    )

    # ┌── 4. OUTPUT (Formatting) ───────────────────
    t_age_str = fmt_latency(t_age.to(millisecond), unit=millisecond, precision=1)
    t_da_str = fmt_latency(t_da.to(millisecond), unit=millisecond, precision=1)
    t_infer_str = fmt_latency(t_infer, unit=millisecond)
    t_validate_str = fmt_latency(t_validate, unit=millisecond)
    t_sum_str = fmt_latency(t_sum, unit=millisecond, precision=1)
```

The scheduling metric that governs every handoff is **replacement latency**\index{Replacement latency!definition} $\ReplacementLatency$: the total elapsed wall-clock time from the initial physical capture of the sensor observation on which a candidate trajectory proposal rests to the formal admission of that proposal into the real-time execution queue. Formulated in the event taxonomy of @tbl-04-event-timing, $\ReplacementLatency$ spans the interval from capture to admission. It represents the direct sum of two distinct intervals derived across the system architecture: the capture-to-dispatch perception age $\DispatchObservationAge$ established in @sec-perception-latency-waterfall and the dispatch-to-admission interval $\DispatchAdmissionInterval$, a design allocation whose stages are listed next and which @sec-placement-dispatch-admission later tests against the hardware:
$$\ReplacementLatency = \underbrace{\DispatchObservationAge}_{\text{capture}\,\to\,\text{dispatch}} + \underbrace{\DispatchAdmissionInterval}_{\text{dispatch}\,\to\,\text{admission}}, \qquad \DispatchAdmissionInterval = \ProposerInferenceTime + \ProposalLinkTransportTime + \ProposalDeserializationTime + \CombinedPlanValidationAllowance + \ActivationStagingTime + \PermissionTickWaitTime$$ {#eq-plan-replacement-latency}
On the physical machine, sensor data is already `{python} PlanningReplacementBudget.t_age_str` old when planning dispatches. The subsequent dispatch-to-admission allocation $\DispatchAdmissionInterval$ of `{python} PlanningReplacementBudget.t_da_str` accounts for the chunk policy's full `{python} PlanningReplacementBudget.t_infer_str` neural network forward pass, `{python} PlanningReplacementBudget.t_validate_str` of whole-plan kinematic validation, and the few milliseconds of inter-board link transport, message deserialization, activation staging, and synchronization wait until the next discrete permission tick that make up the balance, which @sec-placement-dispatch-admission itemizes when it tests the allocation on the selected hardware. These stages combine to yield an overall replacement latency $\ReplacementLatency$ of `{python} PlanningReplacementBudget.t_sum_str`. $\ReplacementLatency$ is a latency, not a period. It exceeds both the `{python} PlanningLeaseRule.t_renew_str` renewal period and the `{python} PlanningLeaseRule.t_lease_str` lease, so the renewal cadence can be sustained only by overlapping requests, several in flight at once, a throughput condition the timeline below returns to. Charging the entire neural inference pass after dispatch intentionally bills the visual encoding stage twice, since that stage is already inside $\DispatchObservationAge$, which makes the budget deliberately conservative. When pipelined stages execute concurrently or contend for shared memory buses, the sum of independent stage percentiles does not equal the percentile of the sum (@sec-body-latency-pipeline). Sizing the planning horizon therefore demands evaluating the empirical end-to-end distribution of $\ReplacementLatency$, measured directly between physical sensor capture interrupts and microcontroller admission timestamps.

::: {.column-margin}
![](images/svg/margin_replacement_latency_envelope.svg){width="100%" fig-alt="One stacked bar on a millisecond scale: 51.6 milliseconds from capture to dispatch plus 63.3 from dispatch to admission, 114.9 in all. The bar runs past a dashed line for the 50 millisecond renewal period and a dotted line for the 60 millisecond lease."}

*A `{python} PlanningReplacementBudget.t_sum_str` replacement path outlasts the `{python} PlanningLeaseRule.t_renew_str` renewal, so requests must overlap.*
:::

Trajectory validation represents the motion planner's dedicated compute contribution within this latency budget. The `{python} PlanningReplacementBudget.t_validate_str` validation allowance covers the combined elapsed contribution of host geometry validation and bounded local MCU admission, including scheduling delays, rather than overhead silently absorbed into the millisecond actuator tick. Its split between processors remains to be qualified. Formal admission requires bounded staging memory, candidate spline and stopping coefficients, and qualified local clearance evidence; the host processor's full, multi-gigabyte scene representation need not reside on the embedded MCU. The real-time scheduler must preserve deterministic per-tick enforcement while background admission executes, refreshing the seam boundary check immediately prior to commitment. System architects must allocate and qualify this compute and memory footprint under worst-case shared-bus interference. Because each term in @eq-plan-replacement-latency represents an illustrative design allocation, neither $\ReplacementLatency$ nor its constituent stages serve as unverified static bounds; both intervals remain explicit qualification obligations on the physical hardware.

Prediction length and execution duration are separate architectural parameters. While the prediction horizon $\ActionChunkHorizon\FiniteChange \TimeInstant$ specifies how far into the future the sequence proposer forecasts, the **executed prefix**\index{Executed prefix!definition} represents only the initial slice dispatched to actuators before an admitted replacement plan supersedes it. Expanding the prediction horizon supplies candidate continuity well past the next planned handoff, but does not grant the robot authority to execute that trajectory unchecked. The production controller targets an admitted renewal every `{python} PlanningLeaseRule.t_renew_str`, enforcing hard lease expiry at `{python} PlanningLeaseRule.t_lease_str` following the most recent admission. The evidence horizon of the upstream target observation can be shorter still.

Compute amortization depends strictly on inference dispatch frequency rather than the raw number of future setpoints generated in a forward pass. Executing a longer trajectory prefix lowers invocation frequency and amortizes accelerator workload, yet it simultaneously inflates closed-loop reaction lag, delaying task corrections when the environment drifts. Conversely, predicting farther into the future while maintaining a high renewal rate increases proposer compute without reducing inference duty. Emergency protective stopping remains governed by an independent hardware permission path and its certified reaction latency. Sizing the prediction horizon therefore balances closed-loop reactivity, pipeline renewal throughput, sensor evidence freshness, and fallback transition rates under realistic system loads; no universal optimal horizon emerges from trajectory buffer capacity alone.

::: {.column-margin .margin-pointer}
↩ Action chunking as a supply lever is established in @sec-brain-action-chunking.
:::

### Tail latency budgeting across a mission {#sec-planning-tail-latency-budgeting}

When the resident fallback works as certified, a late replacement costs availability rather than safety. A missed replanning deadline becomes a collision hazard only if the resident stop is kinematically infeasible, corrupted in memory, or delayed beyond its budgeted stopping distance. Over a long mission, however, the number of handoffs makes tail latency decide whether the mission completes,[^fn-tail-scale-fanout] even when a stopping profile safely absorbs every individual miss. The analysis below therefore bounds how often handoffs miss their deadlines, not how often the machine collides.

[^fn-tail-scale-fanout]: **Tail at scale**\index{Tail latency!fan-out}: @dean2013tail showed that a distributed request fanned out across many servers is bottlenecked by the slowest tail response, transforming rare single-server delays into frequent user-facing latencies. A continuous mission comprising thousands of sequential handoffs maps this same fan-out onto the time domain. Because every individual handoff must meet its admission deadline to avoid triggering a stop, the complete mission inherits the worst-case tail latency, rendering conventional per-handoff p99 benchmarks insufficient for assessing end-to-end mission reliability.

```{python}
#| label: calc-planning-mission-exposure
#| echo: false
#| warning: false
#| message: false
# ┌─────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────
# │ MISSION EXPOSURE OF A P99 REPLACEMENT BUDGET
# ├─────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────
# │ Context: @sec-planning-goal-to-trajectory (design-tail paragraph),
# │          chk-plan-action-chunk-horizon-tail.
# │
# │ Goal:    Show why a per-handoff P99 budget says little about a mission, and
# │          derive the per-handoff design-tail target by the union bound.
# │ Show:    K = 600 s x 5 Hz = 3000; 30 late; 0.99^3000 ~ 8e-14;
# │          1e-3 / 3000 ~ 3.3e-7, i.e. P99.99997.
# │ How:     Generic replanner (not the machine's 20 Hz chunk renewal);
# │          independence assumed, as the prose states.
# └─────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────
from mlsysim import *
from mlsysim.core.units import second, hertz
from mlsysim.fmt import check, fmt, fmt_int, fmt_frequency, fmt_math, sci_latex

class PlanningMissionExposure:
    """Handoff count, late-handoff exposure, and union-bound design target."""

    # ┌── 1. LOAD (Constants) ──────────────────────
    t_mission = 600 * second  # category: illustrative; ten-minute mission
    f_replan = 5 * hertz  # category: illustrative; generic replanner rate
    p_late = 0.01  # category: definitional; exceedance of a P99 budget
    eps_mission = 1e-3  # category: chosen; mission exceedance target

    # ┌── 2. EXECUTE (The Compute) ─────────────────
    n_handoff = round((t_mission * f_replan).to("dimensionless").magnitude)
    n_late = n_handoff * p_late
    p_all = (1 - p_late) ** n_handoff
    eps_handoff = eps_mission / n_handoff
    q_pct = 100 * (1 - eps_handoff)

    # ┌── 3. GUARD (Invariants) ────────────────────
    check(n_handoff == 3000, "handoff count changed")
    check(abs(n_late - 30) < 1e-9, "expected late handoffs changed")
    check(7e-14 < p_all < 9e-14, "all-on-time probability changed")
    check(abs(eps_handoff - eps_mission / 3000) < 1e-15, "per-handoff target changed")
    # margin_handoff_exceedance_ladder.svg fig-alt hand-types 0.01, 0.001 and 3.3e-7.
    check(p_late == 0.01 and eps_mission == 1e-3 and f"{eps_handoff:.1e}" == "3.3e-07", "exceedance-ladder margin fig-alt values are stale")
    check(f"{q_pct:.5f}" == "99.99997", "exceedance-ladder caption quantile P99.99997 out of date")

    # ┌── 4. OUTPUT (Formatting) ───────────────────
    f_replan_str = fmt_frequency(f_replan)
    t_mission_str = fmt_latency(t_mission, unit=second)
    n_handoff_str = fmt_int(n_handoff, commas=False)
    n_late_str = fmt_int(n_late)
    p_late_math = fmt_math(f"\\LateHandoffProbability={fmt(p_late, precision=2)}")
    eps_mission_math = fmt_math(rf"\MissionExceedanceBudget={sci_latex(eps_mission, precision=0)}")
    late_math = fmt_math(rf"\MissionHandoffCount\LateHandoffProbability={n_handoff}\times{fmt(p_late, precision=2)}={fmt_int(n_late)}")
    eps_ratio_math = fmt_math(
        rf"{fmt(p_late, precision=2)}/({sci_latex(eps_handoff, precision=1)})\approx{sci_latex(p_late / eps_handoff, precision=0)}"
    )
    k_math = fmt_math(f"\\MissionHandoffCount={n_handoff}")
    p_all_math = fmt_math(rf"(0.99)^{{{n_handoff}}}\approx{sci_latex(p_all, precision=0)}")
    eps_math = fmt_math(rf"\HandoffExceedanceProbability\le\MissionExceedanceBudget/\MissionHandoffCount\approx{sci_latex(eps_handoff, precision=1)}")
    q_math = fmt_math(rf"\text{{p{fmt(q_pct, precision=5, commas=False)}}}")
```

The component breakdown in @eq-plan-replacement-latency defines the latency of a single replacement cycle. Because an autonomous mission executes this handoff cycle repeatedly, the tail of the latency distribution dictates system behavior. A mission requiring $\MissionHandoffCount$ successive plan handoffs fails its continuous execution target if even one handoff misses its deadline. Partitioning a cumulative mission exceedance budget $\MissionExceedanceBudget$ uniformly across all $\MissionHandoffCount$ handoffs yields an upper bound on allowable per-handoff failure probability via the union bound:

$$\HandoffExceedanceProbability \le \frac{\MissionExceedanceBudget}{\MissionHandoffCount}$$ {#eq-plan-union-bound}

::: {#nbk-planning-handoff-exposure-wall .callout-notebook title="Handoff deadlines across a mission"}

**Problem**: A generic replanner, slower than this machine's chunk renewal, meets a p99 replacement budget on each handoff. Over a ten-minute mission, how likely is it that every handoff arrives on time, and what per-handoff tail must the design target instead?

**Variables**:

- Mission length `{python} PlanningMissionExposure.t_mission_str` and replanning rate `{python} PlanningMissionExposure.f_replan_str` (illustrative)
- Per-handoff exceedance of the p99 budget, `{python} PlanningMissionExposure.p_late_math` (definitional)
- Mission exceedance target `{python} PlanningMissionExposure.eps_mission_math` (chosen)
- Independent misses (assumption)

**Math**:

1. **Handoff count**: `{python} PlanningMissionExposure.t_mission_str` $\times$ `{python} PlanningMissionExposure.f_replan_str` gives `{python} PlanningMissionExposure.k_math`, and `{python} PlanningMissionExposure.late_math` handoffs are expected late.
2. **Every handoff on time**: `{python} PlanningMissionExposure.p_all_math`.
3. **Design tail** (@eq-plan-union-bound): `{python} PlanningMissionExposure.eps_math`, the `{python} PlanningMissionExposure.q_math` quantile, deeper than the p99 budget by `{python} PlanningMissionExposure.eps_ratio_math`.

**Result**: A mission almost never completes with every handoff inside a p99 budget, and the tail a mission target implies lies more than four orders of magnitude deeper.

**Systems insight**: The quantile a design must target is set by how many handoffs a mission makes, not by the per-handoff budget, and it lies beyond what a test campaign of practical size observes. A late handoff must degrade service availability, not safety clearance. Preserving $\StoppingDistance \le \ClearDistance$ relies on the resident stop profile (the pre-validated stopping suffix latched in MCU memory at admission and triggered without the host), not on optimistic assumptions about latency tails.

:::

This per-handoff quantile functions as a **design quantile target**\index{Design quantile target!definition}, a risk allocation across the software stack rather than an observed tail latency. In practice, resource contention across shared memory, PCIe buses, and hardware accelerators introduces temporal correlation, clustering deadline misses and violating independent-failure assumptions. Hardware-in-the-loop stress testing under maximum bus and memory saturation can expose deadline misses, but establishing this deep quantile requires a stated statistical model, sufficient observations, and evidence that the operating conditions match. The mission architecture must tolerate fallback frequencies that the available evidence cannot rule out without requiring human intervention.

::: {.column-margin}
![](images/svg/margin_handoff_exceedance_ladder.svg){width="100%" fig-alt="Three bars measured from probability 1 on a log scale of exceedance probability, so a rarer target draws a longer bar: the p99 per-handoff budget at 0.01, the whole-mission target at 0.001, and the per-handoff design target, 0.001 divided across 3000 handoffs, at 3.3 times 10 to the minus 7, about four and a half orders of magnitude below p99."}

*Spread over `{python} PlanningMissionExposure.n_handoff_str` handoffs, a mission target demands a `{python} PlanningMissionExposure.q_math` deadline, far past p99.*
:::

To maintain continuous tracking, the client dispatches the next planning request at an offset no later than $\ReplanRequestOffset$ after the active chunk begins executing. Plan admission must complete before a hard decision cutoff that precedes physical commitment $\CommitmentInstant$ by the actuator response allowance, rather than running up against the final nominal setpoint. Given a replacement-latency quantile target $\DesignLatencyQuantile(\ReplacementLatency)$ and a safety reserve $\ReplacementTimingReserve$, a sufficient conservative timing requirement is $\CommitmentInstant-\TrackingStartInstant\ge \ReplanRequestOffset+\DesignLatencyQuantile(\ReplacementLatency)+\ReplacementTimingReserve$. This requirement charges the complete capture-to-admission quantile after request dispatch, conservatively charging the preceding capture-to-dispatch age again. That extra age charge is separate from the visual-encoding overlap in @eq-plan-replacement-latency. A tighter dispatch-relative requirement would use an independently characterized dispatch-to-admission distribution; subtracting marginal latency quantiles would not establish it. The reserve parameter $\ReplacementTimingReserve$ includes both scheduling slack before preferred admission and the physical decision-to-onset allowance. Furthermore, executing the resident stop requires an additional time window $\StoppingDuration$ under dedicated MCU authority. Consequently, the time horizon $\TrajectoryRecordDuration$ that an admitted trajectory record must cover, whether stored as dense setpoint arrays or polynomial splines, satisfies the corresponding conservative design requirement:

$$\TrajectoryRecordDuration\ge \ReplanRequestOffset+\DesignLatencyQuantile(\ReplacementLatency)+\ReplacementTimingReserve+\StoppingDuration$$ {#eq-plan-action-chunk-horizon}

```{python}
#| label: calc-planning-arm-timeline
#| echo: false
#| warning: false
#| message: false
# ┌─────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────
# │ AUTHORITY TIMELINE FOR THE CONVEYOR-TRACKING ARM
# ├─────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────
# │ Context: @sec-planning-goal-to-trajectory (horizon paragraph, evidence
# │          age), @sec-planning-behavior-seam (arm case).
# │
# │ Goal:    Hold the arm's timeline inputs in one place so the horizon bound,
# │          the evidence-age check, the C2 arm case, and the trajectory record
# │          read the same values.
# │ Show:    25 ms setpoint period; 60 ms request delay vs. the 50 ms chunk
# │          renewal period; 575 ms motion-and-stop window (the 275 ms
# │          S-curve stop after 300 ms onset); 240 ms preferred admission;
# │          20 ms scheduling slack plus 22 ms response = 42 ms full reserve;
# │          262 ms sufficient minimum onset; selected onset 300 ms
# │          (60 ms after preferred admission); 278 ms latest admission;
# │          400 ms nominal end (H = 16 setpoints).
# │ How:     RM chunk step and horizon; the rest are scenario assumptions;
# │          eq-plan-action-chunk-horizon.
# └─────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────
from mlsysim import *
from mlsysim.core.units import millisecond
from mlsysim.fmt import check, fmt, fmt_frequency, fmt_latency, fmt_int

RM = Embodied.MobileManipulator.WarehouseMobileManipulator

class PlanningArmTimeline:
    """Replacement and stop timeline for the conveyor-tracking arm."""

    # ┌── 1. LOAD (Constants) ──────────────────────
    t_period = RM.chunk_step  # category: chosen; chunk setpoint period, registry
    n_horizon = RM.chunk_horizon  # category: chosen; setpoints per chunk, registry
    t_chunk = RM.chunk_inference_latency  # category: illustrative; P99 chunk pass incl. vision, registry
    t_request = 60 * millisecond  # category: chosen; request delay
    f_renew = RM.chunk_rate  # category: chosen; chunk renewal rate, registry
    q_latency = 160 * millisecond  # category: chosen; design-tail replacement-latency target
    t_schedule_slack = 20 * millisecond  # category: chosen; scheduling slack before preferred admission
    t_response = PlanningLeaseRule.t_dispatch  # category: derived; physical decision-to-onset allowance
    t_stop = PlanningLeaseRule.t_arm_stop  # category: derived; arm S-curve stop duration, calc-planning-lease-rule
    t_blend = PlanningLeaseRule.t_blend  # category: chosen; blend deadline, calc-planning-lease-rule
    t_commit = PlanningLeaseRule.t_commit  # category: chosen; physical suffix onset, calc-planning-lease-rule

    # ┌── 2. EXECUTE (The Compute) ─────────────────
    f_step = (1 / t_period).to("hertz")
    t_renew = (1 / f_renew).to(millisecond)
    request_slack = t_request - t_renew
    t_plan_exp = (n_horizon * t_period).to(millisecond)
    t_replace_min = t_request + q_latency + t_schedule_slack  # preferred admission, not physical onset
    t_reserve = t_schedule_slack + t_response  # full reserve in eq-plan-action-chunk-horizon
    t_onset_min = t_request + q_latency + t_reserve
    commit_slack = t_commit - t_replace_min
    t_stop_end = t_commit + t_stop
    n_window = (t_stop_end / t_period).to("dimensionless").magnitude

    # ┌── 3. GUARD (Invariants) ────────────────────
    check(abs(t_period.to(millisecond).magnitude - 25.0) < 1e-9, "chunk setpoint period changed")
```
