```{python}
    check(n_horizon == 16, "chunk horizon changed")
    check(abs(t_plan_exp.magnitude - 400.0) < 1e-9, "nominal end changed")
    check(q_latency > PlanningReplacementBudget.t_sum > t_chunk, "design-tail target no longer beyond the stage budget")
    check(abs(t_replace_min.to(millisecond).magnitude - 240.0) < 1e-9, "replacement deadline changed")
    check(abs(commit_slack.to(millisecond).magnitude - 60.0) < 1e-9, "preferred-admission-to-onset gap changed")
    check(abs(t_reserve.to(millisecond).magnitude - 42.0) < 1e-9, "full reserve changed")
    check(abs(t_onset_min.to(millisecond).magnitude - 262.0) < 1e-9, "conservative minimum onset changed")
    check(t_onset_min <= t_commit and t_response <= commit_slack, "selected onset must cover the full reserve")
    check(abs(t_stop_end.to(millisecond).magnitude - 575.0) < 1e-9, "arm stop end changed")
    check(abs(n_window - 23.0) < 1e-9, "authority-window duration equivalents changed")
    check(t_replace_min <= t_blend < t_commit < t_plan_exp < t_stop_end, "arm deadline order broken")
    check(abs(t_renew.magnitude - 50.0) < 1e-9, "chunk renewal period changed")
    check(request_slack.magnitude > 0, "request delay no longer exceeds the renewal period")

    # ┌── 4. OUTPUT (Formatting) ───────────────────
    t_period_str = fmt_latency(t_period, unit=millisecond)
    f_step_str = fmt_frequency(f_step)
    n_horizon_str = fmt_int(n_horizon)
    t_chunk_str = fmt_latency(t_chunk, unit=millisecond)
    t_request_str = fmt_latency(t_request, unit=millisecond)
    t_renew_str = fmt_latency(t_renew, unit=millisecond)
    request_slack_str = fmt_latency(request_slack, unit=millisecond)
    q_latency_str = fmt_latency(q_latency, unit=millisecond)
    t_schedule_slack_str = fmt_latency(t_schedule_slack, unit=millisecond)
    t_response_str = fmt_latency(t_response, unit=millisecond)
    t_reserve_str = fmt_latency(t_reserve, unit=millisecond)
    t_onset_min_str = fmt_latency(t_onset_min, unit=millisecond)
    t_stop_str = fmt_latency(t_stop, unit=millisecond)
    t_replace_min_str = fmt_latency(t_replace_min, unit=millisecond)
    t_blend_str = fmt_latency(t_blend, unit=millisecond)
    t_commit_str = fmt_latency(t_commit, unit=millisecond)
    commit_slack_str = fmt_latency(commit_slack, unit=millisecond)
    t_plan_exp_str = fmt_latency(t_plan_exp, unit=millisecond)
    t_stop_end_str = fmt_latency(t_stop_end, unit=millisecond)
    n_window_str = fmt_int(n_window)
```

In the baseline warehouse configuration, the chunk policy outputs a discrete setpoint every `{python} PlanningArmTimeline.t_period_str` across a `{python} PlanningArmTimeline.n_horizon_str`-step horizon, producing `{python} PlanningArmTimeline.t_plan_exp_str` of nominal forward trajectory. Under nominal operation, an admitted replacement supersedes this trajectory after `{python} PlanningArmTimeline.t_renew_str`. If renewal fails, the active lease lapses at `{python} PlanningLeaseRule.t_lease_str` past the preceding admission tick. Unexecuted setpoints beyond that cutoff serve as candidate references for continuous handoffs rather than extended tracking authority.

On this running schedule the second tier, the record's commitment deadline, never acts, because a stalled proposer lets the `{python} PlanningLeaseRule.t_lease_str` chunk lease lapse long before commitment arrives. To show how a record's own deadlines coordinate nominal motion with its stop, the worked timeline therefore uses an **alternate longer-lease schedule**\index{Alternate longer-lease schedule} for the same arm, one whose chunk lease is long enough not to lapse before the commitment cutoff, so the commitment tier can be seen on its own. On this schedule the planner issues its request `{python} PlanningArmTimeline.t_request_str` after the active chunk begins (later than the running machine's `{python} PlanningArmTimeline.t_renew_str` renewal, which only a longer lease permits), budgets `{python} PlanningArmTimeline.q_latency_str` as its design-tail replacement latency $\DesignLatencyQuantile(\ReplacementLatency)$ above the `{python} PlanningReplacementBudget.t_sum_str` nominal sum as a chosen stand-in for the deep quantile that @eq-plan-union-bound implies, and adds `{python} PlanningArmTimeline.t_schedule_slack_str` of scheduling slack to set a preferred admission deadline at `{python} PlanningArmTimeline.t_replace_min_str`. Adding the `{python} PlanningArmTimeline.t_response_str` decision-to-onset response allowance to the scheduling slack gives the `{python} PlanningArmTimeline.t_reserve_str` full reserve of @eq-plan-action-chunk-horizon and a conservative minimum stop onset of `{python} PlanningArmTimeline.t_onset_min_str`. Selecting a slightly later physical stopping onset at `{python} PlanningArmTimeline.t_commit_str` leaves `{python} PlanningArmTimeline.commit_slack_str` between preferred admission and commitment, so replacement admission can close as late as `{python} PlanningLeaseRule.t_alt_admission_cutoff_str` (one `{python} PlanningLeaseRule.t_dispatch_str` decision-to-onset delay before commitment) while the pre-validated `{python} PlanningArmTimeline.t_stop_str` stopping suffix (@sec-planning-c2-stopping-suffix) brings the arm to rest at `{python} PlanningArmTimeline.t_stop_end_str`, provided clearance holds through that entire window.

This alternate profile serves to contrast buffer structure with the production policy. Its window spans `{python} PlanningArmTimeline.n_window_str` setpoint periods, yet it stays compact in memory because the stop is stored as an analytical profile (jerk limits, acceleration limits, and phase durations) rather than as a dense array of setpoints. Set on one time axis, the two schedules spend clearance differently (@fig-11-seam-timeline-fallback). On the running lease, the lease lapses at `{python} PlanningLeaseRule.t_lease_str`, the tick, bus, and onset allowance delays the resident stop to `{python} PlanningLeaseRule.t_lease_path_str`, and the arm uses `{python} PlanningLeaseRule.lease_total_str` of the `{python} PlanningLeaseRule.d_arm_clear_str` clearance, leaving `{python} PlanningLeaseRule.lease_margin_str`. On the alternate schedule, admission must close by `{python} PlanningLeaseRule.t_alt_admission_cutoff_str`, after the preferred `{python} PlanningArmTimeline.t_replace_min_str`, so that the matched stop begins at the `{python} PlanningArmTimeline.t_commit_str` commitment and reaches rest at `{python} PlanningArmTimeline.t_stop_end_str` with `{python} PlanningLeaseRule.commit_margin_str` to spare; the nominal setpoints that run on to `{python} PlanningArmTimeline.t_plan_exp_str` are never executed.

```{python}
#| label: calc-planning-timeline-figure
#| echo: false
#| warning: false
#| message: false
# ┌─────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────
# │ SYNC GUARD FOR THE HAND-DRAWN TWO-SCHEDULE TIMELINE FIGURE
# ├─────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────
# │ Context: @fig-11-seam-timeline-fallback (SVG labels are hand-typed).
# │
# │ Goal:    Fail the build if a cell value the figure draws changes.
# │ Show:    running 50 / 60 / 82 / 357 ms, 82 + 137.5 = 219.5 mm, 80.5 mm;
# │          alternate 240 / 278 / 300 / 400 / 575 ms, 60 + 137.5 = 197.5 mm,
# │          102.5 mm; 300 mm clearance.
# │ How:     Reads PlanningLeaseRule and PlanningArmTimeline; the alternate
# │          cruise is recomputed because PlanningC2Stop is defined later.
# └─────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────
from mlsysim.core.units import millisecond, millimeter
from mlsysim.fmt import check

class PlanningTimelineFigure:
    """Values drawn in fig11_seam_timeline_fallback.svg."""

    # ┌── 1. LOAD (Constants) ──────────────────────
    LR = PlanningLeaseRule  # category: derived; calc-planning-lease-rule
    AT = PlanningArmTimeline  # category: derived; calc-planning-arm-timeline

    # ┌── 2. EXECUTE (The Compute) ─────────────────
    t_run_stop_end = (LR.t_lease_path + LR.t_arm_stop).to(millisecond)
    alt_cruise = (LR.v_arm * (AT.t_commit - AT.t_blend)).to(millimeter)

    # ┌── 3. GUARD (Invariants) ────────────────────
    def _ms(q):
        return q.to(millisecond).magnitude

    for _v, _drawn in (
        (LR.t_renew, 50),
        (LR.t_lease, 60),
        (LR.t_lease_path, 82),
        (t_run_stop_end, 357),
        (AT.t_replace_min, 240),
        (LR.t_alt_admission_cutoff, 278),
        (AT.t_commit, 300),
        (AT.t_plan_exp, 400),
        (AT.t_stop_end, 575),
    ):
        check(abs(_ms(_v) - _drawn) < 1e-9, f"timeline figure label {_drawn} ms is stale")
    check(abs(LR.arm_stop_dist.to(millimeter).magnitude - 137.5) < 1e-9, "figure stop distance is stale")
    check(abs(LR.lease_total.to(millimeter).magnitude - 219.5) < 1e-9, "figure running travel is stale")
    check(abs(LR.lease_margin.to(millimeter).magnitude - 80.5) < 1e-9, "figure running margin is stale")
    check(abs(alt_cruise.magnitude - 60.0) < 1e-9, "figure alternate cruise is stale")
    check(abs(LR.commit_margin.to(millimeter).magnitude - 102.5) < 1e-9, "figure alternate margin is stale")
    check(abs(LR.d_arm_clear.to(millimeter).magnitude - 300.0) < 1e-9, "figure clearance is stale")
```

::: {#fig-11-seam-timeline-fallback fig-env="figure" fig-pos="t" fig-cap="**Two lease schedules for the arm**: On the running lease (top), a stalled proposer lapses the lease 60 ms after the last admission, and the tick, bus, and onset allowance (amber) delays the resident stop to 82 ms. On the alternate schedule (bottom), admission must close by 278 ms so the matched stop begins at the 300 ms commitment; the unused nominal setpoints run to 400 ms. Each margin is charged against its own clearance check and still excludes sensing and model reserves." fig-alt="Two horizontal timelines on a shared axis from 0 to 600 milliseconds. Top: tracking until the lease lapses at 60 ms, a response interval to stop onset at 82 ms, and an S-curve stop at rest by 357 ms, using 219.5 of 300 millimeters of clearance. Bottom: tracking until commitment at 300 ms with preferred admission at 240 and cutoff at 278, nominal end at 400, and a matched stop at rest by 575 ms, using 197.5 of 300 millimeters."}
![](images/svg/fig11_seam_timeline_fallback.svg){width="100%"}
:::

Sustaining the continuous `{python} PlanningArmTimeline.t_renew_str` renewal cadence of the running lease requires verifying pipeline throughput alongside latency. Because the illustrative `{python} PlanningReplacementBudget.t_sum_str` replacement latency exceeds the `{python} PlanningArmTimeline.t_renew_str` renewal period, the system must pipeline consecutive planning requests. Pipelining maintains real-time throughput only when intermediate hardware stages provide non-blocking queue capacity and bounded bus arbitration delay; pipelined concurrency cannot be established from latency sums alone. Until comprehensive load testing validates multi-request pipelining under peak bus contention, the specified resident fallback responds to missed renewal only under its stated state, clearance, sensing, energy, drive-response, deceleration, and jerk assumptions.

Both lease architectures remain bounded by the validity lifespan of upstream perceptual evidence. Even when employing a qualified local object tracker, the tracked evidence horizon derived in @sec-intent-goals-expire is shorter than the alternate commitment duration, so a single vision observation of a target object cannot justify that entire duration. Instead, the manipulator uses a staged perceptual approach: it follows an admitted prefix through a certified clear corridor, triggers fresh visual acquisition from a wrist-mounted camera at closer proximity, and re-anchors subsequent trajectory segments to updated state estimates so that embedded firmware admits the terminal grasp maneuver only when the complete motion profile satisfies current target tolerances within an active validity envelope. Although an overall reaching motion may span several observation cycles, every executed trajectory slice requires fresh evidentiary support; generating a new trajectory proposal cannot refresh stale sensor evidence, and losing perceptual tracking immediately transitions the robot into a state-matched stopping fallback.

On the Push-T manipulation benchmark [@chi2024diffusionpolicy], frequent closed-loop replanning lets an articulated planar arm recover from live disturbances as it guides a T-shaped block toward a designated pose: a diffusion policy generates $\ActionChunkHorizon = 16$ future steps and executes an initial prefix of $\ExecutedActionStepCount = 6$ steps before replanning, recovering dynamically from transient camera occlusions, external block displacements during approach, and perturbations near the terminal pose. However, these empirical trials demonstrate task-level reactive correction rather than certified derivative continuity or deterministic stopping under compute starvation. A safety-critical production system still requires an independently executable stopping suffix verified against known kinematic clearance bounds.

### Conditioning on the state at splice time {#sec-planning-future-state-conditioning}

```{python}
#| label: calc-planning-stale-pose-gap
#| echo: false
#| warning: false
#| message: false
# ┌─────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────
# │ STALE REQUEST-EPOCH POSE GAP
# ├─────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────
# │ Context: @sec-planning-goal-to-trajectory (projected-seam paragraph).
# │
# │ Goal:    Show how far a moving reference runs ahead of a pose captured when
# │          the replacement was requested.
# │ Show:    0.50 rad/s x 80 ms = 0.040 rad (2.29 degrees); up to 28 mm of
# │          tool motion at the 0.70 m planar reach.
# │ How:     Illustrative delay and joint speed; reach from
# │          calc-planning-two-link-arm (lever arm bounded by the reach).
# └─────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────
from mlsysim import *
from mlsysim.core.units import millisecond, second, degree, millimeter, radian
from mlsysim.fmt import check, fmt, fmt_angular_velocity, fmt_angle, fmt_latency, fmt_length

class PlanningStalePoseGap:
    """Reference lag of a stale request-epoch pose."""

    # ┌── 1. LOAD (Constants) ──────────────────────
    t_delay = 80 * millisecond  # category: illustrative; replacement delay
    w_joint = 0.50 * radian / second  # category: illustrative; constant joint speed

    # ┌── 2. EXECUTE (The Compute) ─────────────────
    gap = (w_joint * t_delay).to(radian)
    gap_deg = gap.to(degree)
    d_tool_max = (gap.magnitude * PlanningTwoLinkArm.reach).to(millimeter)  # arc length at the full lever arm

    # ┌── 3. GUARD (Invariants) ────────────────────
    check(abs(gap.magnitude - 0.040) < 1e-12, "stale pose gap changed")
    check(abs(d_tool_max.magnitude - 28.0) < 1e-9, "stale tool displacement bound changed")

    # ┌── 4. OUTPUT (Formatting) ───────────────────
    t_delay_str = fmt_latency(t_delay, unit=millisecond)
    w_joint_str = fmt_angular_velocity(w_joint, precision=2)
    gap_str = fmt_angle(gap, precision=3)
    gap_deg_str = fmt(gap_deg.magnitude, precision=2)
    d_tool_max_str = fmt_length(d_tool_max, unit=millimeter)
```

While a joint rotates at `{python} PlanningStalePoseGap.w_joint_str` during an illustrative `{python} PlanningStalePoseGap.t_delay_str` compute and transport delay (somewhat longer than the `{python} PlanningReplacementBudget.t_da_str` dispatch-to-admission allocation), a joint pose sampled when the replacement request was dispatched lags the advancing reference by `{python} PlanningStalePoseGap.gap_str` (`{python} PlanningStalePoseGap.gap_deg_str`°). Mapped through the arm's forward kinematics (@eq-plan-two-link-kinematics) at its `{python} PlanningTwoLinkArm.reach_str` maximum planar reach, that angular lag displaces the tool center point by up to `{python} PlanningStalePoseGap.d_tool_max_str`, more than the entire lateral swept-volume clearance budgeted for a reach past the conveyor guard (@sec-planning-runtime-monitors, a sideways allowance distinct from the `{python} PlanningLeaseRule.d_arm_clear_str` of free path ahead of the tool that a stop consumes). Conditioning a motion plan on sensor feedback captured when inference begins therefore induces the **stale-state paradox**\index{Stale-state paradox}: by the time the generative policy completes its forward pass, the physical arm has already advanced along its prior trajectory, so initializing the new plan from the request-time state commands the actuators to step backward across the distance traversed during computation, injecting step discontinuities into commanded position, velocity, and acceleration. To eliminate boundary discontinuities, the sequence proposer must instead condition its action generation on the forward-projected reference state[^fn-smith-predictor-delay] of the active trajectory at the designated replanning seam $\SeamInstant$:

$$\FiniteChange \ReferenceJointPosition=\int_{t_0}^{\SeamInstant}\RetiringChunkJointVelocity(\TimeInstant)\,d\TimeInstant,\qquad \ProjectedSeamState=\RetiringChunkReferenceState(\SeamInstant)$$ {#eq-plan-execution-delay-gap}

[^fn-smith-predictor-delay]: **Smith predictor**\index{Smith predictor!dead-time compensation}: @smith1957closer handled known dead time in feedback control loops by projecting a plant model forward across the delay interval rather than closing feedback against delayed measurements. Future-state conditioning adapts this idea to trajectory planning by anchoring prospective trajectories to the reference state expected at the handoff seam. It also inherits the weakness of any dead-time predictor: external disturbances during the delay interval go uncompensated until physical feedback arrives, which is why the MCU must check measured joint states against strict error bounds at activation.

The left-hand integral is the joint-space gap that a stale anchor would leave, the `{python} PlanningStalePoseGap.gap_str` of the example, while the right-hand state is the anchor the proposer uses instead. Because the projected seam state $\ProjectedSeamState$ in @eq-plan-execution-delay-gap exists strictly in reference trajectory space, external contact forces, mechanical compliance, and closed-loop tracking errors invariably displace the physical plant from this nominal point. Rather than presuming an unobservable future measurement, admission verification prior to the seam evaluates a bounded reachable-state envelope, confirming that feasible polynomial bridges and certified stopping profiles exist across all reachable states within that set. At activation, embedded MCU firmware reads fresh optical encoder measurements and state-estimator error bounds to validate the actual boundary discrepancy $(\FiniteChange \JointPosition, \FiniteChange\JointVelocity, \FiniteChange\JointAcceleration)$ against that certified envelope, then instantiates the bounded fifth-degree $\DifferentiabilityClass^2$ bridge of @sec-planning-quintic-splines and checks its joint-space derivatives against actuator velocity, torque, and jerk limits within the reserved real-time tick before dispatching motor commands. If measured tracking errors or bridge derivatives exceed admitted bounds, the MCU rejects the replacement and maintains the active plan only while its tracking error, target evidence, lease duration, and stopping clearances satisfy safety invariants; otherwise, it triggers the pre-latched fallback profile. Matching two *reference* profiles guarantees derivative continuity across reference commands, but it never eliminates physical tracking errors in the underlying mechanical hardware.

Recent generative imitation learning architectures incorporate delay compensation directly into their sampling algorithms. Real-time chunking [@black2025realtime] computes upcoming action sequences concurrently with active chunk execution. Because setpoints scheduled to run during the inference delay window are already committed to the actuator queue, the model fixes those initial steps to their committed values and samples subsequent actions conditioned on this prefix, applying decaying consistency weights across the overlap window. Although empirical evaluations show that control throughput remains stable under artificial latency injection, the formulation provides no formal continuity or stability guarantees. In contrast, bidirectional decoding [@liu2024bidirectional] samples a diverse candidate batch of trajectory chunks, scoring and selecting the proposal whose trajectory matches the previously executed actions most smoothly. Conditioning generation on the committed trajectory prefix promotes smooth kinematic transitions and reduces boundary tracking discrepancies, yet it cannot substitute for formal safety verification. Embedded microcontroller logic must still evaluate actual physical states against the admitted safety envelope before committing any new chunk to execution.

::: {#dfn-planning-future-state-conditioning .callout-definition title="Future-state conditioning"}

***Future-state conditioning***\index{Future-state conditioning!definition} is the practice of generating candidate motion plans anchored to the anticipated state at execution time rather than the stale state measured at plan initiation.

1.  **Significance**: Offsets computational and transport latency $\FiniteChange \PlanningStartInstant$, eliminating boundary step discontinuities at trajectory handoffs without forcing zero-velocity pauses between consecutive chunks.
2.  **Distinction**: Differs from state estimation or Kalman filtering; it is a forward reference-planning technique that propagates an admitted nominal trajectory rather than filtering sensor noise.
3.  **Common pitfall**: Conflating forward-projected reference states with actual physical plant positions. If external contact forces or tracking lag displace the mechanism during planning, activation remains contingent upon the MCU verifying actual encoder feedback and bridge feasibility at the handoff seam.

:::

Trajectory replacement therefore comes down to three sizing decisions. The prediction horizon must be long enough to carry kinematically feasible motion together with a certified stopping profile, the executed prefix short enough to keep closed-loop responses to a changing environment fast, and the renewal cadence one that the pipelined compute can sustain deterministically. Perceptual evidence freshness dictates the maximum lifespan over which any target estimate justifies physical motion. Even when replacement plans arrive strictly within latency budgets, timely delivery alone cannot guarantee that physical joint actuators can track the synthesized trajectory or bridge seamlessly from their measured state.

::: {#chk-plan-action-chunk-horizon-tail .callout-checkpoint title="Action chunk horizon and tail latency"}

Verify your understanding of replacement timing budgets, tail latency exposure, and delay compensation mechanisms before examining kinodynamic feasibility:

- [ ] **Mission length and tail quantiles**: In the stated independent-handoff illustration, what is the probability that one or more missed p99 handoff deadlines occur across `{python} PlanningMissionExposure.n_handoff_str` consecutive cycles, and why does this represent an allocation target rather than an empirical mission collision rate?
- [ ] **Horizon sizing trade-offs**: Why can a long prediction horizon coexist with a short executed prefix, and which scheduling parameter dictates accelerator inference duty?
- [ ] **Projected seam state**: Why must a trajectory synthesized from a forward-projected reference still undergo reachable-set verification at admission and measured state bridge validation at activation?

:::

## Kinodynamic Feasibility {#sec-planning-kinodynamic-feasibility}

A candidate trajectory that clears every obstacle in workspace and arrives before its deadline will still fault on the hardware if it asks a joint for more speed, torque, or current slew than the drive can supply. What an embodied model generates is a geometric and timed proposal, not permission to move. While high-level motion planners and learned policies navigate free configuration space $\FreeConfigurationSpace$, physical actuators operate under fixed electromotive, thermal, and structural limits. Kinodynamic feasibility bridges geometric intent and mechanical reality, ensuring that reference trajectories respect actuator torque limits, velocity boundaries, and transmission dynamics before the low-level controller dispatches setpoints to motor drives.

::: {#dfn-planning-kinodynamic-feasibility-envelope .callout-definition title="Kinodynamic feasibility envelope"}

***Kinodynamic feasibility envelope***\index{Kinodynamic feasibility envelope!definition}\index{Feasibility!kinodynamic} is the set of initial states from which the machine can track a candidate trajectory, including its transition seams and terminal stop, while every joint remains within its configured position, velocity, acceleration, jerk (the rate of change of acceleration), torque, and stator current limits.

1.  **Significance**: Obstacle clearance in configuration space is necessary but insufficient. At the `{python} PlanningTwoLinkArm.v_tool_str` TCP speed limit, a collision-free reach in the arm's weakest kinematic direction at a right-angle elbow demands `{python} PlanningTwoLinkArm.qd_one_good_str` from a single joint against its `{python} PlanningTwoLinkArm.qd_max_str` ceiling; the spatial geometry succeeds while the timing fails. The envelope defines the state region where dynamic models predict trackable motion, which admission and runtime monitors must continuously verify.
2.  **Distinction**: Kinematic reachability evaluates whether a mechanism can geometrically achieve a configuration. Kinodynamic feasibility introduces time and momentum: the time derivatives that a trajectory profile implies, the dynamic torques produced through the manipulator equation, the effective inertia reflected through gear trains, and the physical stopping distance required to brake safely.
3.  **Common pitfall**: Evaluating feasibility solely at discrete waypoints. The continuous-time interpolant between discrete samples can overshoot velocity bounds or demand severe torque steps even when every discrete sample satisfies constraints.

:::

### Rigid-body dynamics and continuous collision checks {#sec-planning-rigidbody-dynamics}

A trajectory can stay completely clear of obstacles in $\FreeConfigurationSpace$ and still fail on the physical machine because it demands actuator torques that saturate motor inverters, induces base accelerations that tip the platform, or drives current slew rates that trip motor protection circuits. Classical kinematic motion planning checked only whether the swept volume avoided obstacles; a moving body with momentum must satisfy configuration-space clearance and time-domain dynamic limits together.

```{python}
#| label: calc-planning-one-joint-dynamics
#| echo: false
#| warning: false
#| message: false
# ┌─────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────
# │ ONE-JOINT DYNAMICS: THE SHOULDER HOLDING THE RATED PAYLOAD AT FULL REACH
# ├─────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────
# │ Context: @sec-planning-rigidbody-dynamics (one-joint reduction),
# │          @sec-planning-time-parameterization (worked phase plane).
# │
# │ Goal:    Size the gravity and inertia terms of the one-joint equation for
# │          the payload alone, as a lower bound on the real joint load.
# │ Show:    3 kg x g x 0.70 m = 20.6 N m (23.7 % of 87 N m);
# │          3 kg x 0.70^2 + 0.1835 = 1.65 kg m^2.
# │ How:     RM arm payload and joint torque limit (registry); planar reach
# │          from calc-planning-two-link-arm; reflected rotor inertia of the
# │          registered Panda-class stand-in joint. Link masses omitted
# │          (not in the manufacturer specification; needs identified link
# │          parameters, e.g. gaz2019dynamic, entered in the registry with source).
# └─────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────
from mlsysim import *
from mlsysim.core.units import meter, newton, standard_gravity
from mlsysim.fmt import check, fmt_torque, fmt_inertia, fmt_percent, fmt_mass

RM = Embodied.MobileManipulator.WarehouseMobileManipulator

class PlanningOneJointDynamics:
    """Payload-only gravity and inertia terms for the shoulder joint at full planar reach."""

    # ┌── 1. LOAD (Constants) ──────────────────────
    m_pay = RM.arm.payload_capacity  # category: datasheet; rated payload, registry
    tau_max = RM.arm.max_torque  # category: datasheet; joints 1-4 torque limit, registry
    r_reach = PlanningTwoLinkArm.reach  # category: datasheet; planar reach, calc-planning-two-link-arm
    j_rotor_ref = Actuators.PandaClassJoint.CSG_25_50_ILM70x18.reflected_inertia  # category: derived; registry stand-in joint
    g0 = standard_gravity  # category: definitional

    # ┌── 2. EXECUTE (The Compute) ─────────────────
    tau_grav = (m_pay * g0 * r_reach).to(newton * meter)
    grav_ratio = (tau_grav / tau_max).to("dimensionless").magnitude
    j_eff = (m_pay * r_reach**2 + j_rotor_ref).to(kilogram * meter**2)

    # ┌── 3. GUARD (Invariants) ────────────────────
    check(abs(tau_grav.magnitude - 20.594) < 1e-3, "payload holding torque changed")
    check(abs(j_eff.magnitude - 1.6535) < 1e-4, "payload plus rotor inertia changed")
    check(grav_ratio < 0.5, "payload gravity no longer a minority of the joint limit")

    # ┌── 4. OUTPUT (Formatting) ───────────────────
    m_pay_str = fmt_mass(m_pay, unit=kilogram, precision=0)
    tau_max_str = fmt_torque(tau_max, precision=0)
    tau_grav_str = fmt_torque(tau_grav, precision=1)
    grav_pct_str = fmt_percent(grav_ratio, precision=1, style="prose")
    j_eff_str = fmt_inertia(j_eff, precision=2)
```

On a single joint, such as the manipulator's shoulder lifting a grasped payload, the balance of torques obeys the scalar equation of motion:

$$\CommandedJointTorque = \EffectiveJointInertia\,\JointAcceleration + \Mass \Gravity \PayloadLeverArm\cos \JointPosition + \JointFrictionTorque$$ {#eq-plan-one-joint-dynamics}

where $\EffectiveJointInertia$ represents the effective inertia driven by the joint, $\Mass$ is a concentrated mass whose center of gravity lies at distance $\PayloadLeverArm$ from the joint axis, $\JointPosition$ is the joint angle measured from the horizontal plane, and $\JointFrictionTorque$ is friction torque opposing motion. Mechanical inertia resists angular acceleration, while gravity exerts a static load proportional to the horizontal moment arm $\PayloadLeverArm\cos \JointPosition$. Holding the rated `{python} PlanningOneJointDynamics.m_pay_str` payload horizontally at the manipulator's full `{python} PlanningTwoLinkArm.reach_str` planar reach requires `{python} PlanningOneJointDynamics.tau_grav_str` of static holding torque, which consumes `{python} PlanningOneJointDynamics.grav_pct_str` of the joint's `{python} PlanningOneJointDynamics.tau_max_str` torque limit before motion begins [@franka2023robot]. Adding the actuator's reflected rotor inertia, the $\GearReductionRatio^2$-amplified rotor term of @sec-body-reflected-rotor-inertia that the seam analysis below prices for a Panda-class joint, to the payload inertia produces an effective joint inertia of `{python} PlanningOneJointDynamics.j_eff_str` that every commanded acceleration must accelerate. Structural link mass and distributed inertia add to this baseline. Because manufacturer datasheets rarely provide link mass distributions, empirical evaluations rely on published identified parameters [@gaz2019dynamic]; an operational deployment requires system identification on the physical arm and attached tooling.

In multi-degree-of-freedom manipulators, dynamic coupling interconnects the joints. The scalar terms generalize into the matrix terms of the **manipulator equation**\index{Manipulator equation}, derived from the Euler-Lagrange equations of motion [@craig2005introduction; @lynch2017modern]:

$$\JointTorque(\TimeInstant) = \GeneralizedInertiaMatrix(\GeneralizedCoordinates)\GeneralizedAccelerations + \CoriolisCentrifugalMatrix(\GeneralizedCoordinates, \GeneralizedVelocities)\GeneralizedVelocities + \GravitationalTorqueVector(\GeneralizedCoordinates) - \ManipulatorJacobian^\top(\GeneralizedCoordinates)\ExternalWrench$$ {#eq-plan-rigidbody-dynamics}

Here, the symmetric, positive-definite inertia matrix $\GeneralizedInertiaMatrix(\GeneralizedCoordinates)$ generalizes scalar inertia $\EffectiveJointInertia$ from @eq-plan-one-joint-dynamics. Off-diagonal elements capture cross-joint inertial coupling (accelerating the elbow induces reaction torques at the shoulder), and matrix values vary continuously as the arm articulates. The quadratic velocity term $\CoriolisCentrifugalMatrix(\GeneralizedCoordinates, \GeneralizedVelocities)\GeneralizedVelocities$ aggregates centrifugal and Coriolis torques, which scale quadratically with joint velocity, while the gravity vector $\GravitationalTorqueVector(\GeneralizedCoordinates)$ generalizes $\Mass \Gravity \PayloadLeverArm\cos \JointPosition$ to represent configuration-dependent static holding torque. The geometric Jacobian from @eq-plan-two-link-kinematics maps an external wrench $\ExternalWrench$ acting on the end effector into equivalent joint torques via the transpose $\ManipulatorJacobian^\top(\GeneralizedCoordinates)$; external contact wrenches that assist motion reduce actuator torque demands, while resistive loads increase them. Evaluating @eq-plan-rigidbody-dynamics along a prospective trajectory $\GeneralizedCoordinates(\TimeInstant)$ is the problem of **inverse dynamics**\index{Inverse dynamics!definition}. The recursive Newton-Euler algorithm computes inverse dynamics for an $\JointCount$-joint serial arm in $\mathcal{O}(\JointCount)$ arithmetic operations per trajectory sample [@luh1980online; @lynch2017modern]. An admission filter scanning an $\TrajectorySampleCount$-sample candidate trajectory therefore performs $\mathcal{O}(\TrajectorySampleCount \JointCount)$ operations whose worst-case execution time must fit within the system's admission latency allowance.

Before dispatching a proposed trajectory chunk, the planning runtime screens it against the kinodynamic feasibility envelope, verifying that the physical state at the handoff seam satisfies position, velocity, torque, stator current, contact force, and collision boundaries over the planning horizon. For robotic arms, the rigid-body model maps joint trajectories $\GeneralizedCoordinates(\TimeInstant)$, $\GeneralizedVelocities(\TimeInstant)$, and $\GeneralizedAccelerations(\TimeInstant)$ to joint torques $\JointTorque(\TimeInstant)$ via @eq-plan-rigidbody-dynamics, which convert to quadrature-axis motor currents ${\TorqueProducingCurrent}_i(\TimeInstant) = \CommandedJointTorque_i(\TimeInstant) / {\JointTorqueConstant}_i$ using the joint-effective torque constant ${\JointTorqueConstant}_i$. (When using motor-side torque constants, the conversion must explicitly incorporate gear ratios and transmission mechanical efficiencies.) Initial screening by an unprivileged planner, however, does not constitute system admission. The real-time safety MCU executes an independent, deterministic verification check, admitting a bounded trajectory chunk only if configured dynamic limits and certified stop clearances hold for the verified initial state. Once admitted, the MCU monitors control tracking error, plan freshness, and stopping distance margins on every servo cycle.

Numerical optimizers can smooth geometric paths and expand obstacle clearance, but motion permission resides strictly in the admitted trajectory chunk and its resident stopping suffix. For example, the cuRobo motion-generation framework uses massively parallel GPU compute to generate collision-free, minimum-jerk trajectories across kinematic configurations [@sundaralingam2023curobo]. Its collision pipeline evaluates signed distance fields across sampled swept-sphere volumes under a linear-motion approximation, leaving continuous inter-sample swept volume evaluation as an open requirement. Following trajectory optimization, cuRobo identifies the limiting time step where joint velocity, acceleration, or jerk encounters actuator bounds, rescaling trajectory duration before re-optimizing. This uniform temporal scaling represents an initial form of the rigorous time parameterization developed in @sec-planning-time-parameterization. Because cuRobo's algorithmic formulation focuses on kinematic derivatives rather than full multi-body dynamics, torque boundaries, winding thermal accumulation, continuous swept-volume containment, and admission deadlines remain external system-level requirements.

Under this systems architecture, the GPU trajectory generator operates as an unprivileged proposer. The real-time safety MCU independently validates prospective trajectories and seam constraints within a strict admission deadline, latching an executable stopping continuation before authorizing motion.

### Overshoot between samples and contracted limits {#sec-planning-intrasample-overshoot}

When the admission filter checks a candidate only at discrete waypoints spaced $\SamplingPeriod$ apart, two consecutive joint samples $\TimeInstant_k = \SetpointSampleIndex \SamplingPeriod$ that sit just below the velocity ceiling $\SpeedBound$ can still bracket an overspeed fault midway between them because physical actuators track a continuous interpolant across $(\TimeInstant_k, \TimeInstant_{k+1})$. If that interpolator can command accelerations up to $\ProfileAccelerationBound$ within a sample period, an acceleration sign reversal across the midpoint lets continuous velocity rise above the values recorded at both endpoints.

Under acceleration-bounded interpolation, the maximum velocity excursion between two consecutive samples sharing equal velocity arises from a bang-bang acceleration reversal: $+\ProfileAccelerationBound$ applied over $[0, \SamplingPeriod/2]$, followed immediately by $-\ProfileAccelerationBound$ over $[\SamplingPeriod/2, \SamplingPeriod]$ to restore endpoint velocity. The velocity excursion reaches its maximum at the midpoint, corresponding to the integrated area of the initial acceleration phase:

$$\FiniteChange \JointVelocity = \ProfileAccelerationBound \cdot \frac{\SamplingPeriod}{2} = \frac{1}{2} \ProfileAccelerationBound \SamplingPeriod$$ {#eq-plan-intrasample-overshoot}

As @eq-plan-intrasample-overshoot demonstrates, two consecutive waypoint samples evaluated just beneath velocity ceiling $\SpeedBound$ can bracket an interior velocity peak that exceeds the limit, tripping drive overspeed protection between individually valid samples. To ensure continuous-time velocity compliance without evaluating an infinite continuum of points, the admission filter tests discrete waypoints against an analytically contracted velocity threshold:

$$|\JointVelocity_k| \le \SpeedBound - \frac{1}{2} \ProfileAccelerationBound \SamplingPeriod$$ {#eq-plan-contracted-velocity-limit}

This contraction creates a safety margin that absorbs the worst-case overshoot any acceleration-bounded interpolator can generate across a sample period $\SamplingPeriod$. A smaller reserve requires additional boundary conditions. If consecutive samples have equal velocity and zero acceleration, and the interpolator enforces $\JerkLimit \le 4\ProfileAccelerationBound/\SamplingPeriod$, the extremal reversal consists of a positive triangular acceleration pulse followed by its negative counterpart, each of base $\SamplingPeriod/2$. Their peaks reach $\ProfileAccelerationBound$ only at equality in the jerk condition, so $\frac{1}{4} \ProfileAccelerationBound \SamplingPeriod$ is a conservative velocity reserve for this restricted interpolation. A jerk bound alone does not justify that reserve when endpoint accelerations are nonzero. For polynomial spline interpolants, the admission filter can instead compute exact interior extrema analytically before certifying continuous-time feasibility.

### Seam acceleration jumps and reflected rotor inertia {#sec-planning-seam-torque-inertia}

When the arm hands off from one action chunk to the next while moving, two chunks that are each feasible in isolation can still form an infeasible seam between them. Whereas matching joint positions alone ($\DifferentiabilityClass^0$ continuity) leaves an unconstrained velocity step across the boundary, matching both position and velocity ($\DifferentiabilityClass^1$ continuity) eliminates velocity jumps only to leave an instantaneous acceleration discontinuity that demands an immediate step in joint torque. Under a rigid-inertia approximation, commanding a velocity step $\FiniteChange\JointVelocity$ across a single servo period $\SamplingPeriod$ requires an inertial torque of:

$$\SeamStepTorque = \EffectiveJointInertia \frac{\FiniteChange\JointVelocity}{\SamplingPeriod}$$ {#eq-plan-seam-torque}

where $\EffectiveJointInertia = \LoadInertia + \GearReductionRatio^2 \RotorInertia$ in @eq-plan-seam-torque represents the total effective inertia referenced to the joint output. This term adds link and payload inertia $\LoadInertia$ to the reflected rotor inertia established in @sec-body-reflected-rotor-inertia, the motor rotor inertia $\RotorInertia$ seen through gear reduction ratio $\GearReductionRatio$. Because the rotor turns $\GearReductionRatio$ times faster than the joint, its kinetic energy, written in joint velocity, carries the factor $\GearReductionRatio^2$:

$$\KineticEnergy = \frac{1}{2} \RotorInertia \RotorAngularSpeed^2 = \frac{1}{2} \RotorInertia (\GearReductionRatio \JointVelocity)^2 = \frac{1}{2} (\GearReductionRatio^2 \RotorInertia) \JointVelocity^2$$

```{python}
#| label: calc-planning-seam-reflected-inertia
#| echo: false
#| warning: false
#| message: false
from mlsysim import *
from mlsysim.core.units import *
from mlsysim.fmt import fmt_torque, fmt_multiple, fmt_angular_velocity, fmt_inertia, fmt_latency, check

class PlanningSeamInertia:
    """Illustrative one-tick velocity request vs. symmetric C2 blend."""

    joint = (
        Actuators.PandaClassJoint.CSG_25_50_ILM70x18
    )  # category: datasheet; CSG-25-50 gear ratio and torque limits, ILM 70x18 rotor plus gear input inertia
    j_reflected = joint.reflected_inertia  # category: derived; N^2 J_rotor, 0.1835 kg m^2
    delta_omega = 0.2 * radian / second  # category: illustrative; reference velocity gap
    dt_tick = 1 * millisecond  # category: chosen; servo tick
    t_blend = 50 * millisecond  # category: illustrative; blend duration
    tau_step = calc_seam_acceleration_torque_jump(joint.gear_ratio, joint.rotor_inertia, (delta_omega / dt_tick).to(radian / second**2))
    tau_blend_mean = calc_seam_acceleration_torque_jump(joint.gear_ratio, joint.rotor_inertia, (delta_omega / t_blend).to(radian / second**2))
    # Symmetric C2 velocity blend: a(u)=6*delta_omega*u*(1-u)/T.
    tau_blend_peak = 1.5 * tau_blend_mean
    peak_reduction = tau_step / tau_blend_peak
    tau_rated = joint.rated_torque  # category: datasheet; L10 rated torque
    tau_peak_rated = joint.peak_torque  # category: datasheet; repeated peak torque
    # One-tick velocity change the whole repeated peak could supply to reflected rotor inertia alone.
    dq_ceiling = (tau_peak_rated * dt_tick / j_reflected).to(radian / second)
    check(abs(tau_step.magnitude - 36.7) < 0.01, "one-tick request changed")
    check(abs(tau_blend_mean.magnitude - 0.734) < 0.001, "blend mean changed")
    check(abs(tau_blend_peak.magnitude - 1.101) < 0.001, "blend peak changed")
    check(abs(peak_reduction.magnitude - 50 / 1.5) < 0.01, "peak ratio changed")
    check(abs(dq_ceiling.magnitude - 0.6921) < 1e-4, "one-tick velocity ceiling changed")
    check(delta_omega < dq_ceiling, "notebook velocity gap no longer below the one-tick ceiling")
    check(tau_step < tau_rated, "one-tick request no longer below the rated torque")
    tau_step_str = fmt_torque(tau_step, precision=1)
    tau_mean_str = fmt_torque(tau_blend_mean, precision=2)
    tau_peak_str = fmt_torque(tau_blend_peak, precision=1)
    reduction_mult_str = fmt_multiple(peak_reduction.magnitude, precision=1)
    j_reflected_str = fmt_inertia(j_reflected, precision=2)
    tau_rated_str = fmt_torque(tau_rated, precision=0)
    tau_peak_rated_str = fmt_torque(tau_peak_rated, precision=0)
    dt_tick_str = fmt_latency(dt_tick, unit=millisecond)
    dq_ceiling_str = fmt_angular_velocity(dq_ceiling, precision=2)
    delta_omega_str = fmt_angular_velocity(delta_omega, precision=1)
    t_blend_str = fmt_latency(t_blend, unit=millisecond)
```

In precision robotic manipulators equipped with high-ratio strain-wave gearing[^fn-strain-wave-gearing] ($\GearReductionRatio = 50\text{--}100$), reflected rotor inertia is magnified by a factor of $2{,}500$ to $10{,}000$. It can then rival or exceed link inertia, most often for an unloaded arm or a folded pose, although a rated payload held at full reach outweighs it: in the one-joint example the payload supplies most of the `{python} PlanningOneJointDynamics.j_eff_str` total, against `{python} PlanningSeamInertia.j_reflected_str` from the rotor. Either way, the reflected term sits in every joint's $\EffectiveJointInertia$ regardless of payload, and on its own it makes seam torque spikes large. At a $\DifferentiabilityClass^0$ boundary, an instantaneous velocity step implies an idealized Dirac acceleration impulse $\UnitImpulseFunction(\TimeInstant)$, which no physical motor drive can supply. At a $\DifferentiabilityClass^1$ boundary, an acceleration jump $\FiniteChange\JointAcceleration$ demands a step change in electromagnetic torque, $\FiniteChange\CommandedJointTorque = \EffectiveJointInertia \FiniteChange\JointAcceleration$. Such abrupt torque transients excite structural resonance in flexible transmissions, accelerate mechanical wear, and degrade control tracking. On the strain-wave joint priced in the notebook below, an unblended one-tick velocity step of `{python} PlanningSeamInertia.delta_omega_str` asks the reflected rotor inertia for a `{python} PlanningSeamInertia.tau_step_str` torque pulse, while a `{python} PlanningSeamInertia.t_blend_str` $\DifferentiabilityClass^2$ quintic bridge closing the same gap peaks at `{python} PlanningSeamInertia.tau_peak_str` (@fig-11-action-chunk-seam-continuity). Commercial industrial arms enforce this exact discipline at their low-level control interfaces. For example, the Franka Research 3 arm samples setpoints at `{python} PlanningOpeningMachine.f_track_str`, comparing each incoming command against the previous cycle; if inter-cycle setpoint differences exceed factory derivative thresholds, the drive immediately aborts motion with an unrecoverable discontinuity fault (such as `joint_motion_generator_velocity_discontinuity`) [@franka2026troubleshooting; @franka2023robot]. An unblended seam can therefore abort nominal tracking before repeated transitions accumulate mechanical fatigue. Physical stopping still requires the drive's qualified response delay and deceleration profile.

[^fn-strain-wave-gearing]: **Strain-wave (harmonic) gearing**\index{Strain-wave gearing!origin}: In the mechanism @musser1959strain patented, an elliptical wave generator flexes a thin toothed cup, the flexspline, so that it meshes with a rigid ring carrying two more teeth, and each turn of the generator advances the cup by only that difference. The result is a high reduction in one compact stage with almost no backlash. The flexspline is also the joint's main compliance, so the same gearing that multiplies rotor inertia by $\GearReductionRatio^2$ supplies the compliant coupling of the two-inertia model below.

When the arm carries an open cup of liquid, steady velocity does not spill the contents, whereas rapid acceleration transitions and high jerk provoke sloshing and spillage (@sec-planning-c2-stopping-suffix models this deceleration threshold directly). A trajectory interface that continuously matches position, velocity, and acceleration constitutes a **$\DifferentiabilityClass^2$ spline seam**\index{C2 spline seam@$\DifferentiabilityClass^2$ spline seam!definition}. Enforcing $\DifferentiabilityClass^2$ continuity eliminates reference acceleration steps and prevents the associated torque jump $\FiniteChange\CommandedJointTorque = \EffectiveJointInertia\FiniteChange\JointAcceleration$. Concurrently, bounding trajectory **jerk**\index{Jerk!definition} ($\JointJerk=\Glyph{\dot{a}}=\dddot{\Glyph{x}}$) limits the rate at which joint acceleration changes. Neither mathematical property alone guarantees payload stability or mechanical longevity, however; an interpolating bridge that matches boundary conditions perfectly can still violate velocity, jerk, actuator torque, or obstacle clearance limits in its interior.

Mechanical transmissions govern how actuator torque couples into physical link motion. In a standard two-inertia drivetrain comprising load inertia $\LoadInertia$, reflected rotor inertia $\ReflectedRotorInertia=\GearReductionRatio^2\RotorInertia$, and torsional coupling stiffness $\TransmissionTorsionalStiffness$, the antiresonance and resonance frequencies [@li2024optimal] are:

$$\DrivetrainAntiresonanceFrequency = \frac{1}{2\pi}\sqrt{\frac{\TransmissionTorsionalStiffness}{\LoadInertia}}, \qquad \DrivetrainResonanceFrequency = \frac{1}{2\pi}\sqrt{\TransmissionTorsionalStiffness\left(\frac{1}{\LoadInertia} + \frac{1}{\ReflectedRotorInertia}\right)}$$

In robot joints constructed with strain-wave gearing, large reflected inertia coupled with flexspline torsional compliance amplifies high-frequency setpoint harmonics. An admission checker must therefore verify prospective bridges against the joint's identified, load-dependent vibrational modes, evaluating derivative extrema, peak torques, and drive current limits against empirical structural parameters. The two frequencies reach the checker through the bridge duration. A short bridge can excite these modes, but duration alone does not determine its spectral content or the joint's response. Identified modal frequencies and damping therefore inform qualified bridge-duration and derivative limits alongside the torque-rate limit. Structural stiffness, resonance modes, and admissible jerk envelopes never transfer between robot platforms without direct system identification.

### Quintic splines and C$^2$ boundary matching {#sec-planning-quintic-splines}

Closing the position, velocity, and acceleration gap between retiring chunk $\Glyph{A}$ and incoming chunk $\Glyph{B}$ over a finite blend duration $\SeamBridgeDuration$ (a physical execution interval distinct from the computational blend deadline $\BlendDeadline$) requires online $\DifferentiabilityClass^2$ trajectory spline blending\index{C2 trajectory spline blending@$\DifferentiabilityClass^2$ trajectory spline blending}: synthesizing a dedicated polynomial bridge $\SeamBridgePosition(\TimeInstant)$ that must undergo the exact same kinodynamic feasibility checks as the primary chunks rather than acting as a cosmetic filter.[^fn-minimum-jerk-reaching]

A localized seam bridge must simultaneously satisfy position, velocity, and acceleration constraints at both boundary states. Because a cubic polynomial possesses only four degrees of freedom, it cannot satisfy six independent boundary conditions; a fifth-degree quintic polynomial provides the six required coefficients. This localized endpoint-matching formulation differs from fitting a globally continuous cubic spline across an entire offline sequence of knots.

[^fn-minimum-jerk-reaching]: **Minimum jerk**\index{Jerk!minimum-jerk trajectory}: @flash1985coordination found that unconstrained human reaching follows the trajectory that minimizes integrated squared jerk, which for a rest-to-rest reach is a quintic polynomial in time. The jerk term of @eq-plan-kinodynamic-projection inherits that smoothness but not a bound, so a minimum-jerk bridge can still exceed the drive's limits, and its extrema are checked through @eq-plan-quintic-jerk.

The six boundary conditions are
$$\JointPosition(0) = \JointPosition_0, \quad \JointVelocity(0) = \JointVelocity_0, \quad \JointAcceleration(0) = \JointAcceleration_0$$
$$\JointPosition(\SeamBridgeDuration) = \JointPosition_1, \quad \JointVelocity(\SeamBridgeDuration) = \JointVelocity_1, \quad \JointAcceleration(\SeamBridgeDuration) = \JointAcceleration_1$$
where $(\JointPosition_0, \JointVelocity_0, \JointAcceleration_0)$ is the terminal physical state of chunk $\Glyph{A}$ at the seam instant, and $(\JointPosition_1, \JointVelocity_1, \JointAcceleration_1)$ is the target state on incoming chunk $\Glyph{B}$ at $\TimeInstant = \SeamBridgeDuration$. The six conditions fix the six coefficients ($\PolynomialTrajectoryCoefficient_0 \dots \PolynomialTrajectoryCoefficient_5$) of the fifth-degree polynomial:
$$\JointPosition(\TimeInstant) = \PolynomialTrajectoryCoefficient_0 + \PolynomialTrajectoryCoefficient_1 \TimeInstant + \PolynomialTrajectoryCoefficient_2 \TimeInstant^2 + \PolynomialTrajectoryCoefficient_3 \TimeInstant^3 + \PolynomialTrajectoryCoefficient_4 \TimeInstant^4 + \PolynomialTrajectoryCoefficient_5 \TimeInstant^5$$

Evaluating boundary conditions at $\TimeInstant = 0$ directly yields the first three coefficients: $\PolynomialTrajectoryCoefficient_0 = \JointPosition_0$, $\PolynomialTrajectoryCoefficient_1 = \JointVelocity_0$, and $\PolynomialTrajectoryCoefficient_2 = \frac{1}{2}\JointAcceleration_0$. The remaining three coefficients $[\PolynomialTrajectoryCoefficient_3, \PolynomialTrajectoryCoefficient_4, \PolynomialTrajectoryCoefficient_5]^\top$ satisfy the $3 \times 3$ linear system evaluated at duration $\Time = \SeamBridgeDuration$:

$$\begin{bmatrix} \SeamBridgeDuration^3 & \SeamBridgeDuration^4 & \SeamBridgeDuration^5 \\ 3\SeamBridgeDuration^2 & 4\SeamBridgeDuration^3 & 5\SeamBridgeDuration^4 \\ 6\SeamBridgeDuration & 12\SeamBridgeDuration^2 & 20\SeamBridgeDuration^3 \end{bmatrix} \begin{bmatrix} \PolynomialTrajectoryCoefficient_3 \\ \PolynomialTrajectoryCoefficient_4 \\ \PolynomialTrajectoryCoefficient_5 \end{bmatrix} = \begin{bmatrix} \JointPosition_1 - \left(\JointPosition_0 + \JointVelocity_0 \SeamBridgeDuration + \frac{1}{2}\JointAcceleration_0 \SeamBridgeDuration^2\right) \\ \JointVelocity_1 - \left(\JointVelocity_0 + \JointAcceleration_0 \SeamBridgeDuration\right) \\ \JointAcceleration_1 - \JointAcceleration_0 \end{bmatrix}$$ {#eq-plan-quintic-spline-matrix}

Analytically inverting @eq-plan-quintic-spline-matrix yields closed-form expressions for $[\PolynomialTrajectoryCoefficient_3, \PolynomialTrajectoryCoefficient_4, \PolynomialTrajectoryCoefficient_5]^\top$, given in @sec-appendix-control-splines, that require deterministic arithmetic operations per joint. Differentiating $\JointPosition(\TimeInstant)$ three times produces the continuous commanded jerk profile:

$$\JointJerk(\TimeInstant) = \dddot{\JointPosition}(\TimeInstant) = 6 \PolynomialTrajectoryCoefficient_3 + 24 \PolynomialTrajectoryCoefficient_4 \TimeInstant + 60 \PolynomialTrajectoryCoefficient_5 \TimeInstant^2$$ {#eq-plan-quintic-jerk}

Because $\JointJerk(\TimeInstant)$ in @eq-plan-quintic-jerk is a quadratic function of time, its extrema over the interval $[0, \Time]$ occur exclusively at the domain boundaries ($\TimeInstant = 0$ or $\TimeInstant = \Time$) or at the interior stationary point $\TimeInstant^* = -\PolynomialTrajectoryCoefficient_4 / (5 \PolynomialTrajectoryCoefficient_5)$ (when $\PolynomialTrajectoryCoefficient_5 \ne 0$ and $\TimeInstant^* \in (0, \Time)$). If $\PolynomialTrajectoryCoefficient_5 = 0$, jerk varies linearly or remains constant, and evaluating the boundaries alone suffices. The safety microcontroller can therefore compute exact peak jerk $|\PeakBridgeJerk|$ analytically in $\mathcal{O}(1)$ operations without executing iterative numerical line searches. An identical principle governs lower derivatives: acceleration extrema occur at the roots of the quadratic jerk, and velocity extrema occur at the roots of cubic acceleration, both solvable in closed form.

Evaluating coupled joint torques across the bridge presents an entirely different challenge. Along a polynomial trajectory $\GeneralizedCoordinates(\TimeInstant)$, the right-hand side of @eq-plan-rigidbody-dynamics is non-polynomial because the inertia matrix $\GeneralizedInertiaMatrix(\GeneralizedCoordinates)$, Coriolis matrix $\CoriolisCentrifugalMatrix(\GeneralizedCoordinates, \GeneralizedVelocities)$, and gravity vector $\GravitationalTorqueVector(\GeneralizedCoordinates)$ contain transcendental trigonometric functions of joint positions. Consequently, peak torque possesses no closed-form analytic solution. The safety monitor therefore evaluates torque at discrete sample waypoints and bounds inter-sample torque variation using the contraction principles established in @sec-planning-intrasample-overshoot.

Bounding trajectory jerk directly protects actuator health, preserves motor inverter voltage headroom, and prevents premature transmission wear. When a trajectory generator outputs time-parameterized splines, it transforms kinematic waypoints into continuous reference functions whose derivatives map directly onto physical electrical and mechanical states. In permanent-magnet synchronous motors operated under field-oriented control, joint torque rate couples to jerk through the time derivative of the manipulator equation: $\JointTorqueSlew(\TimeInstant) = \GeneralizedInertiaMatrix(\GeneralizedCoordinates) \dddot{\GeneralizedCoordinates}(\TimeInstant) + \InertiaMatrixDerivative(\GeneralizedCoordinates) \GeneralizedAccelerations(\TimeInstant) + \dots$. For a single joint with constant effective inertia $\EffectiveJointInertia = \LoadInertia + \GearReductionRatio^2 \RotorInertia$, neglecting changing gravity, friction, and external-load torques reduces the output torque rate to $\CommandedJointTorqueSlew = \EffectiveJointInertia \JointJerk(\TimeInstant)$. Defining a joint-effective torque constant $\JointTorqueConstant$ such that output torque satisfies $\CommandedJointTorque = \JointTorqueConstant \TorqueProducingCurrent$, commanding an output torque rate $\CommandedJointTorqueSlew$ demands a proportional quadrature-axis stator current slew rate:

$$\frac{d\TorqueProducingCurrent}{d\TimeInstant} = \frac{\EffectiveJointInertia}{\JointTorqueConstant} \JointJerk(\TimeInstant)$$

Here, $\JointTorqueConstant$ incorporates both the gear reduction ratio and transmission mechanical efficiency; directly substituting a raw motor-side torque constant without gear scaling would incorrectly pair motor torque with output-side inertia. Motor winding inductance $\PhaseInductance$ and available DC bus voltage impose hard electrical limits on current slew rate. During positive motoring operations with resistive and back-electromotive force (back-EMF) drops, a simplified necessary condition for voltage headroom is:

$$\DcBusVoltage \ge \PhaseInductance \frac{d\TorqueProducingCurrent}{d\TimeInstant} + \PhaseResistance\, \TorqueProducingCurrent + \MotorBackEmfConstant \ElectricalAngularSpeed$$ {#eq-plan-inverter-headroom}

where $\PhaseResistance$ represents phase winding resistance, $\MotorBackEmfConstant$ is the motor back-EMF constant, and $\ElectricalAngularSpeed$ denotes motor electrical speed. In operational motor drives, space-vector pulse-width modulation limits the maximum usable quadrature-axis voltage to a fraction of the total DC bus voltage. A complete electrical feasibility check must evaluate available voltage against the fully coupled, signed motor equations, including regenerative braking and inductive flyback, rather than treat a scalar approximation as sufficient qualification.

::: {.column-margin .margin-pointer}
↩ Phase inductance, back-EMF, and the current-slew limits they impose are established in @sec-body-electrical-time-constants.
:::

An acceleration discontinuity in a motion plan demands an instantaneous step in electromagnetic torque and stator current. Because finite bus voltage and nonzero winding inductance prevent physical inverters from supplying infinite current slew rates ($d\TorqueProducingCurrent/d\TimeInstant$), the physical actuator lags the commanded reference. The resulting tracking error, inverter saturation, and thermal protection response depend on drive gains and mechanical compliance; an unbounded mathematical jerk demand does not instantly cause an overcurrent shutdown, but it induces severe tracking lag, mechanical vibration, and drive stress. A valid bridge must satisfy both continuous mathematical derivative bounds and the physical bandwidth limits of the actuator drive.

Satisfying the six boundary conditions guarantees acceleration continuity at chunk interfaces, but it does not guarantee that interior jerk, torque, or current slew rates remain within actuator ratings. The admission filter evaluates closed-form derivative extrema from @eq-plan-quintic-jerk against the electrical constraints of @eq-plan-inverter-headroom, checks sampled multi-body torques against inter-sample contraction bounds, and rejects any bridge violating physical thresholds. Evaluating a fixed-degree polynomial requires bounded arithmetic operations per joint. Spline coefficient synthesis and trajectory extrema verification take place prior to trajectory dispatch; the qualified worst-case execution bound, accounting for memory access latency and register operations, must remain strictly within the configured admission deadline.

While a local quintic bridge resolves seam continuity through explicit boundary matching, global trajectory representations provide alternative verification properties. **Uniform B-splines**[^fn-spline-shipwright-origin] parameterize joint trajectories as $\GeneralizedCoordinates(\TimeInstant) = \sum_{i=0}^\SplineFinalControlIndex \SplineControlPoint_i {\BsplineBasisFunction}_{i,\SplineDegree}(\TimeInstant)$, where $\SplineControlPoint_i$ represent geometric control points, ${\BsplineBasisFunction}_{i,\SplineDegree}$ are polynomial basis functions of degree $\SplineDegree$, and $\SplineKnotTime_i$ denote knot timestamps. Using simple knot sequences, uniform B-splines ensure $\DifferentiabilityClass^{\SplineDegree-1}$ continuity by construction. Furthermore, the **convex hull property** ensures that the continuous trajectory lies entirely within the convex hull formed by its control points, enabling spatial collision checkers to prune entire collision volumes without dense sampling. Differentiating a B-spline yields a derivative spline whose control points are $\DerivativeSplineControlPoint_i = \frac{\SplineDegree}{\SplineKnotTime_{i+\SplineDegree+1}-\SplineKnotTime_{i+1}}(\SplineControlPoint_{i+1} - \SplineControlPoint_i)$, allowing difference operations on control points to establish conservative upper bounds on velocity, acceleration, and jerk. These geometric bounds accelerate screening, though they do not replace full dynamic inverse dynamics or swept-volume collision checks. In streaming replanning architectures, the trajectory representation must also support rapid coefficient joining within the real-time admission deadline.

[^fn-spline-shipwright-origin]: **Spline** (a draftsman's bending strip): The word named the thin flexible strip that shipwrights and draftsmen bent through fixed points, held in place by lead weights, to draw a fair curve. @schoenberg1946contributions borrowed it for piecewise polynomials, and @deboor1978practical made B-splines practical to compute with a stable recursion. The convex-hull property that construction supplies is what lets a checker bound a whole segment's derivatives from a few control-point differences.\index{Spline!etymology}

@Tbl-11-trajectory-representations separates the continuity supplied by each representation from the dynamic checks still required before execution.

| Representation                                  | Native seam property                                                                                                                                                                                            | Checks before execution                                                                                                                      |
|:------------------------------------------------|:----------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------|:---------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------|
| Cubic polynomial ($\DifferentiabilityClass^1$)  | Matches $\JointPosition, \JointVelocity$; adjoining acceleration need not match.                                                                                                                                | Check acceleration matching and interior limits; position and velocity matching alone are insufficient.                                      |
| Quintic bridge ($\DifferentiabilityClass^2$)    | Matches $\JointPosition,\JointVelocity,\JointAcceleration$ at both ends; jerk is quadratic within each bridge.                                                                                                  | Check interior extrema, torque rates, inverter headroom, and clearance.                                                                      |
| Septic polynomial ($\DifferentiabilityClass^3$) | Can match derivatives through jerk at both endpoints.                                                                                                                                                           | Check interior derivatives and actuator limits; endpoint matching does not bound their magnitudes.                                           |
| Uniform B-spline (degree $\SplineDegree$)       | $\DifferentiabilityClass^{\SplineDegree-1}$ continuity; convex hull bounds spatial curve.                                                                                                                       | Constrain control point differences for velocity/jerk; check global knot system.                                                             |
| Neural action chunk (ACT, Diffusion)            | Discrete samples; continuity depends on interpolation and seam constraints.                                                                                                                                     | Project onto feasibility manifold via numerical solver or $\DifferentiabilityClass^2$ quintic bridge; latch stop.                            |
| Online jerk-limited generator                   | Reaches a target $(\JointPosition,\JointVelocity,\JointAcceleration)$ from any current state within per-axis $\SpeedBound$, $\ProfileAccelerationBound$, $\JerkLimit$ bounds; the generator picks the duration. | Check coupled torque, clearance, evidence age, and the configured limits themselves; kinematic feasibility by construction is not admission. |

: **Trajectory representations and required checks**: Smooth parameterization helps form a candidate but does not by itself prove dynamic feasibility. {#tbl-11-trajectory-representations tbl-colwidths="[24,36,40]"}

```{python}
#| label: calc-planning-quintic-bridge
#| echo: false
#| warning: false
#| message: false
# ┌─────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────
# │ THE SEAM BRIDGE SOLVED AS A QUINTIC: COEFFICIENTS, JERK, AND TORQUE RATE
# ├─────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────
# │ Context: nbk-planning-seam-acceleration-jump-reflected-inertia-torque,
# │          @sec-planning-quintic-splines, chk-plan-seam-feasibility.
# │
# │ Goal:    Instantiate eq-plan-quintic-spline-matrix and eq-plan-quintic-jerk
# │          for the seam notebook's bridge, and screen the one-tick step and
# │          the bridge against the arm's torque-rate limit.
# │ Show:    a3 = 80 rad/s^3, a4 = -800 rad/s^4, a5 = 0; peak acceleration
# │          6.0 rad/s^2; peak jerk 480 rad/s^3; torque rate 88.1 N m/s
# │          (8.8 percent of 1,000 N m/s); one-tick step 36,700 N m/s (36.7x);
# │          halving T: 2.2 N m, 1,920 rad/s^3, 352.3 N m/s.
# │ How:     Zero boundary accelerations and an endpoint on chunk B's
# │          reference (position residual dw T / 2); the 3x3 system is solved
# │          numerically and guarded against its closed form. Torque rate is
# │          J_refl x jerk (rigid reflected inertia only); the FER torque-rate
# │          limit (franka2023robot) is applied to the stand-in joint, as in
# │          calc-planning-time-parameterization.
# └─────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────
import numpy as np
from mlsysim import *
from mlsysim.core.units import millisecond, second, newton, meter, radian, kilogram
from mlsysim.fmt import (
    check,
    fmt,
    fmt_int,
    fmt_latency,
    fmt_torque,
    fmt_torque_rate,
    fmt_percent,
    fmt_multiple,
    fmt_angle,
    fmt_math,
    fmt_angular_acceleration,
)

RM = Embodied.MobileManipulator.WarehouseMobileManipulator

class PlanningQuinticBridge:
    """The seam notebook's C2 bridge as a quintic, with its peak jerk and torque rate."""

    # ┌── 1. LOAD (Constants) ──────────────────────
    d_omega = PlanningSeamInertia.delta_omega  # category: illustrative; reference velocity gap
    t_b = PlanningSeamInertia.t_blend  # category: illustrative; bridge duration
    dt_tick = PlanningSeamInertia.dt_tick  # category: chosen; servo tick
    j_refl = PlanningSeamInertia.j_reflected  # category: derived; N^2 J_rotor of the stand-in joint
    tau_step = PlanningSeamInertia.tau_step  # category: derived; one-tick inertial request
    tau_bridge = PlanningSeamInertia.tau_blend_peak  # category: derived; bridge peak inertial torque
    taud_max = RM.arm.joint_torque_rate_limit  # category: datasheet; FER torque-rate limit, registry (franka2023robot)
    t_short = 10 * millisecond  # category: illustrative; compressed bridge in chk-plan-seam-feasibility

    # ┌── 2. EXECUTE (The Compute) ─────────────────
    _T = t_b.to(second).magnitude
    _dw = d_omega.to(radian / second).magnitude
    _A = np.array([[_T**3, _T**4, _T**5], [3 * _T**2, 4 * _T**3, 5 * _T**4], [6 * _T, 12 * _T**2, 20 * _T**3]])
    _rhs = np.array([_dw * _T / 2, _dw, 0.0])  # position, velocity, acceleration residuals
    a3, a4, a5 = (float(c) for c in np.linalg.solve(_A, _rhs))
    pos_res = (_dw * _T / 2) * radian
    acc_mid = 1.5 * _dw / _T  # rad/s^2 at mid-bridge
    j_peak = abs(6 * a3)  # rad/s^3 at both ends
    _j_end = abs(6 * a3 + 24 * a4 * _T + 60 * a5 * _T**2)
    _jm2 = j_refl.to(kilogram * meter**2).magnitude
    tau_rate_bridge = (_jm2 * j_peak) * newton * meter / second
    tau_rate_step = (tau_step / dt_tick).to(newton * meter / second)
    step_over_limit = (tau_rate_step / taud_max).to("dimensionless").magnitude
    bridge_share = (tau_rate_bridge / taud_max).to("dimensionless").magnitude
    tau_half = 2 * tau_bridge
    j_half = 4 * j_peak
    tau_rate_half = 4 * tau_rate_bridge

    # ┌── 3. GUARD (Invariants) ────────────────────
    check(
        abs(a3 - _dw / _T**2) < 1e-6 and abs(a4 + _dw / (2 * _T**3)) < 1e-3 and abs(a5) < 1e-3, "quintic coefficients disagree with the closed form"
    )
    check(abs(a3 - 80.0) < 1e-6 and abs(a4 + 800.0) < 1e-3, "quintic coefficients changed")
    check(abs(_j_end - j_peak) < 1e-6, "bridge jerk no longer symmetric at the ends")
    check(abs(_jm2 * acc_mid - tau_bridge.to(newton * meter).magnitude) < 1e-9, "quintic peak torque disagrees with the seam cell")
    check(abs(j_peak - 480.0) < 1e-6, "bridge peak jerk changed")
    check(abs(tau_rate_bridge.magnitude - 88.08) < 0.01, "bridge torque rate changed")
    check(abs(tau_rate_step.magnitude - 36700.0) < 5.0, "one-tick torque rate changed")
    check(step_over_limit > 30 and bridge_share < 0.1, "torque-rate verdicts changed")
    check(tau_rate_half < taud_max, "half-duration bridge no longer inside the torque-rate limit")
    _k_short = (t_b / t_short).to("dimensionless").magnitude
    check(tau_rate_bridge * _k_short**2 > taud_max, "checkpoint: compressed bridge no longer exceeds the torque-rate limit")

    # ┌── 4. OUTPUT (Formatting) ───────────────────
    a3_math = fmt_math(
        rf"\PolynomialTrajectoryCoefficient_3=\FiniteChange\JointVelocity/\SeamBridgeDuration^2={fmt(a3, precision=0)}\ \text{{rad/s}}^3"
    )
    a4_math = fmt_math(
        rf"\PolynomialTrajectoryCoefficient_4=-\FiniteChange\JointVelocity/(2\SeamBridgeDuration^3)={fmt(a4, precision=0)}\ \text{{rad/s}}^4"
    )
    pos_res_str = fmt_angle(pos_res, precision=3)
    acc_mid_str = fmt_angular_acceleration(round(acc_mid) * radian / second**2, precision=0)
    j_peak_str = fmt(j_peak, precision=0, suffix=" rad/s³")
    tau_rate_bridge_str = fmt_torque_rate(tau_rate_bridge, precision=1)
    taud_max_str = fmt_torque_rate(taud_max, precision=0, commas=True)
    bridge_share_str = fmt_percent(bridge_share, precision=1, style="prose")
    tau_rate_step_str = fmt_torque_rate(tau_rate_step, precision=0, commas=True)
    step_over_mult_str = fmt_multiple(step_over_limit, precision=1)
    tau_half_str = fmt_torque(tau_half, precision=1)
    j_half_str = fmt(j_half, precision=0, commas=True, suffix=" rad/s³")
    tau_rate_half_str = fmt_torque_rate(tau_rate_half, precision=1)
    t_short_str = fmt_latency(t_short, unit=millisecond)
```

::: {#nbk-planning-seam-acceleration-jump-reflected-inertia-torque .callout-notebook title="The seam spike"}

**Problem**: At a replanning seam the incoming chunk's reference runs `{python} PlanningSeamInertia.delta_omega_str` faster than the active one. Should the joint close that gap in one servo tick or over a $\DifferentiabilityClass^2$ bridge, and what does each ask of the drive?

**Variables**:

- Joint: a CSG-25-50 strain-wave gear driven by a TQ-RoboDrive ILM 70x18 motor, a Panda-class stand-in because Franka does not publish the Panda's joint internals (datasheet parts); reflected rotor inertia $\EffectiveJointInertia = \GearReductionRatio^2 \RotorInertia =$ `{python} PlanningSeamInertia.j_reflected_str` (derived; link and payload inertia excluded, so here $\EffectiveJointInertia$ is the reflected inertia $\ReflectedRotorInertia$ of @sec-body-reflected-rotor-inertia alone)
- Ratings `{python} PlanningSeamInertia.tau_rated_str` rated and `{python} PlanningSeamInertia.tau_peak_rated_str` repeated peak (datasheet); the arm's torque-rate limit `{python} PlanningQuinticBridge.taud_max_str` (datasheet)
- Velocity gap $\FiniteChange\JointVelocity =$ `{python} PlanningSeamInertia.delta_omega_str` (illustrative) and servo tick $\SamplingPeriod =$ `{python} PlanningSeamInertia.dt_tick_str` (chosen)
- Bridge duration $\SeamBridgeDuration =$ `{python} PlanningSeamInertia.t_blend_str` (illustrative), zero acceleration at both ends, ending on chunk B's reference, a position residual $\FiniteChange\JointVelocity\,\SeamBridgeDuration/2 =$ `{python} PlanningQuinticBridge.pos_res_str` (chosen)

**Math**:

1. **One tick** (@eq-plan-seam-torque): $\EffectiveJointInertia\,\FiniteChange\JointVelocity/\SamplingPeriod =$ `{python} PlanningSeamInertia.tau_step_str`, below the rating. Reaching it within the tick needs at least `{python} PlanningSeamInertia.tau_step_str` per `{python} PlanningSeamInertia.dt_tick_str`, or `{python} PlanningQuinticBridge.tau_rate_step_str`, `{python} PlanningQuinticBridge.step_over_mult_str` the torque-rate limit.
2. **Quintic bridge** (@eq-plan-quintic-spline-matrix): With zero boundary accelerations the system gives $\PolynomialTrajectoryCoefficient_5 = 0$, `{python} PlanningQuinticBridge.a4_math`, and `{python} PlanningQuinticBridge.a3_math`.
3. **Bridge peaks**: Acceleration peaks at mid-bridge at $1.5\,\FiniteChange\JointVelocity/\SeamBridgeDuration =$ `{python} PlanningQuinticBridge.acc_mid_str`, a torque of `{python} PlanningSeamInertia.tau_peak_str`. Jerk (@eq-plan-quintic-jerk) peaks at both ends at $6\PolynomialTrajectoryCoefficient_3 =$ `{python} PlanningQuinticBridge.j_peak_str`, a torque rate $\EffectiveJointInertia\,\JointJerk$ of `{python} PlanningQuinticBridge.tau_rate_bridge_str`, `{python} PlanningQuinticBridge.bridge_share_str` of the limit.
4. **Half the duration**: Peak torque scales as $1/\SeamBridgeDuration$ and jerk as $1/\SeamBridgeDuration^2$, so a bridge half as long needs `{python} PlanningQuinticBridge.tau_half_str`, `{python} PlanningQuinticBridge.j_half_str`, and `{python} PlanningQuinticBridge.tau_rate_half_str`, still inside the limit.

**Result**: The one-tick step passes a torque check and asks for `{python} PlanningQuinticBridge.step_over_mult_str` the torque-rate limit; the bridge passes both with a `{python} PlanningSeamInertia.reduction_mult_str` smaller torque peak.

**Systems insight**: Evaluating torque magnitude alone is an inadequate feasibility screen at a trajectory seam. Actuator drives fail on the rate of change of torque, which grows quadratically ($1/\SeamBridgeDuration^2$) as blending duration compresses. When late trajectory admission forces the system to compress bridge duration $\SeamBridgeDuration$, required jerk and torque slew rates increase fourfold for every twofold reduction in duration. An admission monitor must explicitly re-evaluate the compressed bridge rather than inheriting validity from the uncompressed nominal profile. Furthermore, link inertia, payload mass, gravity, and joint friction compound this inertial baseline, requiring independent peak torque and thermal budget verification. The torque verdict of step 1 depends on that exclusion. With the payload inertia of @eq-plan-one-joint-dynamics included, `{python} PlanningOneJointDynamics.j_eff_str` in place of `{python} PlanningSeamInertia.j_reflected_str`, the one-tick request grows by the same ratio and exceeds even the `{python} PlanningSeamInertia.tau_peak_rated_str` repeated peak, so the one-tick step fails the torque check as well.

:::

::: {#fig-11-action-chunk-seam-continuity fig-env="figure" fig-pos="t" fig-cap="**Seam demand and checked bridge**: Both columns close the same `{python} PlanningSeamInertia.delta_omega_str` reference velocity gap on the notebook's strain-wave joint, with torque drawn to one scale against its datasheet ratings. The one-tick step (left) asks the reflected rotor inertia for `{python} PlanningSeamInertia.tau_step_str`, below the `{python} PlanningSeamInertia.tau_rated_str` rating, so the torque-magnitude check alone passes. The notebook's torque-rate calculation rejects the transition, and the drive also rejects its discontinuity. The `{python} PlanningSeamInertia.t_blend_str` $\DifferentiabilityClass^2$ bridge (right) peaks at `{python} PlanningSeamInertia.tau_peak_str`, but its interior jerk, full joint torque, and response still require checking." fig-alt="Two columns of stacked plots against time in milliseconds around a trajectory seam. Top row: reference velocity relative to chunk A. On the left it steps from zero to 0.2 radians per second within one millisecond; on the right an S-shaped bridge rises over 50 milliseconds before chunk B continues. Bottom row: inertial torque request on a shared scale with dashed lines for the rated torque of 51 and the repeated peak of 127 newton-meters.
