On the left a one-millisecond pulse reaches 36.7 newton-meters; on the right a low hump peaks at 1.1 newton-meters."}

```{python}
#| label: plot-planning-seam-continuity
#| echo: false
#| warning: false
#| message: false
# ┌─────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────
# │ SEAM DEMAND VS. C2 BRIDGE, DRAWN TO SCALE
# ├─────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────
# │ Context: @fig-11-action-chunk-seam-continuity.
# │
# │ Goal:    Show the one-tick seam request and the C2 bridge on one torque
# │          scale against the joint's datasheet ratings.
# │ Show:    0.2 rad/s gap; 36.7 N m for one 1 ms tick vs. 1.1 N m peak over a
# │          50 ms bridge; 51 N m rated and 127 N m repeated peak.
# │ How:     PlanningSeamInertia values only; the bridge is the cell's
# │          symmetric profile a(u) = 6 dw u (1 - u) / T, tau = J_refl a.
# └─────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────
import numpy as np
from mlsysim import viz
from mlsysim.core.units import millisecond, radian, second
from mlsysim.fmt import check

SI = PlanningSeamInertia
_dw = SI.delta_omega.to(radian / second).magnitude
_tick = SI.dt_tick.to(millisecond).magnitude
_T = SI.t_blend.to(millisecond).magnitude
_J = SI.j_reflected.to(kilogram * meter**2).magnitude
_rated = SI.tau_rated.to(newton * meter).magnitude
_peak = SI.tau_peak_rated.to(newton * meter).magnitude
_step = SI.tau_step.to(newton * meter).magnitude
_bridge = SI.tau_blend_peak.to(newton * meter).magnitude

t = np.linspace(-30, 90, 2401)
# (a) one-tick step: linear ramp across the tick, constant request during it
v_a = _dw * np.clip(t / _tick, 0, 1)
tau_a = np.where((t >= 0) & (t < _tick), _J * _dw / (_tick * 1e-3), 0.0)
# (b) symmetric C2 bridge over T
u = np.clip(t / _T, 0, 1)
v_b = _dw * (3 * u**2 - 2 * u**3)
tau_b = np.where((t > 0) & (t < _T), _J * 6 * _dw * u * (1 - u) / (_T * 1e-3), 0.0)
check(abs(tau_a.max() - _step) < 1e-6, "plotted one-tick request disagrees with the cell")
check(abs(tau_b.max() - _bridge) < 1e-3, "plotted bridge peak disagrees with the cell")

C = viz.COLORS
viz.set_book_style()
import matplotlib.pyplot as plt

fig, axes = plt.subplots(2, 2, figsize=(6.8, 4.6), sharex=True, gridspec_kw=dict(height_ratios=[1, 1.25], hspace=0.12, wspace=0.12))
PROP, BRIDGE, INK, SOFT = "#B87333", "#1A4D3E", C["primary"], "#4A5568"
for col, (v, tau, title) in enumerate(((v_a, tau_a, "(a) One-tick step"), (v_b, tau_b, "(b) $C^2$ bridge"))):
    av, at = axes[0, col], axes[1, col]
    pre, post = t <= 0, t >= (_tick if col == 0 else _T)
    mid = ~pre & ~post
    mid = mid | np.roll(mid, 1) | np.roll(mid, -1)  # join the segments
    av.plot(t[pre], v[pre], color=PROP, lw=1.6)
    av.plot(t[post], v[post], color=PROP, lw=1.6)
    av.plot(t[mid], v[mid], color=BRIDGE if col else PROP, lw=1.6, ls="-" if col else ":")
    av.text(-27, 0.03 * _dw + 0.02, "chunk A", color=PROP, fontsize=9)
    av.text(88, _dw * 0.84, "chunk B", color=PROP, fontsize=9, ha="right")
    if col:
        av.axvspan(0, _T, color=C["GreenL"], alpha=0.45, lw=0)
        av.text(_T / 2, _dw * 1.12, f"{_T:.0f} ms", color=BRIDGE, fontsize=9, ha="center")
    av.set_title(title, fontsize=9, loc="left")
    av.set_ylim(-0.03, _dw * 1.3)
    at.axhline(_rated, color=SOFT, lw=0.9, ls="--")
    at.axhline(_peak, color=C["RedLine"], lw=0.9, ls="--")
    at.fill_between(t, 0, tau, color=BRIDGE if col else PROP, alpha=0.9, lw=0.8)
    at.plot(t, tau, color=BRIDGE if col else PROP, lw=1.0)
    at.set_ylim(0, _peak * 1.18)
    at.text(-27, _rated + 4, f"rated {_rated:.0f}", color=SOFT, fontsize=9)
    at.text(-27, _peak + 4, f"repeated peak {_peak:.0f}", color=C["RedLine"], fontsize=9)
    if col:
        at.annotate(
            f"peak {_bridge:.1f} N·m",
            xy=(_T / 2, _bridge),
            xytext=(_T / 2 + 8, 22),
            fontsize=9,
            color=BRIDGE,
            arrowprops=dict(arrowstyle="-", color=BRIDGE, lw=0.7),
        )
    else:
        at.annotate(
            f"{_step:.1f} N·m for {_tick:.0f} ms",
            xy=(_tick, _step),
            xytext=(12, _step - 16),
            fontsize=9,
            color=PROP,
            arrowprops=dict(arrowstyle="-", color=PROP, lw=0.7),
        )
    at.set_xlabel("time from seam (ms)", fontsize=9)
    for ax in (av, at):
        ax.tick_params(labelsize=9)
        ax.grid(False)
        for sd in ("top", "right"):
            ax.spines[sd].set_visible(False)
    if col:
        av.tick_params(labelleft=False)
        at.tick_params(labelleft=False)
    av.set_xlim(-30, 90)
axes[0, 1].sharey(axes[0, 0])
axes[1, 1].sharey(axes[1, 0])
axes[0, 0].set_ylabel("$\\Delta\\dot q$ (rad/s)", fontsize=9)
axes[1, 0].set_ylabel("inertial torque (N·m)", fontsize=9)
plt.show()
```

:::

High-frequency chatter in learned policy outputs represents an identical physical hazard under a different guise. Stochastic sampling policies, such as diffusion policies or action-chunking transformers, often generate consecutive trajectory chunks where individual waypoints satisfy static position and velocity limits, yet commanded accelerations reverse sign erratically between steps. Each acceleration reversal demands an immediate torque reversal from the actuator, triggering rapid current transitions and severe $\TorqueProducingCurrent^2 \PhaseResistance$ resistive heating in the motor windings. In physical AI systems, engineers must treat this high-frequency variance as a direct cause of thermal rise and transmission fatigue rather than cosmetic jitter. A trajectory candidate that excites structural resonances or exceeds drive thermal dissipation limits is infeasible, regardless of how closely its geometric path resembles demonstration data.

### Time parameterization under torque and jerk bounds {#sec-planning-time-parameterization}

A collision-free curve through configuration space says where the arm goes, but nothing about how fast it may travel along that curve without saturating a joint's torque limit on the way up or demanding an impossible torque step when it switches to braking. Geometric search and neural proposal generators determine only the spatial path of motion: a curve $\GeneralizedCoordinates(\PathCoordinate)$ parameterized by scalar path coordinate $\PathCoordinate \in [0, 1]$. The timing law $\PathCoordinate(\TimeInstant)$ governs the physical motion, determining every joint velocity, acceleration, and torque required along the trajectory. Establishing a valid timing profile $\PathCoordinate(\TimeInstant)$ subject to physical actuator limits is the problem of **time parameterization**\index{Time parameterization!definition}. Applying the chain rule to the joint coordinates yields:

$$\GeneralizedVelocities = \JointPathTangent(\PathCoordinate)\,\PathVelocity, \qquad \GeneralizedAccelerations = \JointPathTangent(\PathCoordinate)\,\PathAcceleration + \JointPathCurvature(\PathCoordinate)\,\PathVelocity^2$$

where primes denote differentiation with respect to path coordinate $\PathCoordinate$ ($\DerivativeOperator\GeneralizedCoordinates/d\PathCoordinate$ and $\DerivativeOperator^2\GeneralizedCoordinates/d\PathCoordinate^2$). Substituting these path derivatives into the unconstrained manipulator equation from @eq-plan-rigidbody-dynamics expresses joint torque as a function of three path-dependent terms:

$$\JointTorque = \PathAccelerationTorqueCoefficient(\PathCoordinate)\,\PathAcceleration + \PathVelocitySquaredTorqueCoefficient(\PathCoordinate)\,\PathVelocity^2 + \GravitationalTorqueVector(\PathCoordinate)$$ {#eq-plan-path-torque}

with vector coefficients $\PathAccelerationTorqueCoefficient(\PathCoordinate) = \GeneralizedInertiaMatrix(\GeneralizedCoordinates)\JointPathTangent(\PathCoordinate)$, $\PathVelocitySquaredTorqueCoefficient(\PathCoordinate) = \GeneralizedInertiaMatrix(\GeneralizedCoordinates)\JointPathCurvature(\PathCoordinate) + \CoriolisCentrifugalMatrix(\GeneralizedCoordinates,\JointPathTangent)\,\JointPathTangent(\PathCoordinate)$, and $\GravitationalTorqueVector(\PathCoordinate) = \GravitationalTorqueVector(\GeneralizedCoordinates)$. Each actuator torque bound $|\CommandedJointTorque_i| \le {\JointTorqueLimit}_i$ translates into an admissible interval of path acceleration, $\PathAccelerationLowerBound(\PathCoordinate,\PathVelocity) \le \PathAcceleration \le \PathAccelerationUpperBound(\PathCoordinate,\PathVelocity)$, at every coordinate of the **phase plane**\index{Phase plane!time parameterization} $(\PathCoordinate, \PathVelocity)$. Actuator velocity and acceleration limits introduce equivalent bounding intervals. As path velocity $\PathVelocity$ increases, the centrifugal and Coriolis term $\PathVelocitySquaredTorqueCoefficient(\PathCoordinate)\PathVelocity^2$ grows quadratically until the admissible acceleration interval closes entirely ($\PathAccelerationLowerBound = \PathAccelerationUpperBound$). The locus of phase-plane points where this interval collapses defines the maximum velocity curve, representing an upper speed envelope that no feasible parameterization can exceed.

Because total motion duration is $\Time = \int_0^1 \frac{1}{\PathVelocity}\,d\PathCoordinate$, the minimum-time profile maintains the highest permissible path velocity $\PathVelocity$ at every point along the path. Under torque constraints alone, the time-optimal solution takes a bang-bang form [@bobrow1985time]: the system accelerates along the upper bound $\PathAccelerationUpperBound$ until its phase-plane trajectory encounters a braking curve integrated backward from the goal at lower bound $\PathAccelerationLowerBound$, then decelerates along $\PathAccelerationLowerBound$ to reach the target at rest. Switch points mark the phase-plane coordinates where the trajectory transitions between maximum acceleration and maximum braking. The TOPP-RA algorithm [@pham2018new] solves this phase-plane parameterization efficiently by transforming it into a convex optimization problem. By substituting squared path velocity $\SquaredPathVelocity = \PathVelocity^2$ and path acceleration $\PathAccelerationInput = \PathAcceleration$, the torque constraints in @eq-plan-path-torque and the differential step equation $\SquaredPathVelocity_{i+1} = \SquaredPathVelocity_i + 2\,\FiniteChange \PathCoordinate\,\PathAccelerationInput_i$ become linear across a grid of $\PathGridPointCount$ path waypoints. (This linear step relation follows from $d\SquaredPathVelocity/d\PathCoordinate = 2\PathVelocity\,(\DerivativeOperator\PathVelocity/d\PathCoordinate) = 2\PathAcceleration$, matching the kinematic equation $\Glyph{v}^2 = 2\Glyph{a} \Glyph{d}$). A backward integration pass computes the controllable interval of $\SquaredPathVelocity$ at each grid point from which the terminal state remains reachable, solving a single linear program per point; a subsequent forward pass selects the largest admissible acceleration $\PathAccelerationInput$ at each step. The complete pass runs in $\mathcal{O}(\PathGridPointCount)$ time, and an empty feasible interval at any point provides constructive proof that no parameterization satisfies the bounds on that grid. Kinematic variants that constrain only joint velocity and acceleration compute this timing structure with lower overhead [@kunz2012time]; the Kunz and Stilman algorithm serves as the default time-parameterization method in MoveIt 2, which can apply a downstream jerk-limiting filter [@moveit2timeparam].

```{python}
#| label: calc-planning-time-parameterization
#| echo: false
#| warning: false
#| message: false
# ┌─────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────
# │ TIME-OPTIMAL AND JERK-LIMITED SWING OF ONE JOINT, AND ONLINE GENERATOR TIMING
# ├─────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────
# │ Context: @sec-planning-time-parameterization (notebook and online
# │          generation paragraph), tbl-11-practice-2026.
# │
# │ Goal:    Work the phase-plane bang-bang solution for a rest-to-rest swing
# │          of the loaded shoulder, then price the torque-rate (jerk) bound.
# │ Show:    torque-limited 40.2 up / 65.1 rad/s^2 down vs. 7.5 rad/s^2
# │          joint limit; 0.5 rad in 516 ms, peak 1.94 rad/s; 24.8 N m step
# │          at the switch; jerk 604.8 rad/s^3; 528.9 ms jerk-limited (+12.6 ms).
# │ How:     PlanningOneJointDynamics (payload-only, gravity held at its
# │          horizontal value over the swing); FER joint-2 acceleration limit
# │          and torque-rate limit (registry, franka2023robot); rest-to-rest
# │          double-S without cruise, calc_scurve_rest_to_rest_time:
# │          D = a x (x + a/j), T = 2 (x + a/j).
# │          Ruckig timing from berscheid2021jerk, Table III.
# └─────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────
import math
from mlsysim import *
from mlsysim.core.units import millisecond, microsecond, meter, newton, radian, second, rad
from mlsysim.physics.robotics import calc_scurve_rest_to_rest_time
from mlsysim.fmt import (
    check,
    fmt,
    fmt_int,
    fmt_latency,
    fmt_percent,
    fmt_torque,
    fmt_torque_rate,
    fmt_angular_velocity,
    fmt_angle,
    fmt_angular_acceleration,
)

RM = Embodied.MobileManipulator.WarehouseMobileManipulator

class PlanningTimeParam:
    """Phase-plane swing of the loaded shoulder and the cost of a jerk bound."""

    # ┌── 1. LOAD (Constants) ──────────────────────
    d_q = 0.5 * radian  # category: illustrative; swing amplitude
    j_eff = PlanningOneJointDynamics.j_eff  # category: derived; payload plus reflected rotor inertia
    tau_g = PlanningOneJointDynamics.tau_grav  # category: derived; payload holding torque, held constant near horizontal
    tau_max = PlanningOneJointDynamics.tau_max  # category: datasheet; joint torque limit, registry
    qd_max = PlanningTwoLinkArm.qd_max  # category: datasheet; FER joint 2 velocity limit (franka2023robot)
    qdd_max = RM.arm.joint_acceleration_limits[1]  # category: datasheet; FER joint 2 acceleration limit, registry (franka2023robot)
    taud_max = RM.arm.joint_torque_rate_limit  # category: datasheet; FER torque-rate limit, registry (franka2023robot)
    ruckig_mean = 19.8 * microsecond  # category: literature; 7-DoF mean, i7-8700K (berscheid2021jerk, Table III)
    ruckig_worst = 123 * microsecond  # category: literature; 7-DoF worst case (berscheid2021jerk, Table III)
    ruckig_dofs = 7  # category: literature; axes in the benchmark (berscheid2021jerk)

    # ┌── 2. EXECUTE (The Compute) ─────────────────
    a_up = ((tau_max - tau_g) / j_eff).to(second**-2).magnitude * rad / second**2
    a_dn = ((tau_max + tau_g) / j_eff).to(second**-2).magnitude * rad / second**2
    a_bind = min(a_up, a_dn, qdd_max)
    _dq, _a = d_q.magnitude, a_bind.magnitude
    t_opt = (2 * math.sqrt(_dq / _a)) * second
    v_peak = math.sqrt(_a * _dq) * rad / second
    tau_step = (2 * j_eff * a_bind / rad).to(newton * meter)
    t_step = (tau_step / taud_max).to(millisecond)
    j_bound = (taud_max / j_eff).to(second**-3).magnitude * rad / second**3
    _move = calc_scurve_rest_to_rest_time(d_q, a_bind, j_bound)
    t_jerk = _move["duration"].to(second)
    v_peak_jerk = _move["peak_velocity"].to(rad / second)
    t_extra = (t_jerk - t_opt).to(millisecond)
    extra_ratio = (t_extra / t_opt).to("dimensionless").magnitude
    t_ramp = (a_bind.magnitude / j_bound.magnitude) * second  # a / j, one jerk ramp
    t_hold = (t_jerk / 2 - t_ramp).to(millisecond)  # x in D = a x (x + a/j), T = 2 (x + a/j)

    # ┌── 3. GUARD (Invariants) ────────────────────
    check(abs(a_up.magnitude - 40.16) < 0.01, "upward torque-limited acceleration changed")
    check(abs(a_dn.magnitude - 65.07) < 0.01, "downward torque-limited acceleration changed")
    check(a_bind == qdd_max, "the joint acceleration limit no longer binds")
    check(v_peak < qd_max and v_peak_jerk < qd_max, "swing now reaches the joint velocity limit")
    check(abs(t_opt.to(millisecond).magnitude - 516.40) < 0.01, "time-optimal swing changed")
    check(abs(tau_step.magnitude - 24.80) < 0.01, "switch torque step changed")
    check(abs(t_jerk.to(millisecond).magnitude - 528.95) < 0.01, "jerk-limited swing changed")
    check(_move["reaches_max_acceleration"], "jerk-limited swing no longer reaches the acceleration plateau")
    check(ruckig_worst < 1 * millisecond, "online generator worst case no longer inside a 1 ms cycle")

    # ┌── 4. OUTPUT (Formatting) ───────────────────
    d_q_str = fmt_angle(d_q, precision=1)
    a_up_str = fmt_angular_acceleration(a_up, precision=1)
    a_dn_str = fmt_angular_acceleration(a_dn, precision=1)
    qdd_max_str = fmt_angular_acceleration(qdd_max, precision=1)
    t_opt_str = fmt_latency(t_opt, unit=millisecond, precision=1)
    v_peak_str = fmt_angular_velocity(v_peak, precision=2)
    qd_max_str = PlanningTwoLinkArm.qd_max_str
    tau_step_str = fmt_torque(tau_step, precision=1)
    taud_max_str = fmt_torque_rate(taud_max, precision=0)
    t_step_str = fmt_latency(t_step, unit=millisecond, precision=1)
    j_bound_str = fmt(j_bound.magnitude, precision=1, suffix=" rad/s³")
    t_jerk_str = fmt_latency(t_jerk, unit=millisecond, precision=1)
    t_extra_str = fmt_latency(t_extra, unit=millisecond, precision=1)
    extra_pct_str = fmt_percent(extra_ratio, precision=1, style="prose")
    t_ramp_str = fmt_latency(t_ramp.to(millisecond), unit=millisecond, precision=1)
    t_hold_str = fmt_latency(t_hold, unit=millisecond, precision=1)
    ruckig_mean_str = fmt_latency(ruckig_mean, unit=microsecond, precision=1)
    ruckig_worst_str = fmt_latency(ruckig_worst, unit=microsecond)
    ruckig_dofs_str = fmt_int(ruckig_dofs)
```

::: {#nbk-planning-time-optimal-joint-swing .callout-notebook title="Time-optimal swing of one joint"}

**Problem**: The shoulder lifts the rated payload at full planar reach through `{python} PlanningTimeParam.d_q_str`, from rest to rest. How fast can it swing, and what does the fastest timing ask of the drive?

**Variables**:

- Swing $\FiniteChange \JointPosition =$ `{python} PlanningTimeParam.d_q_str` (illustrative), with the joint angle itself as the path parameter ($\PathCoordinate = \JointPosition$, measured from the start)
- Inertia $\EffectiveJointInertia =$ `{python} PlanningOneJointDynamics.j_eff_str` and payload gravity torque $\PayloadGravityTorque =$ `{python} PlanningOneJointDynamics.tau_grav_str`, held at its horizontal value (derived, payload only)
- Joint limits: torque $\JointTorqueLimit =$ `{python} PlanningOneJointDynamics.tau_max_str`, acceleration `{python} PlanningTimeParam.qdd_max_str`, velocity `{python} PlanningTimeParam.qd_max_str`, torque rate $\TorqueRateLimit =$ `{python} PlanningTimeParam.taud_max_str` (datasheet [@franka2023robot])

**Math**:

1. **Binding acceleration**: The torque limit allows $(\JointTorqueLimit-\PayloadGravityTorque)/\EffectiveJointInertia =$ `{python} PlanningTimeParam.a_up_str` upward and $(\JointTorqueLimit+\PayloadGravityTorque)/\EffectiveJointInertia =$ `{python} PlanningTimeParam.a_dn_str` braking, an asymmetry that gravity creates. The published `{python} PlanningTimeParam.qdd_max_str` is tighter than both, so it binds in both directions.
2. **Time-optimal swing**: The accelerating curve $\PathVelocity^2 = 2\ProfileAccelerationBound \PathCoordinate$ meets the braking curve at mid-swing, where speed peaks at $\sqrt{\ProfileAccelerationBound\,\FiniteChange \JointPosition} =$ `{python} PlanningTimeParam.v_peak_str`, below the velocity limit. The swing takes $2\sqrt{\FiniteChange \JointPosition/\ProfileAccelerationBound} =$ `{python} PlanningTimeParam.t_opt_str`.
3. **Switch-point step**: Acceleration reverses from $+\ProfileAccelerationBound$ to $-\ProfileAccelerationBound$, a torque step $2\EffectiveJointInertia{}\ProfileAccelerationBound =$ `{python} PlanningTimeParam.tau_step_str`, which needs at least `{python} PlanningTimeParam.t_step_str` at the torque-rate limit. That limit bounds jerk at $\TorqueRateLimit/\EffectiveJointInertia =$ `{python} PlanningTimeParam.j_bound_str`.
4. **Jerk-limited swing**: A rest-to-rest double-S profile with no cruise covers $\FiniteChange \JointPosition = \ProfileAccelerationBound\,\SCurveAccelerationPhaseTime\,(\SCurveAccelerationPhaseTime + \ProfileAccelerationBound/\JerkLimit)$ in $\Time = 2(\SCurveAccelerationPhaseTime + \ProfileAccelerationBound/\JerkLimit)$, where $\SCurveAccelerationPhaseTime = \Time/2 - \ProfileAccelerationBound/\JerkLimit$ is half the swing less one jerk ramp (the constant-acceleration hold plus one ramp), so $\ProfileAccelerationBound \SCurveAccelerationPhaseTime$ is the peak speed. With $\ProfileAccelerationBound/\JerkLimit =$ `{python} PlanningTimeParam.t_ramp_str`, the swing needs $\SCurveAccelerationPhaseTime =$ `{python} PlanningTimeParam.t_hold_str` and takes `{python} PlanningTimeParam.t_jerk_str`.

**Systems insight**: Enforcing the torque-rate limit incurs an execution penalty of `{python} PlanningTimeParam.t_extra_str`, a modest `{python} PlanningTimeParam.extra_pct_str` increase in motion duration, while eliminating the instantaneous torque step entirely. For the payload alone, torque was not the binding constraint; the published kinematic limits governed the trajectory, though identified link inertia would narrow this torque headroom. A valid time parameterization must incorporate every constraint capable of binding in practice. The theoretical time-optimal profile without a jerk bound is an unexecutable mathematical abstraction that physical drives reject.

:::

In the phase plane the two profiles differ only near their corners (@fig-11-phase-plane-swing). The torque limits alone would permit steeper accelerating and braking parabolas, but the published `{python} PlanningTimeParam.qdd_max_str` acceleration limit contracts both arcs, and the bang-bang path rides them to its `{python} PlanningTimeParam.v_peak_str` switch point, well below the velocity limit. The jerk-limited path rounds the start, the apex, and the finish just inside those arcs. That rounding is where its extra `{python} PlanningTimeParam.extra_pct_str` of duration goes, and it is what removes the `{python} PlanningTimeParam.tau_step_str` torque step at the switch point.

::: {#fig-11-phase-plane-swing fig-env="figure" fig-pos="t" fig-cap="**Phase plane of the shoulder swing**: Path speed $\PathVelocity$ against path position $\PathCoordinate$ for the `{python} PlanningTimeParam.d_q_str` rest-to-rest swing. The joint's `{python} PlanningTimeParam.qdd_max_str` acceleration limit, tighter than either torque-derived bound, sets both the accelerating and braking curves; the bang-bang path follows them to the switch point at `{python} PlanningTimeParam.v_peak_str`, below the velocity limit, in `{python} PlanningTimeParam.t_opt_str`. The jerk-limited path stays inside it and takes `{python} PlanningTimeParam.t_jerk_str`, `{python} PlanningTimeParam.extra_pct_str` longer, with no torque step at the switch." fig-alt="A plot of path speed in radians per second against path position in radians from 0 to 0.5. A horizontal dashed line marks the velocity limit near 2.2. Two dashed gray parabolas rise steeply from each end. Two solid parabolas, one rising from the left and one falling to the right, meet at a peak near 1.9 radians per second at mid-swing, marked as the switch point. A second solid curve with rounded start and peak lies just inside them."}

```{python}
#| label: plot-planning-phase-plane
#| echo: false
#| warning: false
#| message: false
# ┌─────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────
# │ PHASE PLANE OF THE TIME-OPTIMAL AND JERK-LIMITED SHOULDER SWING
# ├─────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────
# │ Context: @fig-11-phase-plane-swing.
# │
# │ Goal:    Draw the notebook's bang-bang solution and its jerk-limited
# │          counterpart in (s, sdot), with the bounds that shape them.
# │ Show:    velocity limit 2.175 rad/s; torque bounds 40.2 / 65.1 rad/s^2;
# │          binding 7.5 rad/s^2 curves meeting at 1.94 rad/s; 516.4 ms vs.
# │          528.9 ms.
# │ How:     PlanningTimeParam values; the jerk-limited path integrates the
# │          double-S jerk schedule (ramp a/j, hold, ramp) and is guarded to end
# │          at the swing amplitude at the cell's duration.
# └─────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────
import numpy as np
from mlsysim import viz
from mlsysim.core.units import millisecond, radian, second
from mlsysim.fmt import check

TP = PlanningTimeParam
_rps, _rps2 = radian / second, radian / second**2
_D = TP.d_q.to(radian).magnitude
_vmax = TP.qd_max.to(_rps).magnitude
_a = TP.a_bind.to(_rps2).magnitude
_aup, _adn = TP.a_up.to(_rps2).magnitude, TP.a_dn.to(_rps2).magnitude
_j = TP.j_bound.to(radian / second**3).magnitude
_T = TP.t_jerk.to(second).magnitude

s = np.linspace(0, _D, 801)
acc = lambda a: np.sqrt(2 * a * s)
brk = lambda a: np.sqrt(np.clip(2 * a * (_D - s), 0, None))
bang = np.minimum(acc(_a), brk(_a))
check(abs(bang.max() - TP.v_peak.to(_rps).magnitude) < 1e-3, "plotted switch speed disagrees with the cell")

# Double-S rest-to-rest: jerk +j, 0, -j over the first half, mirrored in the second.
_tj = _a / _j
_ta = _T / 2 - 2 * _tj
_dt = _T / 20000
tt = np.arange(0, _T + _dt / 2, _dt)
_b = np.cumsum([0, _tj, _ta, _tj, _tj, _ta, _tj])
jerk = np.select([tt < _b[1], tt < _b[2], tt < _b[3], tt < _b[4], tt < _b[5], tt < _b[6]], [_j, 0, -_j, -_j, 0, _j], 0.0)
acc_t = np.cumsum(jerk) * _dt
vel_t = np.cumsum(acc_t) * _dt
pos_t = np.cumsum(vel_t) * _dt
check(abs(pos_t[-1] - _D) < 2e-3 * _D, "jerk-limited path no longer ends at the swing amplitude")
check(vel_t.max() < _vmax, "jerk-limited path reaches the velocity limit")

C = viz.COLORS
viz.set_book_style()
import matplotlib.pyplot as plt

fig, ax = plt.subplots(figsize=(6.8, 3.8))
PROP, STRUCT, SOFT = "#B87333", "#1A4D3E", "#4A5568"
ax.axhline(_vmax, color=C["RedLine"], lw=0.9, ls="--")
ax.text(_D * 0.5, _vmax + 0.06, f"joint velocity limit {_vmax:.3f} rad/s", color=C["RedLine"], fontsize=9, ha="center", va="bottom")
m_up, m_dn = acc(_aup) < _vmax * 1.25, brk(_adn) < _vmax * 1.25
ax.plot(s[m_up], acc(_aup)[m_up], color="#A0AEC0", lw=1.0, ls="--")
ax.plot(s[m_dn], brk(_adn)[m_dn], color="#A0AEC0", lw=1.0, ls="--")
ax.text(0.045, 1.62, f"torque bound\n+{_aup:.1f} rad/s²", color=SOFT, fontsize=9, ha="left", va="center")
ax.text(_D - 0.035, 1.62, f"torque bound\n−{_adn:.1f} rad/s²", color=SOFT, fontsize=9, ha="right", va="center")
ax.plot(s, bang, color=PROP, lw=1.8, label=f"bang-bang, ±{_a:.1f} rad/s², {TP.t_opt.to(millisecond).magnitude:.1f} ms")
ax.plot(pos_t, vel_t, color=STRUCT, lw=1.6, label=f"jerk-limited, {TP.t_jerk.to(millisecond).magnitude:.1f} ms")
ax.plot([_D / 2], [bang.max()], "o", color=PROP, ms=4, zorder=5)
ax.annotate(
    f"switch point, {bang.max():.2f} rad/s",
    xy=(_D / 2, bang.max()),
    xytext=(_D * 0.58, 1.98),
    fontsize=9,
    color=PROP,
    va="center",
    arrowprops=dict(arrowstyle="-", color=PROP, lw=0.7),
)
ax.set_xlim(0, _D)
ax.set_ylim(0, 2.65)
ax.set_xlabel("path position $s = q$ (rad)", fontsize=9)
ax.set_ylabel("path speed $\\dot s$ (rad/s)", fontsize=9)
ax.tick_params(labelsize=9)
ax.grid(False)
for sd in ("top", "right"):
    ax.spines[sd].set_visible(False)
ax.legend(loc="lower center", fontsize=9, frameon=False)
plt.show()
```

:::

The time-optimal bang-bang solution produces precisely the derivative discontinuities that safe seam execution forbids. Every transition between maximum acceleration and maximum braking represents a step change in acceleration, demanding an instantaneous step in electromagnetic torque that actuator drives cannot deliver within finite voltage and current slew limits. Incorporating an explicit jerk bound transforms the problem into a third-order trajectory formulation. As the shoulder swing notebook shows, the time cost of bounding jerk is small next to the torque step it removes. Modern motion pipelines therefore parameterize paths under coupled torque and velocity limits and enforce explicit jerk bounds downstream, or constrain jerk directly during parameterization.

An identical jerk-limited profile, synthesized from the robot's verified state, resolves both seam blending and safe stopping. An **online trajectory generator**\index{Online trajectory generation} receives the instantaneous position, velocity, and acceleration of each joint together with a target boundary state, returning a time-optimal profile that satisfies per-axis velocity, acceleration, and jerk limits [@kroger2010online]. For example, the Ruckig algorithm [@berscheid2021jerk] evaluates arbitrary initial and target states across seven distinct constant-jerk phases, calculating profile durations analytically for most trajectory classes and using a bounded polynomial root solver for asymmetric edge cases. In published benchmarks, Ruckig achieved an average execution latency of `{python} PlanningTimeParam.ruckig_mean_str` and a worst-case latency of `{python} PlanningTimeParam.ruckig_worst_str` for `{python} PlanningTimeParam.ruckig_dofs_str` axes on a desktop processor, making it fast enough to re-solve within a 1 kHz control cycle. This formulation differs structurally from the fixed-duration quintic bridge in @sec-planning-quintic-splines. While the quintic approach fixes blending duration $\SeamBridgeDuration$ upfront and risks exceeding joint limits during aggressive maneuvers (requiring downstream extrema checks to reject invalid solutions), an online trajectory generator solves for minimum duration as an optimization variable, guaranteeing that kinematic derivative bounds hold by construction. The S-curve stopping trajectory examined in @sec-planning-c2-stopping-suffix represents this exact profile structure evaluated toward a zero-velocity terminal state.

Kinematic feasibility by construction, however, does not grant permission to move. An online generator guarantees only the mathematical bounds explicitly configured in its parameters. Single-axis velocity, acceleration, and jerk bounds cannot account for multi-joint dynamic coupling in @eq-plan-rigidbody-dynamics, spatial swept-volume collisions, or stale perception data. Furthermore, configuration errors or numerical solver faults can directly compromise the guarantees the generator claims to provide. Real-time benchmarks reported on high-performance desktop CPUs also do not represent execution latency on a constrained safety MCU. Online generators produce higher-quality proposals that satisfy kinematic constraints by design, but the deterministic safety controller must independently validate dynamic feasibility, collision margins, and temporal deadlines before granting execution permission.

::: {#chk-plan-seam-feasibility .callout-checkpoint title="Followable motion and the seam"}

A collision-free candidate becomes followable only after its joint rates, its seams, and its timing fit the body's limits.

**Pricing the seam**

Even a candidate trajectory that passes every internal dynamic and seam continuity check remains unsafe without an admitted contingency. The system must continuously maintain a certified stopping suffix to handle replacement chunks that fail to arrive before the admission deadline.

## Behavior at the Seam {#sec-planning-behavior-seam}

When the replacement does not arrive, because inference stalls on scheduling interference, a bus fault, or an unhandled exception, the arm reaches the end of its authority with no successor in hand. The runtime must then bring it to rest without violating the limits derived above or exhausting its stopping clearance. Three things decide the outcome: which deadline has passed, which stop the MCU runs, and how much clearance that stop consumes.

### Replacement deadlines and commitment cutoffs {#sec-planning-two-tier-deadlines}

A single timeout cannot protect both a fast control loop against a hung proposer and a moving arm against overrunning its obstacle clearance, because a lease short enough to catch a dropped packet fires long before the geometric point of no return, while a cutoff placed at the point of no return leaves a stalled policy coasting blind in the meantime. The two tiers named with the trajectory record in @sec-planning-handoff, the periodic chunk lease and the commitment cutoff, therefore answer different questions: whether a replacement has renewed tracking authority recently enough, and whether the reserved stop can still begin in time. The planner also uses a soft *blend deadline* ($\BlendDeadline$), a scheduling target for a smooth replacement. Missing that target need not end tracking if the current lease and evidence remain valid and a checked replacement can still arrive before the admission cutoff that precedes physical commitment ($\CommitmentInstant$). The earlier admission cutoff leaves the response interval needed for the matched stopping suffix to begin at commitment, before its reserved clearance is spent.

The two deadlines call for two different stops:

-   **Matched stop suffix (planned termination at $\TimeInstant = \CommitmentInstant$):** A pre-computed, jerk-limited $\DifferentiabilityClass^2$ slowdown along the admitted path, anchored specifically at the nominal state expected at $\CommitmentInstant$, checked at admission to satisfy $\StoppingDistance \le \ClearDistance$. If no successor is admitted before the earlier admission cutoff, the controller dispatches the stop early enough that the body smoothly transfers to this pre-latched suffix at commitment, decelerating to rest without requiring runtime replanning.
-   **State-matched fallback (reactive termination at $\TimeInstant < \CommitmentInstant$):** If the high-rate chunk lease lapses, the parent intent expires, or a runtime safety monitor detects an unmodeled obstacle or torque fault *before* reaching $\CommitmentInstant$, the robot cannot use the matched stop suffix (which is anchored at the future state $\CommitmentInstant$). Instead, the MCU selects or constructs a validated state-matched fallback from current state estimates $(\JointPosition, \JointVelocity, \JointAcceleration)$ within reserved clearance. Encoder-derived velocity and acceleration have their own error bounds; bounded polynomial evaluation does not eliminate sensing, dispatch, or actuator response delay.

Both are the stopping suffix that every admitted trajectory carries (definition \ref{dfn-planning-stopping-suffix}), differing only in the entry state from which they start.

For the running mug reach, a stalled proposer expires the shared lease `{python} PlanningLeaseRule.t_lease_str` after the last admission. The MCU then requests its state-matched fallback; physical onset follows the separately budgeted response delay. All timeout checks use the MCU monotonic clock. The longer-lease comparison isolates the geometric limit: even with tracking evidence continually renewed, the controller must dispatch the matched stop early enough to begin at commitment. A host progress report changes neither cutoff. Both stops also inherit the seam's continuity requirement, and that requirement fixes their shape and therefore their length.

### The C$^2$ stopping suffix and jerk-limited braking {#sec-planning-c2-stopping-suffix}

A moving robot carries continuous momentum. If an emergency brake uses an idealized constant-deceleration profile ($\StopAxisAcceleration(\TimeInstant) = -\CredibleBrakingDeceleration$), the commanded acceleration steps discontinuously from zero to $-\CredibleBrakingDeceleration$ at $\CommitmentInstant$, and steps discontinuously back to zero when velocity reaches zero. This instantaneous switch demands an infinite jerk impulse ($\dddot{\StopAxisPosition} = \infty$) and an instantaneous step jump in actuator braking torque ($\FiniteChange\CommandedJointTorque = \EffectiveJointInertia \CredibleBrakingDeceleration$). A real drive can only approximate that step. Whether the response loses traction, disturbs the payload, or exceeds structural limits depends on the load and controller, so the worked design chooses an explicitly smooth profile.

Two bounds describe what the load and the drive tolerate during that stop: a peak deceleration $\ProfileAccelerationBound$ and a peak jerk $\JerkLimit$, the rate at which deceleration may change. A $\DifferentiabilityClass^2$ stop keeps position, velocity, and acceleration continuous at both ends, so it must ramp its deceleration up from zero and back down to zero, and the jerk bound limits how quickly it can do either. Within those bounds, the shape of the profile decides how far the machine travels. For a cruise entry with position $\StopAxisPosition(\CommitmentInstant) = \CommitmentPathPosition$, cruise speed $\CruiseSpeed > 0$, and zero entry acceleration, one smooth candidate is the lowest-order polynomial that matches position, velocity, and acceleration at both ends, written in the normalized time $\StopProgress = (\TimeInstant - \CommitmentInstant) / \StoppingDuration \in [0, 1]$:

$$\StopAxisPosition(\StopProgress) = \CommitmentPathPosition + \CruiseSpeed \StoppingDuration \left(\StopProgress - \StopProgress^3 + \frac{1}{2} \StopProgress^4\right), \qquad \StopAxisAcceleration(\StopProgress) = -\frac{6 \CruiseSpeed}{\StoppingDuration} \StopProgress(1 - \StopProgress), \qquad \dddot{\StopAxisPosition}(\StopProgress) = -\frac{6 \CruiseSpeed}{\StoppingDuration^2} (1 - 2\StopProgress)$$ {#eq-plan-c2-polynomial-stop}

Its deceleration is an inverted parabola that peaks at the midpoint, $\PeakStopDeceleration = 1.5\,\CruiseSpeed/\StoppingDuration$, and its jerk is largest at the two ends, $6\CruiseSpeed/\StoppingDuration^2$. Holding the peak at $\ProfileAccelerationBound$ gives $\StoppingDuration = 1.5\,\CruiseSpeed/\ProfileAccelerationBound$ and a distance of $\frac{1}{2}\CruiseSpeed \StoppingDuration = 0.75\,\CruiseSpeed^2/\ProfileAccelerationBound$, which is $1.5$ times the constant-deceleration distance $\CruiseSpeed^2/2\ProfileAccelerationBound$. That factor is a property of this polynomial, not of smooth stopping. The polynomial touches its peak deceleration only at the midpoint and spends half the stop below three quarters of it, so it gives away distance that its own bounds would allow it to use.

The profile that uses those bounds fully is the **jerk-limited S-curve**\index{S-curve!jerk-limited stop}\index{Stopping suffix!S-curve} (trapezoidal acceleration, the "double S" velocity profile) [@biagiotti2008trajectory]. It ramps deceleration from zero to $\ProfileAccelerationBound$ at the jerk limit, holds $\ProfileAccelerationBound$, and ramps back to zero at the jerk limit just as velocity reaches zero. Each ramp lasts $\ProfileAccelerationBound/\JerkLimit$. The velocity profile is point-symmetric about its midpoint, so the distance is half the entry speed times the duration:

$$\StoppingDistance(\SpeedAtDetection) = \begin{cases} \dfrac{\SpeedAtDetection^2}{2\ProfileAccelerationBound} + \dfrac{\SpeedAtDetection\,\ProfileAccelerationBound}{2\JerkLimit}, & \SpeedAtDetection \ge \ProfileAccelerationBound^2/\JerkLimit \\[1.2ex] \SpeedAtDetection\sqrt{\SpeedAtDetection/\JerkLimit}, & \SpeedAtDetection < \ProfileAccelerationBound^2/\JerkLimit \end{cases} \qquad \StoppingDuration(\SpeedAtDetection) = \begin{cases} \dfrac{\SpeedAtDetection}{\ProfileAccelerationBound} + \dfrac{\ProfileAccelerationBound}{\JerkLimit}, & \SpeedAtDetection \ge \ProfileAccelerationBound^2/\JerkLimit \\[1.2ex] 2\sqrt{\SpeedAtDetection/\JerkLimit}, & \SpeedAtDetection < \ProfileAccelerationBound^2/\JerkLimit \end{cases}$$ {#eq-plan-c2-stopping-suffix}

Above the threshold speed $\ProfileAccelerationBound^2/\JerkLimit$, the stop costs constant-deceleration braking at $\ProfileAccelerationBound$ plus cruise over half of one jerk ramp, $\ProfileAccelerationBound/2\JerkLimit$, so a finite jerk limit acts like extra reaction time. Below the threshold the stop is too short to reach $\ProfileAccelerationBound$, and its deceleration peaks at $\sqrt{\SpeedAtDetection\,\JerkLimit}$. Among stops that respect both bounds and never reverse, this profile reaches rest in the least time and the least distance. The shape of the stop, not physics, sets the distance beyond $\SpeedAtDetection^2/2\ProfileAccelerationBound$, and for given deceleration and jerk bounds the S-curve spends the least. A slower profile remains admissible, but it must be charged at its own distance.

The jerk bound belongs to the load. The loaded tote rack and the mug tolerate a deceleration only if it is reached gradually, and the registry does not yet hold a measured jerk tolerance for either. The worked design therefore sets each body's $\JerkLimit$ to the peak jerk of @eq-plan-c2-polynomial-stop at that body's peak deceleration and top speed, a jerk the polynomial already asked the load to accept. A loaded stopping trial that measures the tolerable jerk would replace this stipulation, and @eq-plan-c2-stopping-suffix would then give the distance directly.

The stop is also a slowdown along the admitted path, not a new path. The planner fixes the geometry $\GeneralizedCoordinates(\PathCoordinate)$ it checked for clearance, and the S-curve governs only the speed $\PathVelocity(\TimeInstant)$ along that geometry, so the stop sweeps no volume outside the corridor already checked and the one-dimensional comparison $\StoppingDistance \le \ClearDistance$ applies along the path. A stop computed separately for each joint would leave that path and would need its own swept-volume check. A nonzero measured entry acceleration requires a profile matched to the actual $(\JointPosition,\JointVelocity,\JointAcceleration)$ at entry with zero terminal velocity and acceleration; the permission path checks its interior speed, acceleration, jerk, torque, and clearance.

```{python}
#| label: calc-planning-c2-stop-clearance
#| echo: false
#| warning: false
#| message: false
# ┌─────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────
# │ C2 STOP SUFFIX ON THE WAREHOUSE MOBILE MANIPULATOR
# ├─────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────
# │ Context: @sec-planning-behavior-seam (arm case, base budget row, commitment
# │          counterfactual, checkpoint), @sec-planning-summary.
# │
# │ Goal:    Size the jerk-limited S-curve suffix for the arm and the base and
# │          add its term to the base's stopping budget.
# │ Show:    Arm 137.5 mm / 275 ms suffix and 102.5 mm margin; a lease run
# │          200 ms past commitment breaches the 300 mm clearance by 97.5 mm;
# │          base jerk bound 7.11 m/s^3 (the reference polynomial's peak at
# │          1.5 m/s and 2 m/s^2); base S-curve 1031.25 ms / 773.44 mm at
# │          1.5 m/s vs. 843.75 mm for the polynomial; +210.94 mm, running
# │          total 1123.84 mm, 23.84 mm past 1.10 m.
# │ How:     RM/AISLE registry fields; calc_c2_stop_suffix for the reference
# │          polynomial's peak jerk; calc_scurve_stop_distance and
# │          calc_scurve_stop_time for each suffix; calc_safe_stopping_distance
# │          with a_brake for the Ch8 total.
# │
# │ Note:    No aisle-speed value appears here; @sec-enforcement owns the
# │          candidate-speed calculation and outstanding qualification budget.
# └─────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────
from mlsysim import *
from mlsysim.core.units import millisecond, meter, millimeter, second
from mlsysim.fmt import check, fmt_latency, fmt_length, fmt_velocity, fmt_acceleration, fmt_jerk

RM = Embodied.MobileManipulator.WarehouseMobileManipulator
AISLE = Embodied.Scenario.WarehouseAisle

class PlanningC2Stop:
    """Jerk-limited stop suffix for the machine's arm and base, and the budget row it adds."""

    # ┌── 1. LOAD (Constants) ──────────────────────
    # Arm: free-space stop from the machine's TCP speed limit.
    v_arm = RM.tcp_speed_limit  # category: chosen; registry
    a_arm_peak = PlanningLeaseRule.a_arm_stop  # category: illustrative; calc-planning-lease-rule
    j_arm = PlanningLeaseRule.j_arm_stop  # category: derived; reference polynomial's peak jerk
    t_blend = PlanningArmTimeline.t_blend  # category: chosen; calc-planning-arm-timeline
    t_commit = PlanningArmTimeline.t_commit  # category: chosen
    t_plan_exp = PlanningArmTimeline.t_plan_exp  # category: derived
    t_arm_stop = PlanningArmTimeline.t_stop  # category: derived; S-curve duration
    d_arm_clear = PlanningLeaseRule.d_arm_clear  # category: illustrative; obstacle clearance, calc-planning-lease-rule
    t_wait = 200 * millisecond  # category: illustrative; tracking authority run past commitment
    # Base: the stop at the rack end.
    v_drive = RM.base.max_velocity  # category: illustrative; registry drive limit
    a_brake = AISLE.a_brake  # category: illustrative; credible deceleration, loaded, dry floor
    tau_delay = AISLE.tau_delay  # category: derived; pre-brake delay, excl. dispatch-to-admission
    delta_loc = AISLE.delta_loc  # category: illustrative
    delta_margin = AISLE.delta_margin  # category: chosen
    d_clear = AISLE.d_clear  # category: illustrative; rack-end clear distance

    # ┌── 2. EXECUTE (The Compute) ─────────────────
    arm_stop_dist = calc_scurve_stop_distance(v_arm, a_arm_peak, j_arm).to(millimeter)
    arm_poly_dist = calc_c2_stop_suffix(v_arm, a_arm_peak)["distance"].to(millimeter)
    arm_cruise = (v_arm * (t_commit - t_blend)).to(millimeter)
    arm_total = arm_cruise + arm_stop_dist
    arm_margin = d_arm_clear - arm_total
    t_stop_end = (t_commit + t_arm_stop).to(millisecond)
    late_cruise_arm = (v_arm * t_wait).to(millimeter)
    late_breach_arm = late_cruise_arm - arm_margin

    poly_drive = calc_c2_stop_suffix(v_drive, a_brake)
    j_base = poly_drive["peak_jerk"].to(meter / second**3)  # jerk bound: reference polynomial's peak
    v_plateau = (a_brake**2 / j_base).to(meter / second)
    s_drive_time = calc_scurve_stop_time(v_drive, a_brake, j_base).to(millisecond)
    s_drive_dist = calc_scurve_stop_distance(v_drive, a_brake, j_base).to(millimeter)
    poly_drive_dist = poly_drive["distance"].to(millimeter)
    brake_const = (v_drive**2 / (2 * a_brake)).to(millimeter)
    ramp_delay = (a_brake / (2 * j_base)).to(millisecond)
    t_const_drive = (v_drive / a_brake).to(millisecond)
    c2_increment = s_drive_dist - brake_const
    total_prev = calc_safe_stopping_distance(v_drive, tau_delay, a_brake, delta_loc, delta_margin).to(millimeter)
    total_new = total_prev + c2_increment
    excess = total_new - d_clear.to(millimeter)

    # ┌── 3. GUARD (Invariants) ────────────────────
    check(abs(a_arm_peak.to(meter / second**2).magnitude - 5.0) < 1e-9, "arm suffix peak changed")
    check(abs(t_arm_stop.to(millisecond).magnitude - 275.0) < 1e-9, "arm suffix duration changed")
    check(abs(arm_stop_dist.magnitude - 137.5) < 1e-9, "arm suffix distance changed")
    check(abs(arm_poly_dist.magnitude - 150.0) < 1e-9, "arm reference polynomial distance changed")
    check(abs(arm_cruise.magnitude - 60.0) < 1e-9, "arm pre-onset cruise changed")
    check(abs(arm_margin.magnitude - 102.5) < 1e-9, "arm clearance margin changed")
    check(abs(t_stop_end.magnitude - 575.0) < 1e-9, "arm stop end changed")
    check(t_stop_end == PlanningArmTimeline.t_stop_end, "C2 arm stop end disagrees with the timeline cell")
    check(t_blend < t_commit < t_plan_exp < t_stop_end, "arm deadline order broken")
    check(
        abs(arm_stop_dist.magnitude - PlanningLeaseRule.arm_stop_dist.to(millimeter).magnitude) < 1e-9,
        "arm stop disagrees with the lease-rule cell",
    )
    check(
        abs(arm_margin.magnitude - PlanningLeaseRule.commit_margin.to(millimeter).magnitude) < 1e-9,
        "arm margin disagrees with the lease-rule cell",
    )
    check(abs(late_cruise_arm.magnitude - 200.0) < 1e-9, "late-commitment arm cruise changed")
    check(abs(late_breach_arm.magnitude - 97.5) < 1e-9, "late-commitment arm breach changed")
    check(abs(j_base.magnitude - 64.0 / 9.0) < 1e-9, "base jerk bound changed")
    check(v_drive >= v_plateau, "drive-limit stop no longer reaches the deceleration bound")
    check(abs(s_drive_time.magnitude - 1031.25) < 1e-9, "S-curve duration at drive limit changed")
    check(abs(s_drive_dist.magnitude - 773.4375) < 1e-9, "S-curve distance at drive limit changed")
    check(abs(poly_drive_dist.magnitude - 843.75) < 1e-9, "reference polynomial distance at drive limit changed")
    check(abs(brake_const.magnitude - 562.5) < 1e-9, "constant-deceleration braking changed")
    check(abs(t_const_drive.magnitude - 750.0) < 1e-9, "constant-deceleration stop time changed")
    check(abs(c2_increment.magnitude - 210.9375) < 1e-9, "S-curve budget increment changed")
    check(abs(total_prev.magnitude - 912.9) < 5e-3, "Ch8 running total changed")
    check(abs(total_new.magnitude - 1123.8375) < 5e-3, "Ch11 running total changed")
    check(abs(excess.magnitude - 23.8375) < 5e-3, "excess over clear distance changed")
    check(excess.magnitude > 0, "drive limit no longer exceeds the rack-end clear distance")

    # ┌── 4. OUTPUT (Formatting) ───────────────────
    v_arm_str = fmt_velocity(v_arm)
    t_blend_str = fmt_latency(t_blend, unit=millisecond)
    t_commit_str = fmt_latency(t_commit, unit=millisecond)
    t_plan_exp_str = fmt_latency(t_plan_exp, unit=millisecond)
    t_stop_end_str = fmt_latency(t_stop_end, unit=millisecond)
    t_arm_stop_str = fmt_latency(t_arm_stop, unit=millisecond)
    a_arm_peak_str = fmt_acceleration(a_arm_peak)
    j_arm_str = fmt_jerk(j_arm, precision=1)
    arm_stop_dist_str = fmt_length(arm_stop_dist, unit=millimeter, precision=1)
    arm_poly_dist_str = fmt_length(arm_poly_dist, unit=millimeter)
    arm_cruise_str = fmt_length(arm_cruise, unit=millimeter)
    arm_total_str = fmt_length(arm_total, unit=millimeter, precision=1)
    arm_margin_str = fmt_length(arm_margin, unit=millimeter, precision=1)
    d_arm_clear_str = fmt_length(d_arm_clear, unit=millimeter)
    v_drive_str = fmt_velocity(v_drive)
    a_brake_str = fmt_acceleration(a_brake)
    j_base_str = fmt_jerk(j_base, precision=2)
    v_plateau_str = fmt_velocity(v_plateau, precision=4)
    s_drive_time_str = fmt_latency(s_drive_time, unit=millisecond, precision=2, commas=True)
    s_drive_dist_str = fmt_length(s_drive_dist, unit=millimeter, precision=2)
    poly_drive_dist_str = fmt_length(poly_drive_dist, unit=millimeter, precision=2)
    brake_const_str = fmt_length(brake_const, unit=millimeter, precision=1)
    ramp_delay_str = fmt_latency(ramp_delay, unit=millisecond, precision=1)
    t_const_drive_str = fmt_latency(t_const_drive, unit=millisecond)
    c2_increment_str = fmt_length(c2_increment, unit=millimeter, precision=2)
    total_prev_str = fmt_length(total_prev, unit=millimeter, precision=1)
    total_new_str = fmt_length(total_new, unit=millimeter, precision=2)
    d_clear_str = fmt_length(d_clear, unit=meter, precision=2)
    excess_str = fmt_length(excess, unit=millimeter, precision=2)
    t_wait_str = fmt_latency(t_wait, unit=millisecond)
    late_cruise_arm_str = fmt_length(late_cruise_arm, unit=millimeter)
    late_breach_arm_str = fmt_length(late_breach_arm, unit=millimeter, precision=1)
```

In the alternate longer-lease arm case, the blend deadline is `{python} PlanningC2Stop.t_blend_str`, matched commitment `{python} PlanningC2Stop.t_commit_str`, nominal setpoint end `{python} PlanningC2Stop.t_plan_exp_str`, and stop end `{python} PlanningC2Stop.t_stop_end_str`, so the stop lasts `{python} PlanningC2Stop.t_arm_stop_str`. At the arm's `{python} PlanningC2Stop.v_arm_str` TCP speed limit, the S-curve suffix with a `{python} PlanningC2Stop.a_arm_peak_str` deceleration bound and a `{python} PlanningC2Stop.j_arm_str` jerk bound travels `{python} PlanningC2Stop.arm_stop_dist_str`, compared with `{python} PlanningC2Stop.arm_poly_dist_str` for the polynomial of @eq-plan-c2-polynomial-stop with the same peaks. Because the blend deadline is the preferred admission instant on this schedule, the last scheduled validation and clearance evidence finish at `{python} PlanningC2Stop.t_blend_str`, which means the `{python} PlanningC2Stop.arm_cruise_str` of cruise between `{python} PlanningC2Stop.t_blend_str` and physical brake onset at `{python} PlanningC2Stop.t_commit_str` must be charged against that clearance alongside the stop, consuming `{python} PlanningC2Stop.arm_total_str` in all and leaving `{python} PlanningC2Stop.arm_margin_str` of the `{python} PlanningC2Stop.d_arm_clear_str` obstacle clearance before sensing and model error are deducted. Because `{python} PlanningC2Stop.t_commit_str` is **physical suffix onset**, the MCU must close replacement admission and pretrigger any communication or actuator delay $\UnreservedStopDelay$ by that instant minus $\UnreservedStopDelay$; otherwise, the arm travels an extra $\CruiseSpeed\UnreservedStopDelay$, shifts the stop end later, and shrinks the `{python} PlanningC2Stop.arm_margin_str` margin. Nominal setpoints end at `{python} PlanningC2Stop.t_plan_exp_str` while MCU STOP continues to `{python} PlanningC2Stop.t_stop_end_str`, assuming fresh target evidence keeps TRACK valid until stop dispatch (@sec-planning-goal-to-trajectory).

On the running machine, as the alternate schedule's introduction noted, a stall never reaches commitment because the chunk lease lapses first, so its stop is the state-matched fallback. From zero-acceleration cruise the S-curve matches the arm at whatever instant it starts, and it slows the tool along the path already checked, so the state-matched fallback travels the same distance as the matched stop suffix. On the arm, as on the base, the chunk lease is a term of the stopping budget, the rule established in @sec-nervous-lease-sizing; the arm's own speed, stop, and clearance set what that term costs.

```{python}
#| label: calc-planning-stall-runway
#| echo: false
#| warning: false
#| message: false
# ┌─────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────
# │ THE STALL RUNWAY: LEASE PATH PLUS S-CURVE STOP FOR THE ARM
# ├─────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────
# │ Context: nbk-planning-stall-runway in @sec-planning-c2-stopping-suffix.
# │
# │ Goal:    Put the arm's stall arithmetic on the page: response path, the
# │          S-curve branch test and its two terms, and the remaining margin.
# │ Show:    60 + 1 + 1 + 20 = 82 ms, 82 mm; a^2/j = 0.375 m/s < 1.0 m/s;
# │          100 + 37.5 = 137.5 mm in 200 + 75 = 275 ms; 219.5 of 300 mm,
# │          80.5 mm left; response path 59.6 percent of the stop; the margin
# │          equals 80.5 ms of further lease at the TCP limit.
# │ How:     Reads PlanningLeaseRule; the two S-curve terms are
# │          eq-plan-c2-stopping-suffix and are guarded against
# │          calc_scurve_stop_distance / calc_scurve_stop_time.
# └─────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────
from mlsysim.core.units import millisecond, meter, millimeter, second
from mlsysim.fmt import check, fmt_latency, fmt_length, fmt_velocity, fmt_acceleration, fmt_jerk, fmt_percent

class PlanningStallRunway:
    """Worked stall case for the arm: lease path, S-curve stop, and margin."""

    # ┌── 1. LOAD (Constants) ──────────────────────
    LR = PlanningLeaseRule  # category: derived; calc-planning-lease-rule
    v = LR.v_arm  # category: chosen; TCP limit, registry
    a = LR.a_arm_stop  # category: illustrative; arm stop deceleration bound
    j = LR.j_arm_stop  # category: derived; reference polynomial's peak jerk

    # ┌── 2. EXECUTE (The Compute) ─────────────────
    v_thresh = (a**2 / j).to(meter / second)
    d_brake = (v**2 / (2 * a)).to(millimeter)
    d_ramp = (v * a / (2 * j)).to(millimeter)
    t_brake = (v / a).to(millisecond)
    t_ramp = (a / j).to(millisecond)
    path_share = (LR.d_lease_path / LR.arm_stop_dist).to("dimensionless").magnitude
    t_margin = (LR.lease_margin / v).to(millisecond)

    # ┌── 3. GUARD (Invariants) ────────────────────
    check(v >= v_thresh, "arm stop no longer reaches the deceleration bound (plateau branch)")
    check(abs((d_brake + d_ramp - LR.arm_stop_dist).to(millimeter).magnitude) < 1e-9, "S-curve terms disagree with calc_scurve_stop_distance")
    check(abs((t_brake + t_ramp - LR.t_arm_stop).to(millisecond).magnitude) < 1e-9, "S-curve times disagree with calc_scurve_stop_time")
    check(abs(d_brake.magnitude - 100.0) < 1e-9 and abs(d_ramp.magnitude - 37.5) < 1e-9, "stall-runway stop terms changed")
    check(abs(path_share - 82.0 / 137.5) < 1e-9, "response-path share changed")
    check(abs(t_margin.magnitude - 80.5) < 1e-9, "margin in lease milliseconds changed")

    # ┌── 4. OUTPUT (Formatting) ───────────────────
    t_tick_str = fmt_latency(LR.t_tick.to(millisecond), unit=millisecond)
    t_bus_str = fmt_latency(LR.t_bus.to(millisecond), unit=millisecond)
    t_onset_str = fmt_latency(LR.t_onset.to(millisecond), unit=millisecond)
    a_str = fmt_acceleration(a)
    j_str = fmt_jerk(j, precision=1)
    v_thresh_str = fmt_velocity(v_thresh, precision=3)
    d_brake_str = fmt_length(d_brake, unit=millimeter)
    d_ramp_str = fmt_length(d_ramp, unit=millimeter, precision=1)
    t_brake_str = fmt_latency(t_brake, unit=millisecond)
    t_ramp_str = fmt_latency(t_ramp, unit=millisecond)
    t_stop_str = fmt_latency(LR.t_arm_stop, unit=millisecond)
    path_share_str = fmt_percent(path_share, precision=1, style="prose")
    t_margin_str = fmt_latency(t_margin, unit=millisecond, precision=1)
```

::: {#nbk-planning-stall-runway .callout-notebook title="The stall runway"}

**Problem**: The proposer stalls while the arm reaches at its TCP limit, and no replacement is admitted. How much of the obstacle clearance does the arm use between its last admission and rest, and how much remains?

**Variables**:

- Chunk lease $\ChunkLease =$ `{python} PlanningLeaseRule.t_lease_str` (chosen); permission tick `{python} PlanningStallRunway.t_tick_str` (derived) and bus cycle `{python} PlanningStallRunway.t_bus_str` (illustrative); onset `{python} PlanningStallRunway.t_onset_str` (illustrative, the base's registered brake onset charged conservatively to the arm)
- Speed $\SpeedAtDetection =$ `{python} PlanningLeaseRule.v_arm_str` (chosen, TCP limit)
- Deceleration bound $\ProfileAccelerationBound =$ `{python} PlanningStallRunway.a_str` (illustrative) and jerk bound $\JerkLimit =$ `{python} PlanningStallRunway.j_str` (derived, the peak jerk of @eq-plan-c2-polynomial-stop at the same peak)
- Clearance $\ClearDistance =$ `{python} PlanningLeaseRule.d_arm_clear_str` (illustrative)

**Math**:

1. **Response path**: `{python} PlanningLeaseRule.t_lease_str` $+$ `{python} PlanningStallRunway.t_tick_str` $+$ `{python} PlanningStallRunway.t_bus_str` $+$ `{python} PlanningStallRunway.t_onset_str` $=$ `{python} PlanningLeaseRule.t_lease_path_str` from last admission to stop onset, which is `{python} PlanningLeaseRule.d_lease_path_str` at $\SpeedAtDetection$.
2. **Branch test** (@eq-plan-c2-stopping-suffix): $\ProfileAccelerationBound^2/\JerkLimit =$ `{python} PlanningStallRunway.v_thresh_str`, below $\SpeedAtDetection$, so the stop reaches $\ProfileAccelerationBound$.
3. **Stop**: $\SpeedAtDetection^2/2\ProfileAccelerationBound + \SpeedAtDetection\,\ProfileAccelerationBound/2\JerkLimit =$ `{python} PlanningStallRunway.d_brake_str` $+$ `{python} PlanningStallRunway.d_ramp_str` $=$ `{python} PlanningLeaseRule.arm_stop_dist_str`, in $\SpeedAtDetection/\ProfileAccelerationBound + \ProfileAccelerationBound/\JerkLimit =$ `{python} PlanningStallRunway.t_brake_str` $+$ `{python} PlanningStallRunway.t_ramp_str` $=$ `{python} PlanningStallRunway.t_stop_str`.
4. **Clearance**: `{python} PlanningLeaseRule.d_lease_path_str` $+$ `{python} PlanningLeaseRule.arm_stop_dist_str` $=$ `{python} PlanningLeaseRule.lease_total_str` of `{python} PlanningLeaseRule.d_arm_clear_str`.

**Result**: The stall leaves `{python} PlanningLeaseRule.lease_margin_str` of geometric margin, before sensing and model reserves.

**Systems insight**: The travel before the stop begins is `{python} PlanningStallRunway.path_share_str` of the stop itself, and at this speed every millisecond of lease costs a millimeter. The remaining margin equals only `{python} PlanningStallRunway.t_margin_str` of further lease, so the lease length is a term of $\StoppingDistance \le \ClearDistance$ exactly as the deceleration bound is.

:::

While hardware qualification must establish the arm's actual response in place of the charged onset allowance, the two schedules leave different geometric margins because they date their clearance evidence differently (@fig-11-seam-timeline-fallback). Whereas the running lease charges travel from the last admission (`{python} PlanningLeaseRule.d_lease_path_str`) plus the `{python} PlanningLeaseRule.arm_stop_dist_str` stop to keep `{python} PlanningLeaseRule.lease_margin_str`, the alternate schedule charges only the cruise from its blend deadline, when clearance was last checked, to commitment (`{python} PlanningC2Stop.arm_cruise_str`) plus the same stop to keep `{python} PlanningLeaseRule.commit_margin_str`. The alternate schedule's `{python} PlanningLeaseRule.t_alt_admission_cutoff_str` admission cutoff is therefore an offset on its own time axis rather than a lease length that the running clearance could support; any lease, whatever its length, must fit its own evidence age, response travel, stop, and uncertainty reserve, just as the running lease does in the notebook above.

```{python}
#| label: calc-planning-mug-spill
#| echo: false
#| warning: false
#| message: false
# ┌─────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────
# │ DOES THE ARM STOP SPILL AN OPEN MUG?
# ├─────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────
# │ Context: @sec-planning-c2-stopping-suffix (carrying paragraph).
# │
# │ Goal:    Check the free-space arm stop against the quasi-static tilt of a
# │          liquid surface, and size the carry speed that fits the lease path.
# │ Show:    5 m/s^2 raises the liquid 20.4 mm at a 40 mm radius (> 10 mm
# │          freeboard); a <= g h_f / R = 2.45 m/s^2; stop from 1.0 m/s at that
# │          bound 280.4 mm; with 82 mm lease path 362.4 mm > 300 mm; fitting
# │          carry speed 0.885 m/s.
# │ How:     calc_quasistatic_spill_acceleration (free surface normal to
# │          effective gravity, tan theta = a / g);
# │          illustrative mug geometry; jerk bound = reference polynomial's peak
# │          at the same peak and the TCP limit, as for the free-space stop;
# │          calc_scurve_stop_distance and calc_scurve_max_permitted_velocity.
# └─────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────
from mlsysim import *
from mlsysim.core.units import millisecond, meter, millimeter, second, standard_gravity
from mlsysim.physics.robotics import calc_quasistatic_spill_acceleration
from mlsysim.fmt import check, fmt_length, fmt_acceleration, fmt_velocity

class PlanningMugSpill:
    """Quasi-static spill bound for an open mug and the carry speed it implies."""

    # ┌── 1. LOAD (Constants) ──────────────────────
    r_mug = 40 * millimeter  # category: illustrative; inner radius of the mug
    h_free = 10 * millimeter  # category: illustrative; liquid surface below the rim
    a_free = PlanningLeaseRule.a_arm_stop  # category: illustrative; free-space arm stop bound
    v_arm = PlanningLeaseRule.v_arm  # category: chosen; TCP limit, registry
    t_path = PlanningLeaseRule.t_lease_path  # category: derived; lease lapse plus dispatch
    d_clear = PlanningLeaseRule.d_arm_clear  # category: illustrative; obstacle clearance
    g0 = standard_gravity  # category: definitional

    # ┌── 2. EXECUTE (The Compute) ─────────────────
    rise_free = (r_mug * a_free / g0).to(millimeter)
    a_mug = calc_quasistatic_spill_acceleration(r_mug, h_free)
    j_mug = calc_c2_stop_suffix(v_arm, a_mug)["peak_jerk"]
    d_mug = calc_scurve_stop_distance(v_arm, a_mug, j_mug).to(millimeter)
    d_mug_total = (v_arm * t_path).to(millimeter) + d_mug
    v_carry = calc_scurve_max_permitted_velocity(d_clear, t_path, a_mug, j_mug, 0 * meter, 0 * meter).to(meter / second)

    # ┌── 3. GUARD (Invariants) ────────────────────
    check(rise_free > h_free, "free-space stop no longer tips the surface past the rim")
    check(abs(a_mug.magnitude - 2.4517) < 1e-4, "quasi-static spill bound changed")
    check(abs(d_mug.magnitude - 280.42) < 0.01, "mug-limited stop distance changed")
    check(d_mug_total > d_clear, "mug-limited stop now fits at the TCP limit")
    check(abs(v_carry.magnitude - 0.885) < 1e-3, "fitting carry speed changed")
    # margin_mug_carry_clearance_envelope.svg fig-alt hand-types 219.5, 362.4 and 300 mm.
    check(
        [
            round(PlanningLeaseRule.lease_total.to(millimeter).magnitude, 1),
            round(d_mug_total.magnitude, 1),
            round(d_clear.to(millimeter).magnitude),
        ]
        == [219.5, 362.4, 300],
        "mug-carry margin fig-alt values are stale",
    )

    # ┌── 4. OUTPUT (Formatting) ───────────────────
    r_mug_str = fmt_length(r_mug, unit=millimeter)
    h_free_str = fmt_length(h_free, unit=millimeter)
    a_free_str = fmt_acceleration(a_free)
    rise_free_str = fmt_length(rise_free, unit=millimeter, precision=1)
    a_mug_str = fmt_acceleration(a_mug, precision=2)
    d_mug_str = fmt_length(d_mug, unit=millimeter, precision=1)
    d_mug_total_str = fmt_length(d_mug_total, unit=millimeter, precision=1)
    v_carry_str = fmt_velocity(v_carry, precision=2)
```

Although the free-space deceleration bound suits the empty-gripper reach toward the mug, it is too aggressive once the arm carries an open mug of liquid away from the conveyor, because container acceleration tilts the free surface and excites sloshing [@mayer2012walking]. Under a steady deceleration $\SteadyDeceleration$, the free surface settles perpendicular to the effective gravity, tilting by $\tan\FreeSurfaceTiltAngle = \SteadyDeceleration/\Gravity$ and raising the liquid at the wall by $\ContainerInnerRadius\,\SteadyDeceleration/\Gravity$ for inner radius $\ContainerInnerRadius$. In an illustrative mug of `{python} PlanningMugSpill.r_mug_str` inner radius filled to `{python} PlanningMugSpill.h_free_str` below the rim, the free-space stop's `{python} PlanningMugSpill.a_free_str` deceleration raises the liquid `{python} PlanningMugSpill.rise_free_str` at the wall, well past the rim. Keeping even the steady tilt inside the freeboard $\FreeboardHeight$ (a necessary condition, since dynamic sloshing overshoots the steady tilt) limits deceleration to $\Gravity\,\FreeboardHeight/\ContainerInnerRadius$, or `{python} PlanningMugSpill.a_mug_str`. At that gentler bound, with the jerk the polynomial reaches at the same peak, the stop from the `{python} PlanningLeaseRule.v_arm_str` TCP limit lengthens to `{python} PlanningMugSpill.d_mug_str` and, together with the running lease path, demands `{python} PlanningMugSpill.d_mug_total_str` of the `{python} PlanningLeaseRule.d_arm_clear_str` clearance. The loaded carry must therefore run slower than the empty reach: before sensing and model reserves are deducted, the highest speed whose lease path and stop fit that clearance is `{python} PlanningMugSpill.v_carry_str`, and the trajectory record's assumption sidecar must declare which payload regime and measured slosh limit (or lid) the record assumes.

::: {.column-margin}
![](images/svg/margin_mug_carry_clearance_envelope.svg){width="100%" fig-alt="Two horizontal distance bars against a red line at the 300 millimeter clearance: the empty-gripper lease path and stop at 219.5 millimeters, inside the line, and the open-mug lease path and gentler stop at 362.4 millimeters, past it."}

*At the TCP limit, the open mug's gentler stop overruns the clearance the empty reach fits.*
:::

The commitment deadline forbids waiting. In the alternate arm schedule, commitment preserves the `{python} PlanningC2Stop.arm_margin_str` margin computed from clearance dated at `{python} PlanningC2Stop.t_blend_str`. Missing the `{python} PlanningLeaseRule.t_alt_admission_cutoff_str` admission cutoff and delaying stop dispatch by `{python} PlanningC2Stop.t_wait_str` would delay physical stop onset that far past commitment, and cruise at the TCP limit would add `{python} PlanningC2Stop.late_cruise_arm_str` before the same stop and breach the `{python} PlanningC2Stop.d_arm_clear_str` clearance by `{python} PlanningC2Stop.late_breach_arm_str`. A later stop must still match its actual entry state; this counterfactual holds cruise speed constant only to show the lost clearance. An arm that waits that long may already occupy a state from which no admissible control avoids the obstacle.

### Inevitable collision states {#sec-planning-inevitable-collision-states}

An arm or base that is still clear of every obstacle at the current millisecond can already be doomed to hit one if its speed and remaining distance leave no control input inside its drive and traction limits that can bring it to rest in time. Classical path planning misses this trap when it treats obstacle avoidance as a static geometric query that asks only whether the robot's configuration overlaps an obstacle volume at the current instant. Because a mobile manipulator moving with momentum and finite braking torque cannot halt instantaneously, its dynamic state (position, velocity, and acceleration, under its traction limits) can cross a boundary beyond which every admissible control trajectory leads to collision long before geometric contact occurs. Such states are inevitable collision states (ICS)[^fn-ics-viability-kernel] [@fraichard2004inevitable].

::: {#dfn-planning-inevitable-collision-state .callout-definition title="Inevitable collision state"}

***Inevitable collision state***\index{Inevitable collision state!definition}\index{Collision avoidance!inevitable collision state} (ICS) is any dynamic plant state $\MechanicalPlantState(\TimeInstant) \in \PlantStateSpace$ from which every physically admissible future control trajectory $\FutureControlTrajectory \in \AdmissibleControlSet$ inevitably produces collision with an obstacle or constraint boundary:
$$\MechanicalPlantState \in \text{ICS}(\ObstacleStateSet) \iff \forall \ControlInput(\cdot) \in \AdmissibleControlSet, \; \exists \FutureTimeInstant \ge \TimeInstant \text{ such that } \MechanicalPlantState(\FutureTimeInstant) \in \ObstacleStateSet$$
where $\AdmissibleControlSet$ denotes the admissible control input set bounded by actuator torque, traction, and deceleration limits.

1.  **Significance**: Sets the commitment deadline $\CommitmentInstant$ in receding-horizon planning; continuing nominal motion past it without an admitted successor can carry the plant into an ICS, and no later replanning can bring it back out.
2.  **Distinction**: Unlike static geometric collision checks that evaluate only instantaneous spatial overlap ($\MechanicalPlantState \in \ObstacleStateSet$), an ICS identifies dynamically trapped states where current momentum and finite braking torque make future boundary breach physically unavoidable.
3.  **Common pitfall**: Delaying emergency braking in the expectation that an overdue neural planner will complete an evasive path, ignoring that moving mass enters an ICS long before geometric contact occurs.

:::

[^fn-ics-viability-kernel]: **Inevitable collision states and viability**\index{Viability kernel!inevitable collision states}: Within the free states, the complement of the ICS set is what @aubin1991viability calls the viability kernel, the states from which some admissible control keeps the system inside its constraints forever. Planning must therefore keep the commitment state inside that kernel, not merely outside the obstacle, and against static obstacles a verified stop to rest is the witness that it is there.

The commitment deadline $\CommitmentInstant$ and the admission-checked stopping suffix are co-designed precisely so that the machine initiates braking *before* its dynamic state enters an inevitable collision state, $\text{ICS}(\ObstacleStateSet)$. If an action chunk's stopping suffix requires distance $\StoppingDistance > \ClearDistance$, that suffix cannot justify admitting the chunk. Failure of this particular stop does not establish that every admissible maneuver collides, as the definition of an inevitable collision state requires. The architecture nevertheless refuses the proposal because it lacks the independently executable stop on which its permission depends. The safety microcontroller therefore enforces the hard admission invariant:
$$\StoppingDistance(\CommitmentInstant) \le \ClearDistance(\CommitmentInstant)$$ {#eq-plan-commitment-invariant}
If the controller delays braking past commitment in the hope that an overdue neural replanner will deliver an evasive path, physical momentum can carry the machine into an ICS from which no admissible control input can prevent impact. The commitment deadline is the deadline form of this boundary, fixed at planning time. Its set form, the recoverable set of plant states from which the resident stop still succeeds, is the stopping envelope that @sec-enforcement-stopping-envelopes develops for the runtime check.

These deadlines and the stop they protect are fixed at admission, before motion begins. The candidate declares payload, contact, effort, and obstacle assumptions. The MCU first validates its fixed header and lineage, then checks the complete bounded trajectory and suffix, including the seam $(\JointPosition,\JointVelocity,\JointAcceleration)$ against the reachable state envelope from its current estimate, interior extrema, clearance, stopping distance, and a feasible response from every state reachable through physical stop onset. A scan over $\TrajectorySampleCount$ setpoints is $\mathcal{O}(\TrajectorySampleCount)$, even with a fixed maximum $\TrajectorySampleCount$ and measured worst-case execution time; after admission, a distinct $\mathcal{O}(1)$ per-tick check reads the current state and local reference. A replacement received after the blend deadline passes the same check with a compressed bridge, whose higher acceleration and torque its extrema must still clear, and if the check cannot finish before the earlier admission cutoff, the MCU retains the current record only while its own lease, evidence, and fallback remain valid. A candidate received after commitment cannot restore the spent runway.

The planner proposes the suffix, but the MCU latches the validated payload and stop profile into protected memory **before** enabling TRACK and dispatches that resident path before commitment without reading host DRAM, so a host crash, bus stall, or corrupted shared packet cannot erase the stop. If the measured state falls outside the latched suffix's entry region, the MCU uses the state-matched fallback; torque disable or a spring brake is not a universal substitute for a controlled stop, especially with a suspended load (@sec-enforcement-fallback-ladder).

### Base stopping budget under jerk-limited deceleration {#sec-planning-base-stopping-budget}

On the mobile base approaching the rack end at its `{python} PlanningC2Stop.v_drive_str` drive limit, the loaded tote rack tolerates the machine's credible `{python} PlanningC2Stop.a_brake_str` deceleration only when that deceleration is ramped gradually rather than applied as an abrupt step. The base's stop is therefore the S-curve of @eq-plan-c2-stopping-suffix with $\ProfileAccelerationBound$ at `{python} PlanningC2Stop.a_brake_str` and a jerk bound of `{python} PlanningC2Stop.j_base_str`, the peak jerk of the polynomial stop from the `{python} PlanningC2Stop.v_drive_str` drive limit and the stop jerk bound already listed on the machine card (@tbl-01-machine-card), under which every speed above `{python} PlanningC2Stop.v_plateau_str` reaches the deceleration plateau. At the drive limit, this suffix lasts `{python} PlanningC2Stop.s_drive_time_str` and travels `{python} PlanningC2Stop.s_drive_dist_str`, compared with `{python} PlanningC2Stop.brake_const_str` for constant-deceleration braking in @eq-body-stopping-distance and `{python} PlanningC2Stop.poly_drive_dist_str` for the polynomial with the same peaks. Because the jerk ramps cost the equivalent of `{python} PlanningC2Stop.ramp_delay_str` of cruise, the suffix adds `{python} PlanningC2Stop.c2_increment_str` to the budget that @sec-perception-latency-waterfall left at `{python} PlanningC2Stop.total_prev_str`, raising the running total to `{python} PlanningC2Stop.total_new_str` and exceeding the `{python} PlanningC2Stop.d_clear_str` rack-end clear distance by `{python} PlanningC2Stop.excess_str`. Because this partial total still omits the unqualified dispatch-to-admission interval, which can only add travel, the `{python} PlanningC2Stop.excess_str` overrun is a conditional design deficit rather than a complete measured response bound.

Plotted as velocity against time, the area under each curve is its stopping distance, and the jerk ramps appear as the rounded start and finish that stretch the S-curve and the polynomial past the constant-deceleration line (@fig-11-stopping-profiles). Stacked onto the budget's other terms, only the constant-deceleration stop, which no drive can execute, ends inside the `{python} PlanningC2Stop.d_clear_str` rack-end clearance.

::: {#fig-11-stopping-profiles fig-env="figure" fig-pos="t" fig-cap="**Three stops from the drive limit**: Velocity against time for the base's stop from `{python} PlanningC2Stop.v_drive_str` under the same `{python} PlanningC2Stop.a_brake_str` deceleration bound (a), and each stop added to the budget's other terms against the `{python} PlanningC2Stop.d_clear_str` rack-end clearance (b). The area under each velocity curve is its stopping distance. Constant deceleration, which no drive can execute, fits with `{python} PlanningC2Stop.brake_const_str` of braking; the jerk-limited S-curve, the shortest stop under the stipulated bounds, needs `{python} PlanningC2Stop.s_drive_dist_str` and passes the clearance by `{python} PlanningC2Stop.excess_str`; the polynomial with the same peaks needs `{python} PlanningC2Stop.poly_drive_dist_str`." fig-alt="Two stacked panels. Top panel a: three velocity curves falling from 1.5 meters per second to zero. A straight line reaches zero at 750 milliseconds, an S-shaped curve with a straight middle at about 1,031 milliseconds, and a smooth curve at 1,125 milliseconds. Bottom panel b: three horizontal stacked bars, each with a gray segment for the other budget terms and a colored segment for the stop, against a dashed vertical line at 1.10 meters. The constant-deceleration bar ends before the line; the S-curve and polynomial bars cross it, with the overrun hatched."}

```{python}
#| label: plot-planning-stopping-profiles
#| echo: false
#| warning: false
#| message: false
# ┌─────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────
# │ CONSTANT, S-CURVE, AND POLYNOMIAL STOPS FROM THE DRIVE LIMIT
# ├─────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────
# │ Context: @fig-11-stopping-profiles.
# │
# │ Goal:    Show why the stop's shape sets its distance and how the chosen
# │          S-curve pushes the rack-end budget past the clearance.
# │ Show:    1.5 m/s, 2 m/s^2, j = 7.11 m/s^3; 750 / 1031.25 / 1125 ms;
# │          562.5 / 773.44 / 843.75 mm; totals 912.9 / 1123.84 / 1194.15 mm
# │          against 1.10 m.
# │ How:     PlanningC2Stop values; velocity curves from the closed forms of
# │          eq-plan-c2-polynomial-stop and the double-S suffix, guarded to
# │          integrate to the cell's distances.
```
