```{python}
# └─────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────
import numpy as np
from mlsysim import viz
from mlsysim.core.units import millisecond, meter, millimeter, second
from mlsysim.fmt import check

CS = PlanningC2Stop
_v = CS.v_drive.to(meter / second).magnitude
_a = CS.a_brake.to(meter / second**2).magnitude
_j = CS.j_base.to(meter / second**3).magnitude
_mm = lambda q: q.to(millimeter).magnitude
_clear = _mm(CS.d_clear)
_other = _mm(CS.total_prev) - _mm(CS.brake_const)  # delay travel, localization, margin

_T_c = _v / _a
_T_s = CS.s_drive_time.to(second).magnitude
_T_p = 1.5 * _v / _a
t = np.linspace(0, 1.2, 6001)
v_const = np.clip(_v - _a * t, 0, None)
_tj = _a / _j
_t2 = _T_s - _tj
v_s = np.where(
    t < _tj, _v - 0.5 * _j * t**2, np.where(t < _t2, _v - 0.5 * _a * _tj - _a * (t - _tj), np.where(t < _T_s, 0.5 * _j * (_T_s - t) ** 2, 0.0))
)
u = np.clip(t / _T_p, 0, 1)
v_poly = _v * (1 - 3 * u**2 + 2 * u**3)
_dt = t[1] - t[0]
_dist = [np.trapezoid(y, dx=_dt) * 1000 for y in (v_const, v_s, v_poly)]
for _d, _ref in zip(_dist, (CS.brake_const, CS.s_drive_dist, CS.poly_drive_dist)):
    check(abs(_d - _mm(_ref)) < 0.5, "plotted stop profile no longer integrates to the cell's distance")
check(abs(_other + _mm(CS.s_drive_dist) - _mm(CS.total_new)) < 1e-6, "plotted S-curve total disagrees with the cell")

C = viz.COLORS
viz.set_book_style()
import matplotlib.pyplot as plt

fig, (ax, bx) = plt.subplots(2, 1, figsize=(6.2, 5.8), gridspec_kw=dict(hspace=0.45))
NEUT, STRUCT, PROP, SOFT = "#4A5568", "#1A4D3E", "#B87333", "#4A5568"
rows = (
    ("constant", v_const, _T_c, NEUT, "--"),
    ("S-curve", v_s, _T_s, STRUCT, "-"),
    ("polynomial", v_poly, _T_p, PROP, ":"),
)
for name, vv, T, col, ls in rows:
    ax.plot(t * 1000, vv, color=col, lw=1.6, ls=ls)
ax.text(20, 0.18, f"constant, {_T_c * 1000:,.0f} ms", color=NEUT, fontsize=9, ha="left")
ax.text(560, 1.25, f"S-curve, {_T_s * 1000:,.0f} ms", color=STRUCT, fontsize=9, ha="left")
ax.text(760, 0.90, f"polynomial,\n{_T_p * 1000:,.0f} ms", color=PROP, fontsize=9, ha="left")
ax.set_xlim(0, 1200)
ax.set_ylim(0, _v * 1.12)
ax.set_xlabel("time from brake onset (ms)", fontsize=9)
ax.set_ylabel("base speed (m/s)", fontsize=9)
ax.set_title("(a) Stop profiles", fontsize=9, loc="left")

for i, ((name, _, _, col, _), d) in enumerate(zip(rows, (_mm(CS.brake_const), _mm(CS.s_drive_dist), _mm(CS.poly_drive_dist)))):
    y = 2 - i
    bx.barh(y, _other, height=0.55, color=C["grid"], edgecolor="white", lw=0.6)
    bx.text(_other / 2, y, f"{_other:.1f}", color=C["primary"], fontsize=9, ha="center", va="center")
    bx.barh(y, d, left=_other, height=0.55, color=col, edgecolor="white", lw=0.6)
    tot = _other + d
    if tot > _clear:
        bx.barh(y, tot - _clear, left=_clear, height=0.55, facecolor="none", edgecolor=C["RedLine"], hatch="////", lw=0.8)
    bx.text(_other + d / 2, y, f"{d:.1f}" if d % 1 else f"{d:.0f}", color="white", fontsize=9, ha="center", va="center")
    bx.text(-30, y, name, fontsize=9, ha="right", va="center")
    bx.text(max(tot, _clear) + 25, y, f"{tot:,.1f}", fontsize=9, ha="left", va="center", color=C["primary"])
bx.axvline(_clear, color=C["RedLine"], lw=1.1, ls="--")
bx.text(_clear - 20, 2.6, f"rack end {_clear / 1000:.2f} m", color=C["RedLine"], fontsize=9, ha="right", va="bottom")
bx.set_xlim(0, 1450)
bx.set_ylim(-0.5, 2.9)
bx.set_yticks([])
bx.set_xlabel("distance before rest (mm)", fontsize=9)
bx.set_title("(b) Rack-end budget", fontsize=9, loc="left")
for axx in (ax, bx):
    axx.tick_params(labelsize=9)
    axx.grid(False)
    for sd in ("top", "right"):
        axx.spines[sd].set_visible(False)
bx.spines["left"].set_visible(False)
plt.show()
```

:::

Even the shortest stop under the stipulated bounds leaves a `{python} PlanningC2Stop.excess_str` deficit at the `{python} PlanningC2Stop.v_drive_str` drive limit, so the robot cannot cruise at that limit in this aisle under the stated deceleration and jerk bounds. The deficit is narrow and it rests on a stipulated jerk bound, so a measured jerk tolerance could move it in either direction. The machine must either derate its operating speed or detect the boundary with more usable clearance ahead; a longer prediction or evidence lifetime alone creates no stopping room. This is the first law's stopping condition (principle \ref{pri-vol4-irreversibility}) with one more term, because a stop the load can tolerate is a longer stop and the distance it adds comes out of the same clear distance. This calculation concerns the fixed rack-end boundary. A person entering the aisle requires separately qualified moving-actor bounds and crossing control or an operating restriction; this static clearance calculation does not establish that protection. Under the selected body and aisle constraints, reducing speed can recover clearance. @Sec-enforcement-stopping-envelopes adds the tracking allowance and derives a candidate speed; permission to operate still requires complete capture-to-admission timing, positive stopping reserve, and qualification under the declared conditions.

::: {.column-margin .margin-pointer}
↩ The intrusion distance an approaching pedestrian adds to the stopping budget, and the site controls it demands, are established in @sec-memory-belief-through-occlusion.
:::

For either body, the admission and fallback decisions in @tbl-11-seam-fallback-hierarchy are distinct from an emergency power cut.

| State                      | Trigger                                                                                           | MCU action and required evidence                                                                                                                             |
|:---------------------------|:--------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------|:-------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------|
| TRACK, ordinary handoff    | Replacement passes the complete admission check before the admission cutoff preceding commitment. | Latch the new nominal path and its own stop, then transfer at a checked $\DifferentiabilityClass^2$ seam.                                                    |
| TRACK, late candidate      | Candidate arrives after the blend deadline but before the admission cutoff preceding commitment.  | Admit only if the compressed bridge, full path, stop, and timing still fit; otherwise retain the current record only while its own permission remains valid. |
| STOP, matched suffix       | No successor admitted by the earlier cutoff.                                                      | MCU follows its protected suffix from the validated entry state; nominal tracking may end while STOP continues.                                              |
| STOP, earlier invalidation | Lease lapse, intent expiry, contact, state mismatch, or fault before physical stop onset.         | MCU selects the state-matched fallback with reserved clearance.                                                                                              |
| Fault response             | Controlled stop cannot be assured from measured state.                                            | Use the machine-specific risk response (which may include drive inhibit, brake, or compliance) only under its validated load and timing assumptions.         |

: **Tracking and fallback decisions**: A host crash does not remove a latched stop. TRACK is the nominal mode; STOP is the stop rung of the fallback ladder in @sec-enforcement-four-rungs. {#tbl-11-seam-fallback-hierarchy tbl-colwidths="[18,29,53]"}

::: {#chk-plan-fallback-clearance-stopping-budget .callout-checkpoint title="Commitment and full stopping clearance"}

Before committing an autonomous machine to an action chunk, verify your understanding of commitment deadlines, stopping budgets, and trajectory continuity:

- [ ] **Deadline distinction**: Distinguish nominal setpoint end, physical stop completion, and the end of the evidence horizon.
- [ ] **Continuous entry**: Why would a constant-deceleration switch fail $\DifferentiabilityClass^2$ matching at zero-acceleration cruise entry?
- [ ] **Clearance and latency**: The arm's `{python} PlanningC2Stop.arm_margin_str` margin already charges cruise from the blend deadline to commitment. Where must an unreserved delay $\UnreservedStopDelay$ beyond it be charged, and how much of that margin does $\CruiseSpeed\UnreservedStopDelay$ consume?

:::

The mug reach now has a complete execution argument: a timed prefix, a checked seam, and a stop reserved under stated conditions. With those obligations fixed, trajectory generators can be compared by the candidate work they perform rather than by treating their outputs as permission.

## Choosing a Trajectory Generator {#sec-planning-paradigms}

When a mobile manipulator reaches around a conveyor guard, a planner that searches configuration space can run out of time before finding a route, a local trajectory optimizer can get trapped in a non-convex pocket behind the guard, and a learned action-chunk policy can propose a smooth reach that clips the guard or exceeds a joint's torque limit. The three algorithmic families that propose motion, geometric search, continuous optimization, and learned action chunking, each fail in a different way if treated as self-certifying. In all three paradigms, deciding where the body can travel geometrically remains separate from determining how quickly actuators can safely traverse that path. Regardless of which family generates a proposal, the resulting trajectory remains an unverified candidate that requires exhaustive dynamic validation before the execution engine commits it to the hardware.

The conveyor reach also fixes what each family can afford. A replacement must be admitted every `{python} PlanningLeaseRule.t_renew_str`, and `{python} PlanningReplacementBudget.t_validate_str` of every replacement's dispatch-to-admission allocation is already reserved for whole-plan validation, while a chunk policy spends another `{python} PlanningReplacementBudget.t_infer_str` of it on inference. To sustain the intended renewal cadence, the generation pipeline must provide both the allocated latency and the throughput that overlapping requests require. A solver without a bounded completion time needs a timeout that leaves the resident fallback executable; it can also run outside the renewal loop, planning the route around the guard and handing the loop a corridor to follow. That deadline, more than the quality of the motion, sorts the three families below.

Sampling-based geometric planners explore configuration space without requiring an explicit algebraic representation of obstacles. Probabilistic Roadmaps (PRM) [@kavraki1996probabilistic] construct multi-query roadmaps by sampling collision-free configurations and connecting nearby neighbors with local collision-free segments, amortizing graph construction costs across multiple tasks. Conversely, Rapidly-exploring Random Trees (RRT) [@lavalle1998rapidly] target single-query problems by growing a space-filling tree from the initial configuration toward unexplored territory. Its asymptotically optimal counterpart, RRT* [@karaman2011sampling], continuously rewires parent connections within local neighborhoods as samples accumulate, ensuring that the discovered path cost converges almost surely to the theoretical optimum [@karaman2011sampling]. These methods resolve geometric routes through complex obstacle geometry, yet their completeness guarantees remain strictly probabilistic: the probability of discovering a feasible path approaches one only as the number of samples approaches infinity. When a sampling planner exhausts its computation budget without finding a path, its timeout provides no proof that the route is obstructed. The admission logic must therefore treat planner silence as an unresolved proposal rather than a verified safety determination. Furthermore, evaluating configuration samples and connecting edges requires repeated collision queries against environment geometry, usually accelerated by enclosing the manipulator links in bounding spheres or capsules, and these queries dominate the planner's run time. Even when successful, search yields only an un-timed geometric path with discontinuous derivative transitions. The system must still apply time parameterization, smooth corner blends, joint torque verification, and a valid stopping continuation before dispatching the trajectory to physical actuators.

The complementary classical formulation is **constrained continuous trajectory optimization**, exemplified by Covariant Hamiltonian Optimization for Motion Planning (CHOMP) [@ratliff2009chomp], TrajOpt [@schulman2014motion], and receding-horizon Model Predictive Control (MPC) [@tedrake2023manipulation; @lynch2017modern]. Rather than evaluating discrete graph nodes, continuous trajectory optimization represents motion as a continuous, time-indexed curve $\GeneralizedCoordinates(\TimeInstant)$ and minimizes an objective functional that balances dynamic smoothness against obstacle proximity:

$$\min_{\GeneralizedCoordinates(t)} \quad \TrajectoryOptimizationObjective[\GeneralizedCoordinates] = \int_0^\Time \left( \frac{1}{2} \|\dddot{\GeneralizedCoordinates}(\TimeInstant)\|^2 + \ObstacleCostWeight \ObstacleProximityCost(\GeneralizedCoordinates(\TimeInstant)) \right) d\TimeInstant$$

subject to physical boundary conditions and actuator invariants:
$$\GeneralizedCoordinates(0) = \GeneralizedCoordinates_0, \quad \GeneralizedVelocities(0) = \GeneralizedVelocities_0, \quad \GeneralizedAccelerations(0) = \GeneralizedAccelerations_0$$
$$\GeneralizedCoordinates(\Time) = \GoalConfiguration, \quad \GeneralizedVelocities(\Time) = \ZeroVector, \quad \GeneralizedAccelerations(\Time) = \ZeroVector$$
$$|\GeneralizedVelocities(\TimeInstant)| \le \JointVelocityLimit, \quad |\GeneralizedInertiaMatrix(\GeneralizedCoordinates)\GeneralizedAccelerations + \CoriolisCentrifugalMatrix(\GeneralizedCoordinates, \GeneralizedVelocities)\GeneralizedVelocities + \GravitationalTorqueVector(\GeneralizedCoordinates)| \le \JointTorqueUpperLimit$$

While CHOMP performs functional gradient descent and TrajOpt solves sequential convex subproblems using signed-distance collision constraints, both rely on local optimization. Consequently, non-convex obstacle geometry can trap the solver in infeasible local minima or geometric dead ends. Graphs of Convex Sets (GCS) resolve this susceptibility when the collision-free configuration space can be partitioned beforehand into convex regions. Finding the global sequence of regions and optimizing the polynomial spline within them then formulates as a mixed-integer convex program whose convex relaxation can be solved efficiently [@marcucci2023motion]. Because generating these convex decompositions requires substantial offline computation, GCS suits static structures such as the conveyor guard far better than dynamic, rapidly shifting environments. Although geometric search or learned policies can propose alternative routes around unforeseen obstructions, any candidate motion must still undergo explicit verification against dynamic torque limits and actuator constraints.

Repeatedly re-optimizing from an updated state estimate forms the operational foundation of classical **Model Predictive Control (MPC)**\index{Model Predictive Control!receding horizon}[^fn-mpc-process-origin]\index{Trajectory optimization!collocation and MPC}. In this receding-horizon paradigm, an optimizer computes an optimal trajectory over a finite horizon $\Time$, dispatches an initial prefix to the actuator controllers, and re-solves the problem from the newly observed state on the subsequent cycle. The objective functional ranks candidate motions by performance, while hard constraints eliminate trajectories that exceed physical limits. Classical discrete-time MPC frames this trade-off as a constrained numerical optimization problem over steps $\HorizonStepIndex = 0, \dots, \MpcPredictionHorizon-1$ [@tedrake2023manipulation; @lynch2017modern]:

[^fn-mpc-process-origin]: **Model predictive control**\index{Model Predictive Control!origin}: MPC began in the process industries of the 1970s, in refineries and chemical plants whose slow dynamics left seconds to minutes for each solve; @qin2003survey trace its industrial lineage from the first IDCOM and dynamic matrix control installations. Moving the same receding-horizon loop onto an arm tracked at `{python} PlanningOpeningMachine.f_track_str` shrinks that time to milliseconds, which is why a solver's deadline, and not its optimum, decides what reaches admission.

$$\begin{aligned}
\min_{\MpcControlSequence} \quad & \sum_{k=0}^{\MpcPredictionHorizon-1} \ell(\MechanicalPlantState_k, \ControlInput_k) + \MpcTerminalCost(\TerminalPlantState) \\
\text{subject to} \quad & \MechanicalPlantState_{k+1} = \DiscretePlantDynamics(\MechanicalPlantState_k, \ControlInput_k), \quad \HorizonStepIndex = 0, \dots, \MpcPredictionHorizon-1 \\
& \MechanicalPlantState_k \in \SafeStateSet, \quad \ControlInput_k \in \AdmissibleControlSet, \quad \HorizonStepIndex = 0, \dots, \MpcPredictionHorizon-1 \\
& \TerminalPlantState \in \TerminalInvariantSet
\end{aligned}$$ {#eq-plan-mpc-formulation}

The variables in @eq-plan-mpc-formulation decouple the predicted state sequence $\MechanicalPlantState_k$ from the selected control inputs $\ControlInput_k$. The dynamic transition map $\DiscretePlantDynamics(\MechanicalPlantState_k, \ControlInput_k)$ propagates the system state forward, requiring every intermediate step to remain admissible. The stage cost $\ell(\MechanicalPlantState_k, \ControlInput_k)$ penalizes tracking error and control effort, while the safe state set $\SafeStateSet$ enforces collision margins derived from the spatial perception pipeline. The admissible control set $\AdmissibleControlSet$ bounds actuator torques and voltages according to verified hardware limits.

The terminal constraint forces the horizon endpoint into a **terminal invariant set**, $\TerminalPlantState \in \TerminalInvariantSet$. In classical control theory, *recursive feasibility* guarantees that if a feasible solution exists at control cycle $\ControlCycleIndex$, a feasible solution remains provably discoverable at cycle $\ControlCycleIndex+1$. Establishing this property requires an accurate dynamic model and a terminal set $\TerminalInvariantSet$ within which an invariant fallback control law maintains safety indefinitely. In an embodied robotic system, this terminal invariant is implemented through a validated braking continuation that brings the machine to rest within verified spatial clearance ($\StoppingDistance \le \ClearDistance$). Bringing the machine to a standstill does not guarantee indefinite safety on its own, because dynamic obstacles can move into the workspace of a stationary robot unless external interlocks preserve the boundary.

Continuous-time optimal control problems are typically transcribed into finite-dimensional nonlinear programs through **direct shooting** or **direct collocation**.[^fn-plan-collocation-defects] Direct shooting forward-integrates the control trajectory $\ControlInput(\TimeInstant)$, yielding a compact optimization problem that can nonetheless become ill-conditioned over long horizons. Direct collocation parameterizes both states and controls using piecewise polynomial splines, enforcing dynamic defect constraints $\PlantDynamicsFunction(\MechanicalPlantState_k, \ControlInput_k) - \PlantStateRate_k = \ZeroVector$ at interior knots to generate large, sparse nonlinear programs that converge rapidly near smooth trajectories [@hargraves1987direct]. However, theoretical MPC guarantees hold only when the dynamic model is accurate, constraints are satisfied, and the numerical solver finishes before its real-time deadline. Contact transitions, stick-slip friction, and unexpected loads degrade solver convergence, often causing iterations to time out. Learned action chunking eliminates online numerical solves during inference, but neural policies do not enforce the terminal invariant constraint $\TerminalPlantState \in \TerminalInvariantSet$; an unvalidated action chunk can easily end at high velocity where the robot lacks adequate braking room.

[^fn-plan-collocation-defects]: **Direct collocation defects in real-time solvers**\index{Direct collocation!defect constraints}: Direct collocation, introduced for trajectory optimization by @hargraves1987direct, turns a continuous-time control problem into a finite nonlinear program by requiring the defect $\CollocationDefect_k = \PlantStateRate(\TimeInstant_k) - \PlantDynamicsFunction(\MechanicalPlantState_k, \ControlInput_k) = \ZeroVector$ at each collocation point. Contact transitions and unmodeled friction make the problem non-smooth, and the solver then loses its fast local convergence and needs more iterations than a fixed control deadline may allow.

Decoupling generation into a learned proposer and a constrained optimizer reconciles statistical representation with physical safety. The learned policy acts as a proposer, generating behavioral candidates conditioned on raw visual tokens and task semantics. A constrained trajectory generator then adjusts the proposed trajectory to satisfy boundary conditions, actuator limits, and spatial clearances. Because this numerical projection can become infeasible or miss its real-time deadline, it operates entirely on the untrusted proposal side of the architecture, upstream of independent safety admission.

Mathematically, this dual-stage architecture formulates trajectory generation as a constrained projection operator $\FeasibleTrajectoryProjection(\LearnedActionProposal)$:

$$\GeneralizedCoordinates^*(\TimeInstant) = \FeasibleTrajectoryProjection(\LearnedActionProposal) = \arg\min_{\GeneralizedCoordinates(t)} \int_0^\Time \|\GeneralizedCoordinates(\TimeInstant) - \LearnedNominalTrajectory(\TimeInstant)\|_{\StateTrackingWeightMatrix}^2 d\TimeInstant + \int_0^\Time \|\dddot{\GeneralizedCoordinates}(\TimeInstant)\|_{\JerkWeightMatrix}^2 d\TimeInstant$$ {#eq-plan-kinodynamic-projection}

The projection begins at the planned activation seam, so its initial-state constraints refer to that seam rather than to the state measured when the planning request begins. Upstream synthesis uses the projected reference and its reachable-state envelope; at activation, the MCU instantiates and checks the bounded bridge against measured state. The candidate remains subject to physical boundary conditions and safety invariants across the execution interval $\TimeInstant \in [0, \Time]$:
$$\GeneralizedCoordinates(0) = \SeamActualConfiguration, \quad \GeneralizedVelocities(0) = \SeamActualVelocities, \quad \GeneralizedAccelerations(0) = \SeamActualAccelerations$$
$$\GeneralizedCoordinates(\TimeInstant) \in \FreeConfigurationSpace, \quad |\GeneralizedVelocities(\TimeInstant)| \le \JointVelocityLimit, \quad |\GeneralizedInertiaMatrix(\GeneralizedCoordinates)\GeneralizedAccelerations + \CoriolisCentrifugalMatrix(\GeneralizedCoordinates, \GeneralizedVelocities)\GeneralizedVelocities + \GravitationalTorqueVector(\GeneralizedCoordinates)| \le \JointTorqueUpperLimit$$
$$\StoppingDistance(\GeneralizedCoordinates(\CommitmentInstant), \GeneralizedVelocities(\CommitmentInstant)) \le \ClearDistance(\CommitmentInstant)$$

In @eq-plan-kinodynamic-projection, the primary term penalizes tracking deviation from the learned nominal trajectory $\LearnedNominalTrajectory(\TimeInstant)$ using positive semidefinite state weights $\StateTrackingWeightMatrix$, while the regularization term penalizes joint jerk $\|\dddot{\GeneralizedCoordinates}(\TimeInstant)\|_{\JerkWeightMatrix}^2$ to minimize mechanical vibration and wear. The weighted quadratic norm is defined as $\|\WeightedNormArgument\|_{\NormWeightMatrix}^2 = \WeightedNormArgument^\top \NormWeightMatrix \WeightedNormArgument$, and $\FeasibleTrajectorySet$ denotes the feasible set of trajectories satisfying the displayed physical constraints. These constraints enforce the dynamic invariants that unconstrained learned models cannot guarantee: $\DifferentiabilityClass^2$ continuity with the currently executing state, collision avoidance within the free configuration space $\FreeConfigurationSpace$, kinematic joint speed bounds, full rigid-body inverse dynamics torque limits, and certified stopping viability at the commitment horizon $\CommitmentInstant$. Even when the optimizer finds a feasible trajectory, that solution remains contingent on model assumptions regarding payload mass and obstacle positions; the independent admission gate must verify those assumptions before granting hardware permission.

Altering the proposer modifies the computational budget and latency profile, but leaves the physical safety obligations unchanged. Action Chunking with Transformers (ACT) [@zhao2023learning] infers an entire chunk of future joint setpoints in a single forward pass and smooths replanning boundaries by ensembling overlapping temporal chunks. However, simple coordinate averaging across predictions fails to enforce higher-order boundary derivatives, which can induce severe acceleration transients at chunk transitions. Diffusion policies [@chi2024diffusionpolicy] capture complex, multimodal behavioral distributions through iterative score-based denoising, but the multiple neural network evaluations required during inference add substantial latency to the replacement planning path. Alternatively, a neural model can warm-start a numerical trajectory optimizer by providing initial collocation knots. While a good warm-start drastically reduces sequential quadratic programming iterations, an out-of-distribution observation can seed the optimizer in an infeasible basin of attraction, causing solver divergence and missed execution deadlines. Generator selection therefore balances configuration-space exploration, constrained local tracking, and multimodal perceptual synthesis against the strict temporal deadlines required to validate and admit candidate trajectories.

@Tbl-11-planning-paradigms compares the inputs, constraints, and seam obligations of the synthesis methods. Its sampling-based MPC row, model predictive path integral control (MPPI), rolls many sampled control sequences through the dynamics model and returns their cost-weighted average; it reappears as a base controller in @sec-planning-mobile-base.

| Trajectory paradigm                         | Input representation                                                                | Dynamic and safety guarantees                                       | Dominant workload        | Boundary continuity across replanning                                                     |
|:--------------------------------------------|:------------------------------------------------------------------------------------|:--------------------------------------------------------------------|:-------------------------|:------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------|
| Sampling-Based Graph Search (PRM, RRT*)     | Configuration samples $\GeneralizedCoordinates \in \FreeConfigurationSpace$         | Route quality depends on the search; dynamics need separate checks  | Collision queries        | Piecewise-linear ($\DifferentiabilityClass^0$); discontinuous $\GeneralizedAccelerations$ |
| Classical Numerical MPC                     | Low-dimensional state vector $\MechanicalPlantState \in \mathbb{R}^\StateDimension$ | Constraint and stability guarantees depend on model and assumptions | Constrained solve        | Continuity requires explicit boundary constraints                                         |
| Sampling-Based MPC (MPPI)                   | State vector and a Euclidean signed distance field (ESDF)                           | Constraint treatment depends on the formulation and solver          | Rollouts or optimization | Requires spline smoothing or terminal costs                                               |
| Generative Action Chunking (ACT, Diffusion) | High-dimensional multimodal tokens (vision, text)                                   | Empirical demonstration distribution; no formal safety guarantee    | Model inference          | Discrete samples; requires checked interpolation and seam                                 |

: **Comparison of trajectory generation paradigms**: Search, optimization, and learned proposals perform different candidate-generation work. Solve time and supported constraints depend on the implementation and problem; every selected pipeline still needs checked dynamics, seams, and stopping clearance. {#tbl-11-planning-paradigms tbl-colwidths="[22,23,23,14,18]"}

The mechanisms in this chapter are durable; the systems that implement them change quickly. @Tbl-11-practice-2026 records the named systems a practitioner meets today, each tied to the mechanism it implements.

```{python}
#| label: calc-planning-practice-2026
#| echo: false
#| warning: false
#| message: false
# ┌─────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────
# │ STATE OF PRACTICE, AS OF 2026: REPORTED FIGURES FROM EACH SYSTEM'S PAPER
# ├─────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────
# │ Context: tbl-11-practice-2026.
# │
# │ Goal:    Hold the literature values the dated table quotes.
# │ Show:    pi0 chunk H = 50; 50 Hz robots re-infer after 25 actions (0.5 s);
# │          Ruckig 19.8 us mean / 123 us worst for 7 DoFs.
# │ How:     black2024pi0 (sec. IV and inference section);
# │          PlanningTimeParam for the Ruckig figures (berscheid2021jerk).
# └─────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────
from mlsysim.core.units import second, hertz
from mlsysim.fmt import check, fmt_int, fmt_frequency, fmt_latency

class PlanningPractice2026:
    """Literature figures for the dated state-of-practice table."""

    # ┌── 1. LOAD (Constants) ──────────────────────
    pi0_horizon = 50  # category: literature; action chunk length H (black2024pi0)
    pi0_rate = 50 * hertz  # category: literature; control rate of the 50 Hz robots (black2024pi0)
    pi0_executed = 25  # category: literature; actions executed before re-inference at 50 Hz (black2024pi0)

    # ┌── 2. EXECUTE (The Compute) ─────────────────
    pi0_reinfer = (pi0_executed / pi0_rate).to(second)

    # ┌── 3. GUARD (Invariants) ────────────────────
    check(abs(pi0_reinfer.magnitude - 0.5) < 1e-12, "pi0 re-inference interval changed")
    check(pi0_executed < pi0_horizon, "pi0 no longer executes a prefix of its chunk")

    # ┌── 4. OUTPUT (Formatting) ───────────────────
    pi0_horizon_str = fmt_int(pi0_horizon)
    pi0_rate_str = fmt_frequency(pi0_rate)
    pi0_executed_str = fmt_int(pi0_executed)
    pi0_reinfer_str = fmt_latency(pi0_reinfer, unit=second, precision=1)
```

| Job in this chapter              | System                                             | Mechanism                                                                          | Reported figure                                                                                                                                                                                                                              |
